ety: Transliteration of Georgian სააკაშვილი (saaḳašvili).

s.def: A transliteration of the Georgian surname სააკაშვილი (saaḳašvili).
ex: Mikheil Saakashvili

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Sabbatarian.
Alternative letter-case form of Sabbath.
ex: Far-right activists had organised their protest for the Jewish sabbath in an area with a 40% Jewish population.

ety: From Middle English sabat, sabbat, sabath, from Old English sabat and Old French sabbat, both from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”), with the spelling ending in -th, probably influenced by the traditional transliteration of the Hebrew as shabbāth, being attested since the 14th century and widespread since the 16th. Doublet of Shabbat. Possibly from the Sumerian sa-bat ("mid-rest").

s.def: Saturday, observed in Judaism as a day of rest and worship.
Friday, observed in Islam as a day of rest and worship.
Sunday, observed in Christianity as a day of rest and worship.
ex: Jerusalem is a city of three Sabbaths–Friday (Muslim), Saturday (Jewish), and Sunday (Christian).

s.def: A meeting of witches. (Also called a witches' Sabbath, Shabbat, sabbat, or black Sabbath.)
Among the ancient Jews and Hebrews, the seventh year, when the land was left fallow.
Synonym of uposatha, a regular day of fasting, devotion, or other religious observance.

ety: From Latin sabbaticus + -al.

s.def: Relating to the Sabbath.
Relating to a sabbatical.
An extended period of leave from a person's usual pursuits.
A sabbatical year (ancient religious observance).

ety: Attested since 1275, from Middle English sable, from Old French sable and martre sable (“sable marten”), in reference to the animal or its fur; from Medieval Latin sabelum, from Middle Low German sabel (compare Middle Dutch sabel, Middle High German zobel, whence German Zobel); ultimately from a Slavic word (compare Russian со́боль (sóbolʹ), Polish soból, Czech sobol). Compare also Middle Persian smwl (*samōr).

s.def: animal
A small carnivorous mammal of the Old World that resembles a weasel, Martes zibellina, from cold regions in Eurasia and the North Pacific islands, valued for its dark brown fur.
Any other marten, especially Martes americana (syn. Mustela americana).
A pelt of fur of a sable or of one of another species of martens; a coat made from this fur.
ex: "Ye must avenge my sister's son's death; I will sables and martins bestow."
Lovers dallied upon divans spread with sables.

s.def: An artist's brush made from the fur of the sable, the kolinsky sable-hair brush.
A black colour on a coat of arms.
A dark brown colour, resembling the fur of some sables.
Black garments, especially worn in mourning.
The sablefish.
Sable-coloured, black.
ex: When I behold the violet past prime, And sable curls all silver'd o'er with white
Night, sable goddess! from her ebon throne, / In rayless majesty, now stretches forth / Her leaden sceptre o'er a slumbering world.

ety: Early 17th century, borrowed from Middle French sabot (see French sabot below). Doublet of sabaton and ciabatta.

s.def: A wooden shoe.
ex: She was a tiny little woman and wore big sabots and a big scoop.

s.def: A carrier around a projectile in a firearm, cannon or other type of artillery piece that precisely holds the projectile within the barrel.
ex: discarding sabot

s.def: To enclose (a projectile) in a sabot.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French sabotage.

s.def: A deliberate action aimed at weakening someone (or something, a nation, etc) or preventing them from being successful, through subversion, obstruction, disruption, and/or destruction.
To deliberately destroy or damage something in order to prevent it from being successful.
ex: The railway line had been sabotaged by enemy commandos.
Our plans were sabotaged.

s.def: A person who intentionally causes the destruction of property in order to hinder the efforts of their enemy.
Alternative spelling of Sabra.

ety: Borrowed from Hebrew צַבָּר (tsabár, “prickly pear cactus”), from Arabic صَبَّار (ṣabbār, “cactus”).

s.def: A female given name.

ety: Borrowed from French sabre, from German Säbel, from Polish szabla, from Hungarian szablya. Cognate with Danish sabel, Russian са́бля (sáblja), Serbo-Croatian сабља, Sicilian sciàbbula.

s.def: A light sword with a curved blade, sharp along the front edge, part of the back edge, and at the point.
A modern fencing sword modeled after the sabre.
Having massive curved upper canine teeth.
ex: One such was Eusmilus, a sabre-toothed killer known as a nimravid.

s.def: Any of numerous species of extinct cat-like mammals, of the †Machairodontinae subfamily of the Felidae, characterized by massive, but short, legs and two large canine teeth, each about seven inches long and shaped like a sabre.

ety: Borrowed from Latin sabulosus, from sabulum (“sand”).

s.def: Sandy or gritty.
ex: ...or fills up the tubular vessels there with sabulous matter.

ex: Holonyms: monosaccharide, oligosaccharide, polysaccharide

s.def: A polarimeter used to measure the sugar content of a liquid.

s.def: Of or relating to sugar; sugary.
Containing a large or excessive amount of sugar.
Excessively sweet in action or disposition, especially if romantic or sentimental to the point of ridiculousness; sickly sweet, syrupy.
Resembling granulated sugar; saccharoid.
Something which is saccharine or sweet; sugar.
Sentimentalism.
Of or relating to saccharin (“a white, crystalline powder, C₇H₅NO₃S, used as an artificial sweetener in food products”).
Alternative spelling of saccharin.

ety: Borrowed from Latin sacculus (“a little sack or bag”), diminutive of saccus (“a bag, sack”). Doublet of sacculus.

s.def: A small sac, pouch, or cyst.

The smaller of the two fluid-filled sacs forming part of the labyrinth of the inner ear (the other being the utricle). It contains a region of hair cells and otoliths which send signals to the brain concerning the orientation of the head.

ety: From Middle English sacerdotale, from Old French sacerdotal, from Latin sacerdōtālis (“priestly”).

s.def: Of or relating to priests or a high religious order; priestly.
ex: ...some of the figures are costumed in the style of religious art, with flowing sacerdotal garments.

ety: Borrowed from Narragansett sachem; compare Mi'kmaq saqamaw (“chief”) and Unami sakima (“chief”), all ultimately from Proto-Algonquian *sa·kima·wa. Doublet of sagamore.

s.def: A chief of one or several Native American tribe(s), especially of the Algonquians; a sagamore.
ex: If a sachem was too harsh, a tribesman might leave and join another tribe.

s.def: A boss, a leader.
An eminent member of a group, or an eminent person in society; a sagamore.
A high-ranking officer of the Tammany Hall political organization.
A butterfly of the Americas, Atalopedes campestris.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French sachet.

s.def: A cheesecloth bag of herbs or spices added during cooking and then removed before serving.
A small scented cloth bag filled with fragrant material such as herbs or potpourri.
A small, sealed packet containing a single-use quantity of any material.
ex: My burger arrived with a plastic sachet of tomato ketchup.

ety: From Middle English sak, sek, sach, zech (“bag, sackcloth”), from Old English sacc (“sack, bag”) and sæċċ (“sackcloth, sacking”); both from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from late Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), borrowed from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic, possibly Phoenician or Hebrew. Cognate with Dutch zak, German Sack, Swedish säck, Danish sæk, Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk sekk, Faroese and Icelandic sekkur, Hebr…

s.def: A bag; especially a large bag of strong, coarse material for storage and handling of various commodities, such as potatoes, coal, coffee; or, a bag with handles used at a supermarket, a grocery sack; or, a small bag for small items, a satchel.
To plunder or pillage, especially after capture; to obtain spoils of war from.
ex: The barbarians sacked Rome in 410 CE.
My sister wants to sack Tokyo.
It [a lyre] was part of the spoils which he had taken when he sacked the city of Eetion […]

s.def: To discharge from a job or position; to fire.
ex: He was sacked last September.
Waste my time working for cowards and creeps / Oh I wish that they'd sack me and leave me to sleep

s.def: A sack coat; a kind of coat worn by men, and extending from top to bottom without a cross seam.

A kind of loose-fitting gown or dress with sleeves which hangs from the shoulders, such as a gown with a Watteau back or sack-back, fashionable in the late 17th to 18th century; or, formerly, a loose-fitting hip-length jacket, cloak or cape.

The amount a sack holds; also, an archaic or historical measure of varying capacity, depending on commodity type and according to local usage; an old English measure of weight, usually of wool, equal to 13 stone (182 pounds), or in other sources, 26 stone (364 pounds).
ex: The American sack of salt is 215 pounds; the sack of wheat, two bushels. — .
Generally, however, the stone or petra, almost always of 14 lbs., is used, the tod of 28 lbs., and the sack of thirteen stone.

s.def: The plunder and pillaging of a captured town or city.
ex: the sack of Rome

s.def: Loot or booty obtained by pillage.
A successful tackle of the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
One of the square bases anchored at first base, second base, or third base.
ex: He twisted his ankle sliding into the sack at second.

ety: From French sacqueboute, from Middle French sacquer (“to pull”) + bouter (“to push”).

s.def: A brass instrument from the Renaissance and Baroque Eras, and an ancestor of the modern trombone. It was derived from the medieval slide trumpet.

ety: From Middle English sakcloth, sekcloth, sekclath, sekklath. By surface analysis, sack + cloth.

s.def: A coarse hessian style of cloth used to make sacks.
Garments worn as an act of penance.
ex: After he realised the gravity of his crime he spent some time wearing sackcloth and ashes.
No more ashes, no more sackcloth / And an armband made of black cloth / Will someday never more adorn a sleeve

s.def: Cheap rough cloth such as would be used to make bags (sacks).
ex: The farmer grabbed a handful of sacking and rubbed down the cow.

s.def: Firing or termination of an employee.
ex: He followed his sacking with a good drink.

s.def: present participle and gerund of sack
Alternative spelling of sack (“a short, loose-fitting garment for women and children”).

ety: From Modern Latin sacrālis, from Latin sacrum (“sacred, holy”) + -ālis.

s.def: Of the sacrum.
Sacred.
ex: An old site with sacral connotations.
Compromise is awkward when religion is involved, and the several South Asian writing systems are considered sacral.

s.def: Any of the sacral bones that make up the sacrum.

ety: From Middle English sacrament, from Old French sacrement, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum (“sacrament”), from Latin sacrō (“hallow, consecrate”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”), originally sum deposited by parties to a suit.

s.def: A sacred act and the attendant ceremony, considered (theology) an outward sign of divine grace, instituted by Jesus Christ.
The Eucharist.
The consecrated Eucharist (especially the bread).
Anything regarded as possessing a sacred character or mysterious significance.
The oath of allegiance taken by soldiers in Ancient Rome; hence, any sacred ceremony used to impress an obligation; a solemn oath-taking; an oath.
ex: I'll take the sacrament on 't.

ety: From Latin sacrārium.

s.def: In Ancient Rome, a place where sacred objects were kept, either in a temple (the adytum) or in a house (holding the penates)

The area surrounding the altar of a Christian church; the sanctuary or piscina. Sometimes specifically a drain directly to the earth, perhaps including reference to a basin, for washing vessels from consecration.
The complex sacrum of any bird.

ety: From Middle English sacred, isacred, past participle of sacren, sakeren (“to make holy, hallow”), equivalent to sacre + -ed.

s.def: Characterized by solemn religious ceremony or religious use, especially, in a positive sense; consecrated, made holy.
ex: a sacred place
a sacred day
sacred service

s.def: Religious; relating to religion, or to the services of religion; not secular
ex: Smit with the love of sacred song.

s.def: Spiritual; concerned with metaphysics.
Not to be profaned or violated; inviolable.
ex: Secrets of marriage still are sacred held.
The sacred project of sociology is simply to help people enjoy being fully what they are.

s.def: Consecrated; dedicated; devoted
ex: A temple, sacred to the queen of love.

s.def: Solemnly devoted, in a bad sense, as to evil, vengeance, curse, or the like; accursed; baleful.
ex: But, to destruction sacred and devote.

s.def: Designated or exalted by a divine sanction; possessing the highest title to obedience, honor, reverence, or veneration; entitled to extreme reverence; venerable.
ex: Such neighbor nearness to our sacred [royal] blood Should nothing privilege him.

s.def: simple past and past participle of sacre

A wading bird of species Threskiornis aethiopicus, of the family Threskiornithidae, which breeds in sub-Saharan Africa, southeastern Iraq and formerly in Egypt, where it was venerated and often mummified as a symbol of the god Thoth.

ety: Calque of Ancient Greek ἱερὸς πόλεμος (hieròs pólemos)

s.def: Any of three wars fought (in 595-585 BCE, 449 BC-448 BCE and 357-346 BCE) by the Amphictyonic Council.

s.def: A human being or an animal, or a physical object or immaterial thing (see etymology 1 sense 1.3), offered to a deity.
To intentionally allow (a piece) to be captured by the opponent in order to improve one's position in the game.
(transitive) to offer (a human being or an animal, or an object) to a deity; (transitive) to offer a human being or an animal, or an object, to a deity
Originally, the killing (and often burning) of a human being or an animal as an offering to a deity; later, also the offering of an object to a deity.
The offering of devotion, penitence, prayer, thanksgiving, etc., to a deity.
Jesus Christ's voluntary offering of himself to God the Father to be crucified as atonement for the sins of humankind.

The rite of Holy Communion or the Mass, regarded as (Protestantism) an offering of thanksgiving to God for Christ's crucifixion, or (Roman Catholicism) a perpetual re-presentation of Christ's sacrificial offering.
ex: The pretensions of the holy see, the authority of tradition, purgatory, transubstantiation, the sacrifice of the mass, […] were copiously discussed.

s.def: The destruction or surrender of anything for the sake of something else regarded as more urgent or valuable; also, the thing destroyed or surrendered for this purpose.
ex: the sacrifice of one’s spare time in order to volunteer

s.def: Ellipsis of sacrifice bunt or sacrifice hit (“a play in which the batter intentionally hits the ball softly with a hands-spread batting stance at the cost of an out to advance one or more runners”).

In full sacrifice bid: a bid of a contract which is unlikely to be fulfilled, that a player makes in the hope that they will incur fewer penalty points than the points likely to be gained by opponents in making their contract.

ety: Borrowed from Latin sacrificiālis (“sacrificial”), from sacrificium (“sacrifice”), from sacrificus (“sacrificial”), from sacrificō (“sacrifice”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”) + faciō (“do, make”). By surface analysis, sacrifice + -ial.

s.def: Used as a sacrifice.
ex: The sacrificial coating protects the hull, but because it takes the damage the hull doesn't, we must replace it annually.
The ceremony involves the ritual slaying of a sacrificial lamb.

s.def: Relating to sacrifice.
ex: The old sacrificial well is still there, but animals aren't thrown into it to appease monsters anymore.

ety: Circa 1300, original sense “stealing something sacred”. From Middle English sacrilege, from Old French sacrilege, from Latin sacrilegium, from sacrilegus (“sacrilegious”). Sense of “profanation” from late 14th century.

s.def: Desecration, profanation, misuse or violation of something regarded as sacred.

ety: From French sacristain, Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer. Doublet of sexton.

s.def: The person who maintains the sacristy and the sacred objects it contains.
ex: And hence the custom and law began That still at dawn the sacristan, Who duly pulls the heavy bell, Five and forty beads must tell Between each stroke
[…] every evening as the temple was closed for the night the sacristan paused: "Pindar to supper with the god!" he cried.
The church was looked after by an old sacristan who lived in a cottage on the shore of the lake.

ety: From Anglo-Norman sacrestie, from Medieval Latin sacristia.

s.def: A room in a church where sacred vessels, books, vestments, etc. are kept. Sometimes also used by clergy to prepare for worship or for meetings.

ety: From sacrum.

s.def: Of or relating to the sacrum.

ety: Etymology tree English sacro- Proto-Indo-European *welH-der. Ancient Greek εἴλω (eílō) Ancient Greek εἰλέω (eiléō) Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós)der.? Latin īle Latin -acus Latin īliacuslbor. French iliaquebor. English iliac English sacroiliac From sacro- + iliac.

The region of the sacrum and the ilium in the lower back.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sacrōsānctus.

s.def: Beyond alteration, criticism, or interference, especially due to religious sanction; inviolable.
ex: After decades of being considered politically sacrosanct, why are homeowner mortgage write-offs suddenly on the chopping block?
For me, it is sacrosanct. It’s our history, it’s our cultural heritage. I do not believe in censorship in that way.

s.def: Sacred, very holy.

ety: From Latin os sacrum (“holy bone”), a calque of Ancient Greek ἱερὸν ὀστέον (hieròn ostéon). Apparently so called either because the sacrum was the part of the animal offered in sacrifice or because of a putative belief that it is where a person's soul resides. A third explanation is that the term is a translation of Ancient Greek ἱερόν (hierón), which has two meanings: “holy, sacred”, and “big” — big being a more appropriate description of the sacrum — but compare.

s.def: A large triangular bone at the base of the spine, located between the two ilia (wings of the pelvis) and formed from vertebrae that fuse in adulthood.

ety: From Middle English sad, from Old English sæd (“satisfied, full, sated, unable to handle more, weary”), from Proto-West Germanic *sad, from Proto-Germanic *sadaz (“sated, satisfied”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂- (“to satiate, satisfy”). Cognate to Saterland Frisian sääd, West Frisian sêd, Dutch zat, German Low German satt, German satt. s.def: Emotionally negative.
ex: She gets sad when he's away.

s.def: Sated, having had one's fill; satisfied, weary.
Steadfast, valiant.
Dignified, serious, grave.
ex: Therfore it nedeth that better prouysion. Were founde for youthe by sad and wyse counsayle

s.def: Naughty; troublesome; wicked.
Unfashionable; socially inadequate or undesirable.
ex: I can't believe you use drugs; you're so sad!
You’d have to be really sad to wear a shirt like that.

s.def: Soggy (to refer to pastries).
Heavy; weighty; ponderous; close; hard.
ex: Chalky lands are naturally cold and sad.

s.def: To make melancholy; to sadden or grieve (someone).
Expressing contempt, ridicule or disgust; bah!

ety: Transliteration of Arabic صَدَّام (ṣaddām).

s.def: A male given name from Arabic of Arabic usage.

ety: From Middle English saddenen, equivalent to sad + -en.

s.def: To make sad or unhappy.
ex: It saddens me to think that I might have hurt someone.
I was saddened that you felt so little for me.

s.def: To become sad or unhappy.
ex: He saddens, all the magic light ⁠Dies off at once from bower and hall, ⁠And all the place is dark, and all The chambers emptied of delight: […]
Hyacinth perfume tickled her senses, making her feel giddy, but she saddened when she saw how uncared for the garden was.

s.def: To darken a color during dyeing.
ex: Curve (E) is seen at a glance to represent green saddened down to its fifth shade, and reduced with white to its fourth tint.

s.def: To render heavy, hard, or cohesive; to compress or thicken.
ex: ... the soil below will, instead of being brought up, be trampled and saddened.

ety: From Middle English sadel, from Old English sadol, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz (“saddle”). s.def: A seat for a rider, typically made of leather and raised in the front and rear, placed on the back of a horse or other animal, and secured by a strap around the animal's body.
ex: I saw many brave men cut down, many fall mortally wounded from their saddles.

s.def: Something resembling a saddle (sense 1) in appearance or shape.
ex: With Lizzie leading, they scrambled quickly over several false peaks towards the saddle.

s.def: seat for a rider placed on the back of a horse or other animal
(transitive) to put a saddle on (an animal)
A timeslot between two popular programmes, in which another programme can be scheduled to encourage people to watch it.
ex: In "hammocking," a new program is placed in the "saddle" between two established hits, or "tent poles."

s.def: To put a saddle (noun sense 1) on (an animal).
To put (something) on to another thing like a saddle on an animal.
To enter (a trained horse) into a race.
Chiefly followed by with: to burden or encumber (someone) with some problem or responsibility.
ex: He has been saddled with the task of collecting evidence of the theft.
They went shopping and left me saddled with two children to look after.
He is saddled with house payments now, so he can't afford to spend more money.

s.def: Chiefly followed by on or upon: to place (a burden or responsibility) or thrust (a problem) on someone.
a blanket that is placed under a saddle as a cushion and to protect the horse's back.
A horse that has been specially trained for riding, specifically the American Saddlebred.
ex: I shall expect a new saddle horse, a suit of fine lace, and an infinite number of the most valuable Jewels.

s.def: A pad placed under a saddle on a horse, like a saddle blanket but thicker.
The base on which the rest of the saddle is built, usually based on wood or a similar synthetic material, and is eventually covered in leather or a leatherlike synthetic.
The tulip tree.

An anticline.

A raccoon oyster.

Wearing a saddle.

ety: From Middle English sadeler, sadelere, equivalent to saddle + -er. Cognate with Old Norse sǫðlari (“saddler”).

an event in which schoolchildren travel to a location separate from their normal learning environment under the authority of the staff of their school and with the purpose of learning by experience.

ety: From school + book.

ety: From school + fellow.

ety: Compound of school + girl.

ety: From Middle English scoleman (attested in names), from Old English scōlman, scōlmann (“student, scholar”), equivalent to school + -man.

ety: From Middle English skolemayster, scolemaister, scol-meister, equivalent to school + master. Cognate with West Frisian skoalmaster (“schoolmaster”), Dutch schoolmeester (“schoolmaster”), Low German Schoolmeester, Schoolmeister (“schoolmaster”), German Schulmeister (“schoolmaster”).

ety: Attested ca. 1715, of uncertain origin. Said to be derived from dialectal scoon (“to skim over water”). Compare also shunt (“to cause to move (suddenly)”).

A glass of beer, of a size which varies between states (Wikipedia).

ety: From German schottische (“Scottish”), as in der schottische Tanz (“the Scottish dance”). First attested in 1849. Doublet of Scottish, Scotch, and Scots. The Oxford English Dictionary comments that the “quasi-French pronunciation […] has no justification”.

ety: Borrowed from German Schuss (literally “shot”).

ety: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

ety: From Middle English science, scyence, borrowed from Old French science, escience, from Latin scientia (“knowledge”), from sciēns, the present participle stem of scire (“to know”).

ety: Variant of sipe, from Middle English *sipen, from Old English sipian, from Proto-Germanic *sipōną, derivative of *sīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb-, *sib- (“to pour out, drip, trickle”). A dark, slightly reddish, brown colour.
A sepia-coloured drawing or photograph.

ety: From Ancient Greek σῆψις (sêpsis, “putrefaction”), from σήπω (sḗpō, “to make rotten”), from σήψ (sḗps, “a kind of lizard; also a kind of serpent whose bite was alleged to cause putrefaction”).

ex: Imagine the sepsis of helpless loathing [Jimmy Connors] must have inspired in his opponents during his "great runs" at the US Open.

ety: From Middle English septenarie, septenary, from Classical Latin septēnārius (“consisting of seven each”), from septēnus (“seven each; seven at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary). ety: From Latin septuagenarius (“containing 70”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives and representative nouns), either directly or via French septuagénaire, from Latin septuagenus (“70 each”) + -arius (“-ary”), from Latin septuāginta (“seven tens, 70”).

ety: Derived from Latin sequāx (“a follower”), from sequī (“to follow”), + -acious (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Following neatly or smoothly.

ety: From Middle English sequele, sequelle, sequile, from Middle French sequele, sequelle and its etymon, Latin sequēla, from sequī (“to follow”). Doublet of sequela.

ety: Formed as series + -al, on model of Latin seriālis, from seriēs + -ālis. Cognate to Italian seriale. First use appears c. 1823. See cite below.

s.def: Of or relating to a grammatical aspect relating to an action that is habitual and ongoing.

s.def: Who performs a specified action or course of action repeatedly or regularly.
ex: The serial killer had a string of victims across seven states.

Either of a pair of words that occur together as an idiomatic expression or collocation, as in "hammer and sickle", "short and sweet", or "spick and span".

ety: Adopted in the 16th century, probably via Latin Sibēria, from Russian Сиби́рь (Sibírʹ) + -ia. In origin the Tatar name of a 14th-century fortress at Qashliq (Tobolsk) which became the capital of the 16th-century Khanate of Sibir, in 16th century Russian usage extended to the entire area of what is now Tyumen Oblast, and with the ongoing Russian conquest of Siberia by the 19th century to the larger area of Russia's Asian territories beyond the Ob River. The figurative sense in English arises in…

s.def: The region of Russia in Asia, stretching from the Urals to the Pacific Ocean.
A species of flying squirrel (Pteromys volans), common in Siberia and northeastern Europe.
A medium-sized spitz breed of dog originally used for herding reindeer and pulling sleighs.
Calliope calliope, a flycatcher breeding in western Siberia and overwinters in South Asia.
A tiger of a population of species Panthera tigris tigris, now confined to Outer Manchuria in Russia.

ety: From Latin sībilāns, present active participle of sībilō (“to hiss”).

s.def: Characterized by a hissing or hushing sound such as the s or sh in sack or shack.
A consonant having a hissing or hushing sound such as the s or sh in sack or shack.
ex: Groove fricatives all have more or less of an [s]-like quality, and are for this reason sometimes called sibilants.

ety: First use appears c. 1903, a modern revival of Old English sibling (“relative, a relation, kinsman”), equivalent to sib + -ling. Compare Middle English siblynges pl, sib, sibbe (“relative; kinsman”), German Sippe. The term apparently meant merely kin or relative until the 20th century when it was applied in a way that aided the study of genetics, which led to its specialized use. For example, the OED has a citation in 1902 in which sibling must be defined for those who do not know the intended…

s.def: A person who shares a parent; one's brother or sister who one shares a parent with.
ex: None of my siblings are married yet.
She also had one sibling, her younger brother Joshua, who was born a year after her.

s.def: A node in a data structure that shares its parent with another node.
The most closely related species, or one of several most closely related species when none can be determined to be more closely related.
ex: Bush suggested that this difference might represent a case of chromosomal polymorphism or, more likely, sibling species.

ety: From Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

s.def: A pagan female oracle or prophetess, especially the Cumaean sibyl.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sīc (“thus, so”).

s.def: Thus; as written; used to indicate, for example, that text is being quoted as it is from the source.
ex: whole bussiness: Quoted sic in George F. Willison, Saints and Strangers (New York: Reynal and Hitchcock, 1945)
In the posting, Matthews said he wished that, “more blacks [sic] people would look into ancient beliefs of pre Christian Africa.”

To mark with a bracketed sic.
To incite an attack by, especially a dog or dogs.
ex: He sicced his dog on me!

ex: Sic ’em, Mitzi.

Causing or promoting drying

ety: From Latin Sicilia + -an. By surface analysis, Sicily + -an.

s.def: Of, from or relating to Sicily, Italy.
The language of Sicily.
A sub-age from 0.781 to 0.26 million years ago, a subdivision of the Pleistocene.
A native or inhabitant of Sicily, Italy.
Any chess opening that starts 1 e4 c5.
ex: Palmgren was playing white and had opened the Sicilian quite correctly.

ety: From Middle English Sicilie, Sicilye, from Old English Sicilia, from Latin Sicilia, from Ancient Greek Σικελία (Sikelía), from Σίκελος (Síkelos, “Sicel”). Doublet of Sicilia.

s.def: The largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, an autonomous region of Italy, close to Africa and separated from Tunisia and Libya by the Strait of Sicily.
Synonym of Kingdom of Sicily, a former kingdom controlling the island and some of southern Italy in the medieval and early modern period
Synonym of Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, a former kingdom controlling the island and most of southern Italy in the 19th century
Synonym of Kingdom of Naples, a former kingdom controlling southern Italy and claiming sovereignty over the island in the early modern period

ety: From Middle English sik, sike, seek, seke, seok, from Old English sēoc (“sick, ill”), from Proto-West Germanic *seuk, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sewg- (“to be troubled or grieved”). See also West Frisian siik, Dutch ziek, German siech, Norwegian Bokmål syk, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish sjuk, Danish syg; also Middle Irish socht (“silence, depression”), Old Armenian հիւծանիմ (hiwcanim, “to be weakening”). The "very good, excellent" sense is an ameliorative semantic sh…

s.def: In poor health; ill.
ex: We have to care for the sick.

s.def: Having an urge to vomit.
ex: My daughter was violently sick three times in the night.
I feel sick, like I might vomit, and I'm more tired than I can ever remember feeling.

s.def: Mentally unstable, disturbed.
ex: You sick bastard!
What a sick, sick feeling / To let you go, my dear

s.def: In bad taste.
ex: That’s a sick joke.

s.def: [with of] Tired of or annoyed by (something that has lasted a long time or often recurs).
ex: sick and tired of the whining—sick of waiting—'sick of politics
I’ve heard that song on the radio so many times that I’m starting to get sick of it.
I’m so sick of that same old love, the kind that breaks your heart.

s.def: Very good, excellent, awesome, badass.
ex: This tune is sick.
He showed off his sick surfing skills.
Dude, this car's got a sick subwoofer!

s.def: In poor condition.
ex: sick building syndrome; my car is looking pretty sick; my job prospects are pretty sick

Vomit.

s.def: (especially in the phrases on the sick and on long-term sick) Any of various current or former benefits or allowances paid by the Government to support the sick, disabled or incapacitated.
The adverse environmental conditions in a building that pose a health risk to its occupants, such as inadequate ventilation or inadequate cleaning.
The symptoms experienced by people who work there.
Paid absence from work specifically to recover from illness.

ety: Calque of Russian больно́й челове́к Европы (bolʹnój čelovék Jevropy), a phrase coined by Czar Nicholas I of the Empire of Russia, referring to the poor state of the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century.

s.def: The Ottoman Empire.
Any European country undergoing economic difficulty.

ety: From Middle English seke bed, equivalent to sick + bed.

s.def: A bed used by a person who is sick.
A place for convalescence.

ety: From Middle English sekenen, equivalent to sick + -en. Cognate with Danish sygne (“to pine”), Swedish sjukna (“to fall ill; become sick”), Norwegian sykne, Icelandic sjúkna (“to sicken; become sick”).

s.def: To make ill.
ex: The infection will sicken him until amputation is needed.

s.def: To become ill.
ex: I will sicken if I don’t get some more exercise.
The judges that sat upon the jail, and numbers of those that attended,[…] sickened upon it and died.

s.def: To fill with disgust or abhorrence.
ex: His arrogant behaviour sickens me.

City took control, pinning a tiring Celtic back and threatening to sicken them with a winner.

s.def: To be filled with disgust or abhorrence.
ex: Mine eyes did sicken at the sight.

s.def: To become disgusting or tedious.
ex: The toiling pleasure sickens into pain.

s.def: To become weak; to decay; to languish.
ex: All pleasures sicken, and all glories sink.

ety: By surface analysis, sicken + -ing.

s.def: present participle and gerund of sicken
Causing sickness or disgust.
ex: sickening cruelty
sickening toxic fumes

s.def: Amazing, fantastic.
ex: Richard Cranium does sickening stuff (if your budget permits), stones from Charles Brennan and lots of imagination.

s.def: The act of making somebody sick.

ety: Etymology tree English sick Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -isch English -ish English sickish From sick + -ish.

s.def: Somewhat sick, but not seriously so.
ex: His heart was thumping harder than ever, and it was impossible to tell if the sickish, pukey feeling deep down in his belly was relief or terror.

ety: From Middle English sikel (also assibilated in sichel), from Old English sicol, siċel, from Proto-West Germanic *sikilu, itself borrowed from Latin sēcula (“sickle”) or sīcīlis (“sickle”). Cognate with Dutch sikkel, German Sichel. Remotely related with English scythe and saw.

s.def: An implement having a semicircular blade and short handle, used for cutting long grass and cereal crops.
ex: Coordinate term: scythe

s.def: Anything resembling a sickle, especially:
ex: Then, ere the silver sickle of that month Became her golden shield, I stole from court With Cyril and with Florian, unperceived.

s.def: To cut with a sickle.
ex: Near-synonyms: reap, mow

s.def: Of red blood cells: to assume an abnormal crescent shape.
ex: Even the cells of heterozygotes will sickle if the oxygen tension is low enough.

s.def: To deform (as with a red blood cell) into an abnormal crescent shape, to cause to sickle.
The most common form of sickle-cell disease, with anemic effects.

ety: From Middle English seekly, sekely, siklich, sekeliche, equivalent to sick + -ly. Possibly a modification of Old English sīcle (“sickly”) and/or derived from Old Norse sjúkligr (“sickly”). Cognate with Dutch ziekelijk, Middle High German siechlich, Danish sygelig, Swedish sjuklig, Icelandic sjúklegur. The verb is from the adjective.

s.def: Frequently ill or in poor health; weakly.
ex: a sickly child
[...] the sharp-scented bottle of crystals that sickly Cousin Bertha had carried to ward off fainting spells.

s.def: Not in good health; (somewhat) sick.
ex: For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep [i.e. have died].
Miguel’s temperature was normal that day, though he was still sickly and restless.

s.def: Characterized by poor or unhealthy growth. (of a plant)
ex: [...] the good wheat on this land had turned sickly and yellow.
With the aid of the marigolds the roses flourished; in the control beds they were sickly and drooping.

s.def: Appearing ill, infirm or unhealthy; giving the appearance of illness.
ex: a sickly pallor
Yossarian [...] could not wipe from his mind the excruciating image of the barefoot boy with sickly cheeks [...]

s.def: Shedding a relatively small amount of light; (of light) not very bright.
ex: The Moon grows sickly at the sight of day.
Night, and all her sickly dews, Her Spectres wan, and Birds of boding cry,
Mr. Moore haunted his mill, his mill-yard, his dye-house, and his warehouse, till the sickly dawn strengthened into day.

s.def: Lacking intensity or vigour.
ex: a sickly smile
a sickly winter sun
What man of soul would [...] run, Day after day, the still-returning round Of life’s mean offices, and sickly joys; But in compassion to mankind?

s.def: Associated with poor moral or mental well-being.
ex: These were not the ravings of imbecility, the sickly effusions of distempered brains;
[...] I know how you came to despise all that sickly Wagnerian idiocy and bombast.
That he had some sickly compulsion neurosis, they said, was very plain for all eyes to see.

s.def: Tending to produce nausea.
ex: a sickly smell; sickly sentimentality
‘Oh, what is that glides quickly where velvet flowers grow thickly, Their scent comes rich and sickly?’—‘A scaled and hooded worm.’
[…] it warn’t no perfumery neither, not by a long sight. I smelt sickly eggs by the barrel, and rotten cabbages, and such things;

s.def: Overly sweet.
ex: […] he was again tasting the sickly welter of melted ice cream on his plate.
The honey tasted sickly in his mouth.

s.def: Marked by the occurrence of illness or disease (of a period of time).

ety: Inherited from Middle English sikness, from Old English sēocnes, sēocness, sēocnys, sēocnyss. By surface analysis, sick + -ness.

s.def: The quality or state of being sick or diseased; illness; an illness.
ex: I do lament the sickness of the king.
18th century, Alexander Pope, Epistle to Miss Blount Trust not too much your now resistless charms; Those, age or sickness soon or late disarms.
Sickness is a dangerous indulgence at my time of life.

s.def: Nausea; qualmishness; as, sickness of stomach.
The analogical misuse of a rarer or marked grammatical case in the place of a more common or unmarked case.

ety: From sick + room.

s.def: A room to be used by someone who is ill.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side From Middle English side, from Old English sīde (“side, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ (“side, flank, edge, shore”), derived from *sīdaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Siede (“side”), West Frisian side (“side”), Dutch zijde, zij (“side”), German Low German Sied (“side”), German Seite (“side”),…

s.def: A bounding straight edge of a two-dimensional shape.
ex: A square has four sides.

s.def: A flat surface of a three-dimensional object; a face.
ex: A cube has six sides.
He said, “Where we’re at right now was back in 2008 all covered with ice. From here to there at the side, the glacier shrank about 20 to 30 meters.”

s.def: One possible aspect of a concept, person, or thing.
ex: Look on the bright side.
She has a mean side (to her).

s.def: One half (left or right, top or bottom, front or back, etc.) of something or someone.
ex: Which side of the tray shall I put it on? The patient was bleeding on the right side.

s.def: A region in a specified position with respect to something.
ex: Meet me on the north side of the monument.

s.def: The portion of the human torso usually covered by the arms when they are not raised; the areas on the left and right between the belly or chest and the back.
ex: Meronyms: flank, loin; latus, lumbus
I generally sleep on my side.
Roll the patient onto the left side so that head, shoulders, and torso move at the same time without twisting.

s.def: One surface of a sheet of paper (used instead of "page", which can mean one or both surfaces.)
ex: John wrote 15 sides for his essay!

s.def: One set of competitors in a game.
ex: Which side has kick-off?

s.def: A sports team.
A group of morris dancers who perform together.
Beside or alongside one another; close to one another and abreast.
ex: The new houses were built side by side, facing the lake.

s.def: In peace.
With a common purpose.
ex: The soldiers of XX and YY were fighting side by side against a common enemy.

s.def: A serving of food meant as an accompanying dish.
ex: She has mashed potatoes as a side dish every day for lunch.

s.def: An unintended consequence, or secondary result, of any action, in addition to the main or intended consequence of that action.
ex: The processing of certain raw materials - pulp and paper, oil, and alumina, for example - can have substantial environmental side effects.

s.def: unintended consequence of any action

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-der. Proto-Germanic *augô Proto-West Germanic *augā Old English ēage Middle English eye English eye English side-eye From side + eye.

s.def: A sidelong look, particularly of animosity, judgment, or suspicion.
ex: Near-synonyms: evil eye, stink eye (see more there)

s.def: To look at out of the corner of one's eye, particularly with animosity, or in a judgmental or suspicious manner.
ex: When I'm working my attention isn't caught straight ahead into the blinkered page, it's side eyeing whatever's peripheral, whatever's random.
"She'll be all right", says [Tionne] Watkins, side-eyeing [Rozonda] Thomas with a cat-like grin.

s.def: A species of jackal (Lupulella adusta, syn. Canis adustus), native to central and southern Africa.

ety: From side + board.

s.def: A piece of dining room furniture having drawers and shelves for linen and tableware; originally for serving food.
ex: He procured himself a glass of water from the sideboard, drank half of it and began to pace the room nervously as he talked.

s.def: A board or similar barrier that forms part of the side of something.
A set of cards that are separate from a player's primary deck, used to customize a match strategy against an opponent by enabling a player to change the composition of the playing deck.
ex: Many of your best chances to overcome opposing decks lie in the development of a strong sideboard.
If you plan on playing in tournaments, you'll want to construct a sideboard for your deck.
They can have a 15-card sideboard or no sideboard. The sideboard can be used to replace cards in the deck after each game.

s.def: To include (a card) in one's sideboard.
ex: Hopefully you now have a strong grasp on how to sideboard effectively.
This will cause an opponent to suffer from a number of his newly sideboarded cards, now useless to him.
Frantic Purification can be sideboarded to destroy an enchantment, but it shouldn't be drafted unless you have no choice.

s.def: To add sideboards to.
ex: The additional load capacity made available by sideboarding is gained by making the scraper bowl taller without increasing the bowl width.

ety: Reformed from burnside, named after American Army general Ambrose Burnside (1824–1881), noted for his unusual facial hair.

s.def: Facial hair reaching from the top of the head down the side of the face to the side of the chin.

ety: From side + car.

s.def: A one-wheeled attachment to the side of a motorcycle to allow for a separate seat for a passenger or cargo space.
A cocktail made with cognac (or brandy), triple sec liqueur, and lemon juice.
A software component that runs in a separate process from the rest of the software, to provide isolation and encapsulation.
ex: Using generic sidecars for multiple microservices may introduce functionality overhead.

ety: From side (noun) + -ed (“having”).

s.def: Having the specified type of side or sides or number of sides.
simple past and past participle of side

ety: From side + kick, which in the late 19th and early 20th century was a slang term for the front side pocket of a pair of trousers, known as the pocket safest from theft. Thus, by analogy, a "side-kick" was a person's closest companion.

s.def: An assistant to another person, especially to a superior or more important person.
ex: If representation and recruitment is an objective, self-styled mavericks like Kelly and his Queensland sidekick George Christensen have some utility.

s.def: In literature, theatre, etc., a good foil of the protagonist, a character who helps emphasize the traits of the main character.
ex: So even though he had – no question – the best lines in Friends, he was never what he would have been in an earlier era: the sidekick.

ety: From side + light.

s.def: A light found at the side of something; especially of a vehicle.
ex: If it starts getting misty, put your sidelights on.

s.def: A window found at one or both sides of a door.
A piece of incidental information that helps one understand a subject.

ety: From side + line.

s.def: A line at the side of something.
Something that is additional or extra or that exists around the edges or margins of a main item.
ex: She started the business as a sideline to her regular work and it ended up becoming the greater source of income.
Soup need not be just a sideline to a meal; if you like, it can be the main course.
I often do electronic repairs as a sideline.

s.def: A line for hobbling an animal by connecting the fore and the hind feet of the same side.
A line defining the side boundary of a playing field. Used in Canadian football, field lacrosse and basketball.
The area outside the playing field beyond each sideline.
ex: The coach stood on the sidelines and bellowed commands at the team.

s.def: The outside or perimeter of any activity.
ex: to relegate to the sidelines
She installed the whole fixture while he simply watched from the sidelines.
Conservative Catholics, Relegated to Sidelines, Denounce Papal Gathering [title]

s.def: A secondary road, especially a byroad at right angles to a main road.
A side hustle.
To place on the sidelines; to bench or to keep someone out of play.
ex: The coach sidelined the player until he regained his strength.

s.def: To remove or keep out of circulation or out of the focus.
ex: The illness sidelined him for weeks.
During 1971-72, spare Type 4s on other regions enabled the whole class to be sidelined, with Class 43s going first.
Prigozhin’s exclusion from Ukraine would sideline one of Russia’s most recognisable war figures.

ety: From Middle English sidlyng (early 14th century), from side + -lyng (modern English side + -ling).

s.def: directed toward one side
inclined; having an inclination
in a sidelong direction
obliquely; askew
Archaic form of siding (“side branch of railway track”).
ex: Upon the main stem […] there is also but one track of Rails with sidelings and turnouts.

ety: From side + lock.

s.def: sidelock
A lock of hair worn at the side of the head.
ex: observation of the Sabbath (rather than the décadi) and the wearing of Jewish side-locks and beards were regarded as ‘uncivic’ offences.

s.def: The design of a gun that has the lockwork mounted to the inside of a plate; compare boxlock.

ety: 1520s, from Middle English sidlyng (early 14th century), from side + -lyng (“(frequentative)”) (modern English -le (“(frequentative)”)). Reanalyzed as side + long.

s.def: Directed to the side; sideways.
ex: He cast me a sidelong glance.

s.def: Slanting or sloping; oblique.
Indirect; suggestive; not straightforward.
ex: She made some sidelong remarks about his manhood.

s.def: Along the side of something.
Towards the side; sideways.
obliquely

ety: From side (“incidental; indirect”, adjective) + quest (noun).
