In fictional or historical writings about chivalric romances: a quest embarked upon by a knight or other person which is not the main quest.
A quest given to a player which has no direct bearing on the outcome of the main campaign or story of a video game, but often provides additional rewards.
ex: Completion of a sidequest often results in the acquisition of money or items that are otherwise unavailable, or unlocks another sidequest.
The following items are either the objects of a quest or vital components of an optional sidequest.

ety: From Latin sīdereus + -al (cf. Latin sīderālis), from sīdus (“star, constellation”), of unknown ultimate origin, likely a substrate language such as Pre-Greek.

s.def: Of or relating to the stars.
Relating to a measurement of time relative to the position of the stars.
Relating to a measurement of time relative to the point of the vernal equinox.
Time measured by the apparent diurnal motion of the vernal equinox; approximated by that based on the rotation of planet Earth relative to the seemingly fixed stars.

ety: From Latin sīdus, sideris, ("constellation").

s.def: Related to stars or constellations, as sidereal relationships.
Related to iron or steel, as in siderosis (fibrosis caused by iron deposits)

ety: From Ancient Greek σίδηρος (sídēros, “iron”) + -lite.

s.def: An iron meteorite; a siderite.

ety: From side + saddle.

s.def: A saddle, usually for a woman, in which the rider sits with both legs on the same side of the horse.
The technique of riding a horse with both legs on the same side of the horse.
On, or as if on, such a saddle.
ex: He rode sidesaddle to avoid worsening his injured leg.
He had his daughter riding sidesaddle on the bicycle frame while he pedaled.
Undoing the last few straps, Eragon swung his right leg over Saphira's spine, so he was sitting sidesaddle, and prepared to jump off her back.

ety: From side + slip.

s.def: A flight manoeuvre that uses opposing rudder and aileron inputs to move the aircraft sideways without turning it.
A flight condition where an aircraft's longitudinal axis is not aligned with its direction of motion relative to the surrounding air.
The angle between an aircraft's longitudinal axis and its direction of motion relative to the surrounding air.
To perform, or place an aircraft in, a sideslip.

ety: Corruption of synod's man.

s.def: An assistant to a churchwarden, one of whose duties is to collect offerings during a service.

ety: From side + splitting.

s.def: Exceptionally funny; hilarious.
ex: We saw a sidesplitting film last night.

s.def: Of laughter, intensely uncontrollable and genuine.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side English step English sidestep From side + step.

s.def: A step to the side.
A physical motion or metaphorical act to avoid or dodge something.
To step to the side.
ex: I […] knocked and waited. […] He sidestepped, and I went in.

s.def: To avoid or dodge.
ex: They sidestepped the issue.

ety: From side + swipe.

s.def: A blow with the side of something, such as the side of car that is changing lanes incautiously.
A catty or sarcastic remark.
ex: give a sideswipe
receive a sideswipe
Calvin Harris's number-ten hit Acceptable in the 80s is both a wry sideswipe and a celebration of the scene;[…]

s.def: To give a blow with the side, as to strike with the side of a car when turning.
ex: As he turns left from Central into Jackson he nearly sideswipes a milk truck idling yards out from the kerb.

ety: From side + track.

s.def: A second, relatively short length of track just to the side of a railroad track, joined to the main track by switches at one or both ends, used either for unloading freight, or to allow two trains on a same track to meet (opposite directions) or pass (same direction); a railroad siding.
Any auxiliary railroad track, as differentiated from a siding, that runs adjacent to the main track.
A smaller tunnel or well drilled as an auxiliary off a main tunnel or well.
An alternate train of thought, issue, topic, or activity, that is a deviation or distraction from the topic at hand or central activity, and secondary or subordinate in importance or effectiveness.
ex: Stay focused on the story; you keep getting lost in all of these little sidetracks.
"However, I am down a side-track. What I wanted to say to you is that you must not take Bolsover's little spirit circus too seriously."

s.def: To divert (a locomotive or train) on to a lesser used track in order to allow other trains to pass.

To divert or distract (someone) from a main issue or course of action with an alternate or less relevant topic or activity; or, to use deliberate trickery or sly wordplay when talking to (a person) in order to avoid discussion of a subject.
ex: Sorry I'm late. I got sidetracked helping my friend move some furniture.
The politician sidetracked the reporter with a story about duck hunting instead of a direct response to the question that was asked.
I hope you can sidetrack the teacher with questions so we don't have to take the exam.

s.def: To sideline; to push aside; to divert or distract from, reducing (something) to a secondary or subordinate position.
ex: The project was sidetracked in favor of a more popular program.
He has sidetracked this debate for far too long.

s.def: To deviate briefly from the topic at hand.
ex: Just to sidetrack a little bit from the subject I will explain my reasoning.
To sidetrack for a moment, let me commend this team for their outstanding efforts.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side English walk English sidewalk From side + walk.

s.def: A paved footpath located at the side of a road, for the use of pedestrians.
ex: Stay on the sidewalk.
Morning commuters in parts of Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas discovered slick sidewalks and icy roadways Monday.

s.def: Any paved footpath, even if not located at the side of a road.

ety: From side + -ward. Compare Middle English liftsideward (“leftward”, adjective).

s.def: Toward a side.
Toward a side.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-redup. Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷléh₂ Proto-Germanic *hweulō Old English hwēol Middle English whel English wheel English -er English sidewheeler From side + wheel + -er.

s.def: A vessel (especially a paddle steamer) propelled by a pair of paddle wheels positioned one on each side

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side English -ing English siding From side + -ing (“material, collection”).

s.def: A building material which covers and protects the sides of a house or other building.
ex: Ugh. If there's one thing I can't stand it's cheesy vinyl siding.

s.def: present participle and gerund of side
ex: Whenever he hears an argument, he can't help siding with one party or the other.

s.def: A second, relatively short length of track just to the side of a railroad track, joined to the main track by switches at one or both ends, used either for loading or unloading freight, storing trains or other rail vehicles; or to allow two trains on a same track to meet (opposite directions) or pas…
ex: They slept where they could, sometimes in an empty truck on a siding near the station, sometimes in a cart behind a warehouse; [...]

ety: From Latin Sidon and Ancient Greek Σιδών (Sidṓn), from Phoenician 𐤑𐤉𐤃𐤅𐤍 (ṣydwn).

s.def: Former name of Saïda: a city in Lebanon; a former city-state in Phoenicia.

ety: From Middle English sege, from Old French sege, siege, seige (modern French siège), from Vulgar Latin *sēdicum, from Latin sēdicŭlum, sēdēcula (“small seat”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”). The military sense of the term is derived from the notion of an army "sitting down" in front of its target.

s.def: Military action.
ex: They sued for peace after the long siege.
The Peloponnesian war is a proper subject for history, the siege of Athens for an epic poem, and the death of Alcibiades for a tragedy.
Liu Pang's general Han Hsin won the strategic city of Hsing-yang for him, but Hsiang-Yü put Liu Pang under siege there.

s.def: A seat.
ex: To th'vpper part, where was aduaunced hye / A stately siege of soueraigne maiestye; / And thereon sat a woman gorgeous gay[…].

s.def: A place with a toilet seat: an outhouse; a lavatory.
To assault or blockade a city or fortress with the intent of conquering by force or attrition; to besiege.

ety: PIE word *h₁én From siege + engine (“large construction used in warfare”).

s.def: A large weapon of war used during ancient and medieval times to batter fortifications, settlements, etc.; specifically, a trebuchet or other type of catapult.
ex: The cavalry were on the wings and the siege-engines, mangonels and catapults, planted on sand-dunes.

s.def: A siege weapon, consisting of a wheeled wooden tower with ladders inside, which was parked next to walls so assailants could safely scale them.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish sierra, from Latin serra (“saw”), referring to the saw-tooth profile of the crestline of the range seen from a distance.

s.def: A rugged range of mountains.
ex: Holonym: cordillera
Meronym: sawback

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Sierra from the NATO/ICAO Phonetic Alphabet.
A scombroid fish.
A relatively low-quality grade of Spanish saffron.

ety: From Italian sierra (“mountain range”) + leone (“lion”) (via Venetian), itself from Portuguese Serra Leoa (“lioness mountains”), as the area was described to the rest of Europe by Venetian explorer Alvise Cadamosto; in reference to the Lion Mountains (named by Pedro de Sintra in 1462).

s.def: A country in West Africa. Official name: Republic of Sierra Leone.

ety: From Sierra Leone + -an.

s.def: A native or inhabitant of Sierra Leone.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish siesta, from Latin sexta (“the sixth hour from dawn, noon, midday”). Doublet of sext.

s.def: A nap, especially an afternoon one taken during the hottest part of the day in some cultures.
ex: When it's time for siesta, you can watch them go by / Beautiful faces, no cares in this world

s.def: Laid-back attitudes to work or laziness, especially by a Hispanic person.
to take a siesta; to nap.

ety: From Middle English sive, syfe, from Old English sife, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi (“sieve”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyp-, *seyb- (“to pour, sieve, strain, run, drip”). Akin to German Sieb, Dutch zeef, Proto-Slavic *sito (Russian си́то (síto), сев (sev), се́ять (séjatʹ)).

s.def: A device with a mesh, grate, or otherwise perforated bottom to separate, in a granular material, larger particles from smaller ones, or to separate solid objects from a liquid.
ex: Near-synonyms: sifter, strainer, temse
Use the sieve to get the pasta from the water.
The philosopher Demonax said of two dunces, 'one appeared to be milking a he-goat while the other was holding a sieve for him.'

s.def: A process, physical or abstract, that arrives at a final result by filtering out unwanted pieces of input from a larger starting set of input.
ex: Given a list of consecutive numbers starting at 1, the Sieve of Eratosthenes algorithm will find all of the prime numbers.

s.def: A kind of coarse basket.
A person, or their mind, that cannot remember things or is unable to keep secrets.
An intern who lets too many non-serious cases into the emergency room.
ex: To be a sieve was to lack clinical judgment, courage, and group loyalty all at once.

s.def: A collection of morphisms in a category whose codomain is a certain fixed object of that category, which collection is closed under precomposition by any morphism in the category.
To strain, sift or sort using a sieve.
ex: Serpulorbis grandis feeds on plankton that it seives ^([sic]) from the water like a clam does.

s.def: To concede; to let in.

ety: From Middle English syften, from Old English siftan, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.

s.def: To sieve or strain (something).
To separate or scatter (things) as if by sieving.
To examine (something) carefully.
ex: But if we still carry on our sifting humour, and ask, What is the foundation of all conclusions from experience ? this implies a new question.
It immediately occurred to him to sift her on the subject of Isabella and Theodore.

s.def: To move data records up in memory to make space to insert further records.
An act of sifting.

ety: From sift + -er.

s.def: One who sifts.
ex: He was employed as a sifter.

s.def: A tool for sifting, especially one for powdered cooking ingredients.
ex: Near-synonym: sieve

s.def: Any lamellirostral bird, as a duck or goose, so called because it sifts or strains its food from the water and mud by means of the lamellae of the beak.

ety: From Middle English sighen (“to sigh”), back-formation from sighte, past tense form of siken, from Old English sīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīkan, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to pour out”).

s.def: To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual, and immediately expel it; to make a deep single audible respiration, especially as the result or involuntary expression of fatigue, exhaustion, grief, sorrow, frustration, or the like.
ex: When she saw it wasn't damaged, she sighed with relief.
He sighed. It was going to be a long night.
He sighed over the lost opportunity.

s.def: To make a sound like sighing.
ex: The wind sighed in the trees.
And the coming wind did roar more loud, / And the sails did sigh like sedge.
The winter winds are wearily sighing.

s.def: To exhale (the breath) in sighs.
ex: She sighed a sigh that was nearly a groan.
sigh a note and sing a note
She sighed her relief when she found her missing toddler.

s.def: To lament; to grieve.
ex: He sighed deeply in his spirit.

s.def: To utter sighs over; to lament or mourn over.
ex: Ages to come, and men unborn, / Shall bless her name, and sigh her fate.
In Lisbon, Queen Luisa, who had sighed so long for a French marriage, declared that an angel from heaven could not have brought better news.

s.def: To express by sighs; to utter in or with sighs.
ex: "I guess I have no choice," she sighed.
She sighed her frustrations.
They […] sighed forth proverbs.

s.def: A deep, prolonged audible inhale and exhale of breath; as when fatigued, frustrated, grieved, or relieved; the act of sighing.
a manifestation of grief; a lament.
A person who is bored.
An expression of fatigue, exhaustion, grief, sorrow, frustration, or the like, often used in casual written contexts.
ex: Sigh, I'm so bored at work today.

ety: From Middle English sighte, from Old English sihþ (“something seen; vision”), from Proto-West Germanic *sihti (“seeing, sight”), equivalent to see + -t. Cognates Cognate with Cimbrian gazicht (“sight, vision; pupil”), Dutch gezicht (“face; sight, vision”), zicht (“sight, vision”), German Gesicht (“face; sight, vision”), Sicht (“view; sight; visibility”), Luxembourgish Gesiicht (“face”), Siicht (“view; sight”), Yiddish געזיכט (gezikht, “face”), Danish sigt (“sight; visibility”), Norwegian Bokmål…

s.def: The sense or faculty by which objects are perceived through the agency of light; the sense by which we see.
ex: Sight is a precious gift.
He is losing his sight and now can barely read.

s.def: An act, instance, opportunity or possibility of seeing; the perception of objects by the eye; view (see also idiomatic expressions such as in sight, out of sight, catch sight of, etc.)
ex: The sight of him in his new uniform made us all proud.
I need to have sight of the certificate before proceeding.
to gain sight of land, to lose sight of the aircraft

s.def: Something seen.
ex: The sight in front of me seemed somehow familiar.

s.def: Something worth seeing; a spectacle, either good or bad.
ex: We went to London and saw all the sights – Buckingham Palace, Tower Bridge, and so on.
You really look a sight in that ridiculous costume!
And Moses saide, I will nowe turne aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.

s.def: A device used in aiming a projectile, through which the person aiming looks at the intended target; see also in one's sights.
ex: He's a really remarkable man and it's very hard to get him in one's sights; […]

s.def: A small aperture through which objects are to be seen, and by which their direction is settled or ascertained.
ex: the sight of a quadrant
their eyes of fire sparking through sights of steel

s.def: a great deal, a lot; frequently used to intensify a comparative.
ex: a sight of money
This is a darn sight better than what I'm used to at home!
"If your mother put you in the pit at twelve, it's no reason why I should do the same with my lad." "Twelve! It wor a sight afore that!"

s.def: In a drawing, picture, etc., that part of the surface, as of paper or canvas, which is within the frame or the border or margin. In a frame, the open space, the opening.
The instrument of seeing; the eye.
Mental view; opinion; judgment.
ex: In their sight it was harmless.
a very heinous Sin in the Sight of God
That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.

s.def: present participle and gerund of sight-read

ety: Etymology tree English sight Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English sightless From sight + -less.

s.def: Without sight; blind; unseeing.
Synonym of invisible.
ex: The toiling world is sightless to those who cannot see.

ety: From Middle English sightlye, equivalent to sight + -ly. Cognate with German sichtlich (“visible”).

s.def: Attractive, pleasing to the eye; affording gratification to the sense of sight; aesthetically pleasing.
ex: Many brave, sightly horses.
'Your face -ain't sightly,' said Ole Pa.

s.def: Offering a good view.
ex: 30 acres land, situated high and sightly, commanding an unobstructed view of the surrounding country, […]
This is one of the most sightly locations in Boston for an imposing religious group having an unobstructed view from practically all directions.

s.def: Open to sight; conspicuous.
ex: There is also a soldiers' monument on a sightly situation on Grand Avenue.
He lived in the William Church, Jr., house which still occupies a sightly spot on West Hill.

ety: From sight + seeing.

s.def: The activity of going out looking at things; tourism.
ex: Sightseeing is a frequent reason to visit San Francisco.

s.def: present participle and gerund of sightsee

ety: Borrowed from Latin sigillum (“little sign”). Doublet of seal and sigillum.

s.def: A seal, signature or signet.
An occult or magical sign, image or symbol.
A nonalphanumeric symbol affixed to an identifier (such as a variable name) to indicate a property such as type or scope.

ety: From Ancient Greek σῖγμα (sîgma), probably from the root σῑγ- (sīg-) as seen in σίζω (sízō, “to hiss”) + -μα (-ma, nominal suffix).

s.def: The eighteenth letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets (Σ, σ), the twentieth letter of Old and Ancient.
The symbol Σ, used to indicate summation of a set or series.
The symbol σ, used to indicate one standard deviation from the mean, particularly in a normal distribution.
A sigma male (a self-reliant and assertive male).
Possessing characteristics of a sigma male.

ety: Etymology tree English sigma Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātuslbor. English -ate English sigmate From sigma + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Shaped like the Greek letter sigma.
To modify (a Greek word) by adding a sigma, or by changing another letter to sigma.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek σῖγμᾰ (sîgmă) Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-) Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *wéydos Proto-Hellenic *wéidos Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos) Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-ēs Proto-Hellenic *-ēs Ancient Greek -ης (-ēs) Ancient Greek -ειδής (-eidḗs) Ancient Greek σῑγμοειδής (sīgmoeidḗs)bor. English sigmoid Borrowing from Ancient Greek σῑγμοειδής (sīgmoeidḗs, “of the shape of sigma”), from σῖγμᾰ (sîgmă, “sigma”) + -ο- (-o-)…

s.def: Semi-circular, like the uncial or lunate sigma (similar to English C).
Curved in two directions, like the letter "S", or the Greek ς (sigma); having a serpentine shape.
Relating to the sigmoid colon.
Ellipsis of sigmoid colon.
Ellipsis of sigmoid function.

ety: From Middle English signe, sygne, syng, seine, sine, syne, from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (“sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. Doublet of signum and signal. Partially displaced native token.

s.def: A clearly visible object, generally flat, bearing a short message in words or pictures.
ex: The sign in the window advertised a room for rent.
I missed the sign at the corner so I took the wrong turn.
The shops were, therefore, distinguished by painted signs, which gave a gay and grotesque aspect to the streets.

s.def: a fact that shows that something exists or may happen
To make a mark
ex: Meantime revolving in his thoughtful mind / The scar, with which his manly knee was sign'd […].

s.def: to make (a document) official by writing one's signature
A visible fact that shows that something exists or may happen.
ex: Their angry expressions were a clear sign they didn't want to talk.
Those clouds show signs of raining soon.
Those clouds show little sign of raining soon.

s.def: A mark or another symbol used to represent something.
ex: The sharp sign indicates that the pitch of the note is raised a half step.
I gave them a thumbs-up sign.

s.def: Physical evidence left by an animal.
ex: The hunters found deer sign at the end of the trail.

s.def: A wonder; miracle; prodigy.
An astrological sign.
ex: Your sign is Taurus? That's no surprise.

s.def: Positive or negative polarity, as denoted by the + or - sign.
ex: I got the magnitude right, but the sign was wrong.

s.def: The sign language (sense 1) that is used locally or that is mistakenly believed to be the only one.
ex: I'm taking night classes to learn sign language.

s.def: Any of several natural languages, typically used by the deaf, in which words consist of hand shapes, motions, positions, and facial expressions.
ex: It is safe to say that the academic world is now convinced that sign languages are real languages in every sense of the term.

s.def: Sign languages (sense 1) considered collectively.
ex: There are some unique properties found in sign language compared to spoken language.

s.def: Communication through gestures as a substitute for language, for example, between monks under a vow of silence or during trade amongst different linguistic groups.
ex: Even Maxwell the trader, who has been most among them, is compelled to resort to the curious sign language common to most of the prairie tribes.

ety: A calque translation of Latin signum crucis.

s.def: A gesture of the hand moving over the front of one's body, or over an object, in the shape of a cross made as part of ritual or to invoke divine protection.
To make a decision that dooms one to certain death.

ety: From Old French segnal, seignal or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s). Doublet of signum and sign.

s.def: A sign made to give notice of some occurrence, command, or danger, or to indicate the start of a concerted action.
ex: All obeyed / The wonted signal and superior voice / Of this great potentate.

s.def: An electromagnetic action, normally a voltage that is a function of time, that conveys the information of the radio or TV program or of communication with another party.
ex: My mobile phone can't get a signal in the railway station.

s.def: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.
Any variation of a quantity or change in an entity over time that conveys information upon detection.
An on-off light, semaphore, or other device used to give an indication to another person.
An action, change or process done to convey information and thus reduce uncertainty.
A token; an indication; a foreshadowing; a sign.
ex: The weary sun […] / Gives signal of a goodly day to-morrow.
There was not the least signal of the calamity to be seen.
Did I get it wrong all along? / You were sending signals / You sent certain signals to me

s.def: Useful information, as opposed to noise.
A simple interprocess communication used to notify a process or thread of an occurrence.
A signalling interaction between cells
An American crayfish, Pacifastacus leniusculus, having a large claw that it waves to attract a mate.

ety: Etymology tree English signal Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English signalize From signal + -ize.

s.def: To distinguish, to make noteworthy.
ex: [T]he reign of the Tudors was often signalized by the valour of our soldiers and sailors […].

s.def: To display or make known (an attribute, quality, etc.); to call attention to.
To point out; to take special note of.
ex: This expression rex Anglorum is rightly signalised by historians as a milestone in our history.

s.def: To communicate with (someone) by means of a signal.
ex: a ship signalizes its consort

s.def: To indicate; to be a sign of.
To furnish (a traffic intersection) with a traffic signal.

ety: Etymology tree English signal Proto-Indo-European *mon- Proto-Germanic *mann- Proto-West Germanic *mann Old English mann Middle English man Middle English -man English -man English signalman From signal + -man.

s.def: Somebody employed to operate the signals and points of a railway.
A member of the armed forces responsible for signalling.
Somebody employed to direct rigging or crane operations by providing a different point of view.

ety: From Latin signatorius.

s.def: One who signs or has signed something.
ex: Near-synonyms: undersigned, subscriber
John Hancock is famous for being the first signatory to the American Declaration of Independence, and for writing his name large.

s.def: Relating to a seal; used in sealing.
ex: signatory Rings

s.def: Signing; joining or sharing in a signature.
ex: signatory powers

ety: Borrowed from Middle French signature, or from Medieval Latin signātūra, future active periphrastic of verb signāre from signum (“sign”), + -tūra, feminine of -tūrus, future active periphrastic suffix. Displaced native Old English handseten (literally “hand setting”).

s.def: A person's name, written by that person, used as identification or to signify approval of accompanying material, such as a legal contract.
An act of signing one's name; an act of producing a signature.
The part of a doctor’s prescription containing directions for the patient.
Signs on the stave indicating key and tempo, composed of the key signature and the time signature.
A group of four (or a multiple of four) sheets printed such that, when folded, they become a section of a book.
A pattern used for matching the identity of a virus, the parameter types of a method, etc.
Data attached to a message that guarantees that the message originated from its claimed source.
A mark or sign of implication.
ex: the natural and indelible signature of God, which human souls […] are supposed to be stamped with
The TACOM Vehicle Signature Reduction program is concerned with reducing the noise signature detectability of military vehicles in combat.

s.def: A distinguishing feature or product.
ex: A great beginning is the goose-liver terrine with truffles, one of the chef's signatures.

s.def: A tuple specifying the sign of coefficients in any diagonal form of a quadratic form.

ety: From sign + board.

s.def: A board carrying a sign, or on which signs may be posted.
Having a signature; endorsed.
ex: The signed check could be cashed.

s.def: Having both positive and negative varieties.
ex: It wasn't until they tried to subtract 3 from 1 that the elementary school students realized they needed signed numbers.

s.def: Furnished with signs and signposts; signposted.
ex: Turn left on poorly signed Highway 292 and proceed on this winding road for about 12 miles.

ety: From Old French signet (“small seal”), from Medieval Latin signētum, diminutive of Latin signum (“sign”).

s.def: An object (especially a ring) formerly used to impress a picture into the sealing wax of a document as a proof of its origin.
ex: I had my fathers Signet in my Purse, / Which was the Modell of that Danish Seale:
To carry pure death in an earring, a casket, A signet, a fan-mount, a filigree basket!

ety: Inherited from Middle English significaunce, from Middle French significance, from Old French significance, from Latin significantia. Doublet of signifiance.

s.def: The extent to which something matters; importance
ex: As a juror your opinion is of great significance for the outcome of the trial.

s.def: Meaning.
ex: the significance of her gesture was unclear

ety: From Latin significans, present participle of significare, from signum (“sign”) + ficare (“do, make”), variant of facere.

s.def: Having a noticeable or major effect.
ex: That was a significant step in the right direction.
The First World War was a significant event.

s.def: Signifying something; carrying meaning.
ex: a significant word or sound
a significant look
It was well said of Plotinus, that the stars were significant, but not efficient.

s.def: Reasonably large in number or amount.
Having a covert or hidden meaning.
Having a low probability of occurring by chance (for example, having high correlation and thus likely to be related).
Of a digit or figure, see significant figure.
That which has significance; a sign; a token; a symbol.
ex: In dumb significants proclaim your thoughts.
And in my glass significants there are

s.def: One's exclusive romantic partner.
A person with whom one has an important bond of some kind.
ex: Dr. Nogueira said it was always preferable to have coaches drawn from a school's staff because a coach "is a significant other" to a student.

ety: From Old French significacion, from Latin significātiō.

s.def: The act of signifying, or something that is signified; significance.
Evidence for the existence of something.
A meaning of a word.

ety: Latin sīgnificātīvus: compare French significatif.

s.def: That tends to signify or indicate; indicative
ex: The holy Symbols, or Signs, are not inanes significationes, barely significative.

s.def: That has meaning or significance; significant
ex: Neither in the degrees of kindred they were destitute of significative words.

ety: Inherited from Middle English signifien, from Old French signifier, from Latin significare.

s.def: To create a sign out of something.
To give (something) a meaning or an importance.
To mean; to betoken.
ex: Life’s […] a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.

s.def: To show one’s intentions with a sign etc.; to indicate, announce, or portend.
ex: I’ll to the king; and signify to him / That thus I have resign’d my charge to you.
For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him.
Tapping at the window, he signified that she should open the casement, and when she had done this he handed in the key to her.

s.def: To make a difference; to matter (in negative or interrogative expressions).
ex: “He was Charles. You can read it there. Charles Hale.” / “That don’t signify,” Ida said. “A man always has a different name for strangers. […]”

ety: Borrowed from Italian signor, apocopic form of signore. Doublet of senior and señor.

s.def: Alternative form of signore, a courtesy title used towards an Italian man.

ety: Borrowed from Italian signora.

s.def: Mrs; madam; title of address or respect for women in Italy.
An Italian woman.

ety: Borrowed from Italian signore. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, sir, and sire.

s.def: A courtesy title for Italian men.
ex: When you walk in a dream but you know you're not dreaming, Signore, scuzza me but you see, back in old Napoli, that's amore!

ety: Borrowed from Italian signorina.

s.def: A courtesy title for an unmarried woman of Italian origin.
maitake, hen of the woods (mushroom)

ety: From sign + post.

s.def: A post bearing a sign that gives information on directions.
A word or phrase within a clue that serves as an indicator, rather than being fodder.
To install signposts on.
ex: The route wasn't signposted, and we got lost on the way.

s.def: To direct (somebody) to services, resources, etc.
To signal (something) intentionally, as if with a signpost.
The function that determines the sign of a real number, yielding −1 if negative, +1 if positive, or otherwise zero.

ety: From Turkish Siirt, from Ottoman Turkish سعرد (Siird).

s.def: A municipality, the capital of Siirt district and Siirt Province, Turkey, with a mixed population of Kurds, Turks, and Arabs.
A province in southeastern Turkey.
A district of Siirt Province, Turkey.

ety: Alteration (probably by influence of silo) of ensilage (1881), itself from French ensilage, from ensiler (“put in a silo”), from Spanish ensilar.

s.def: Fermented green forage fodder stored in an airtight silo or clamp.
ex: Compared to the corn silages, the sweetclover silages are much higher in digestible crude protein, but lower in total digestible nutrients.

ex: The idea for The Sims was one that had been simmering in Wright's mind for quite some time, and was initially conceived as an architecture simulation.

s.def: To cook or undergo heating slowly at or below the boiling point.
ex: The soup simmered on the stove.
That way, the heat can circulate under the meat and prevent it from simmering in its juices.

s.def: To cause to cook or to cause to undergo heating slowly at or below the boiling point.
ex: Simmer the soup for five minutes, then serve.
There are other easy ways you can bake and simmer and sauté wild game without qualifying as a gourmet cook.

s.def: To be on the point of breaking out into anger; to be agitated.
ex: Maybe that really did happen, and Robin's anger at his wife had simmered for this long?

s.def: To remain angry with someone or something past the point of exhaustion; to resign oneself to holding a grudge, especially after some failed attempts to resolve a situation.
ex: I tried to get through to him; all that's left for me to do is simmer.

s.def: The state or process of simmering.
ex: The kettle was kept on the simmer.

s.def: Someone who plays a sim (a simulation game), particularly The Sims.

ety: Most likely a late-19th-century blend of simon (“dollar”), from simon (“sixpence coin”) (17th-century British slang, perhaps related to simony?), and Napoleon (“French gold coin worth 20 francs, bearing the image of Napoleon III”). Perhaps from New Orleans. The gaming sense may have been chosen for its similarity to Sim.

s.def: A dollar.
ex: That'll cost you five simoleons.
"T'ought I was lyin' about the money, did ye? Well, you can frisk me if you wanter. Dat's the last simoleon in the treasury. Who's goin' to pay?"
We gladly did so with the result that we got a menu worth a dollar and a half or two dollars for a single simolean. Can you beat that?

s.def: A fake, theoretical, or unofficial unit of currency.
ex: The game franchise demands that its participants to simulate the "rat race," earning Simoleons, remodeling their homes, and buying properties.

ety: From Simon + says.

s.def: A children's game where players must carry out only those commands that are preceded by the utterance "Simon says".

ety: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.

s.def: The buying or selling of spiritual or sacred things, such as ecclesiastical offices, pardons, or consecrated objects.
ex: He openly practiced simony; in other words, he sold benefices.

ety: Borrowed from Italian simpatico or Spanish simpático (“nice, likeable”), ultimately from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “sympathy”, literally “suffering together”).

s.def: Having a compatible temperament or pleasing qualities.
Compatible (with a person, thing, etc).
ex: "Basically, right now, you and math are just not...simpatico."

ety: Uncertain; compare (probably from) Danish simper / semper (“coy”), German zimper (“elegant, dainty”).

s.def: To smile in a foolish, frivolous, self-conscious, coy, obsequious, or smug manner.
ex: How the fools kotowed and simpered while I looked over their jewels and speculated upon how much I could get for them!
a whimpering, simpering child

s.def: To glimmer; to twinkle.
ex: Yet can I mark how stars above / Simper and shine.

s.def: A foolish, frivolous, self-conscious, or affected smile; a smirk.
ex: He paused, and then a strange expression appeared on his lips. It was very like a simper.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sem- Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-der. Latin sem- Proto-Italic *-plosder. Latin -plus Latin simplusbor. Old French simplebor. Middle English symple English simple Inherited from Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”, literally “onefold”) (as opposed to duplex (“double”, literally “twofold”)), from semel (“the same”) + plicō (“to fold”). See same and fold. Compare single, singular, simultaneous, etc. Partially displaced native…

s.def: Uncomplicated; lacking complexity; taken by itself, with nothing added.
Easy; not difficult.
ex: There is no simple way to define precisely a complex arrangement of parts, however homely the object may appear to be.

s.def: Free from duplicity; guileless, innocent, straightforward.
ex: Full many fine men go upon my score, as simple as I stand here, and I trust them.

s.def: Without ornamentation; plain.
Feeble-minded; foolish.
Undistinguished in social condition; of no special rank.
ex: Garak: Who would want to kill me, a simple tailor? / Odo: A simple tailor? A simple tailor who used to be an agent of the Obsidian Order!

s.def: Structurally uncomplicated.
ex: a simple ascidian

s.def: Trivial; insignificant.
ex: ‘That was a symple cause,’ seyde Sir Trystram, ‘for to sle a good knyght for seyynge well by his maystir.’

s.def: Mere; not other than; being only.
ex: A medicine […] whose simple touch / Is powerful to araise King Pepin.

s.def: A herbal preparation made from one plant, as opposed to something made from more than one plant.
ex: Dere is some simples in my closet, dat I vill not for the varld I shall leave behind.
I know there are some simples, which in operation are moistening and some drying.
The first fellow that picked an herb to cure himself had a bit of pluck. Simples. Want to be careful.

s.def: A device that only requires the application of a single force to work.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see simple, machine.

ety: “Simple” because the tense is formed without any auxiliary verb.

s.def: A tense used to describe something that happened in the past, formed by the inflection of a single word, without any auxiliary verb such as be or have.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sem- Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-der. Latin sem- Proto-Italic *-plosder. Latin -plus Latin simplusbor. Old French simplebor. Middle English symple English simple English -ton English simpleton From simple + -ton (as in a surname). Compare French simplet, Italian semplicione.

s.def: A simple-minded person lacking common sense.

ety: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin simplex (“plain, simple; single”). The first part, sim-, comes from Proto-Indo-European *sem-, *sm̥- (“one; together”). The second part, -plex, may be from *pleḱ- (“to weave”). The noun is derived from the adjective. The plural forms simplices and simplicia are learned borrowings from Latin simplicēs (masculine or feminine) and simplicia (neuter), respectively plural forms of simplex. Noun sense 1 (“generalization of a triangle or tetrahedron to a…

s.def: Having a single structure; not composite or complex; undivided, unitary.

Of an eye: (supposedly) having pigment on only the posterior surface of the iris and not the anterior surface, and thus appearing blue; this was later found to be inaccurate, as eye colour is due to the amount of pigment in the anterior surface of the iris; also, of eye pigmentation: present only o…
Of a circuit or device: involving signals which travel in one direction at a time; unidirectional.
Of a polyploid organism: having one dominant allele at a given locus on all homologous chromosomes.
Synonym of heterozygous (“of an organism: having two different alleles in a given gene”).
Of a word: having no (derivational) affixes; simple, monomorphemic, uncompounded.
Of an apartment (or, sometimes, another type of property): having only one floor or storey; single-storey.
A generalization of a triangle or tetrahedron to an arbitrary dimension; more accurately, the convex hull of n+1 affinely independent points in n-dimensional space.
A word which is not compound and contains no derivational affixes (inflectional affixes are usually disregarded); a monomorphemic word.
ex: The word weak is a simplex. Its derivative weaken is not.

s.def: In full simplex sentence: in transformational grammar: a simple sentence which is the product of a few transformations; a kernel sentence.

ety: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). See simple. By surface analysis, simple + -icity. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.

s.def: quality or state of being simple, unmixed, or uncompounded; as, the simplicity of metals or of earths
The state or quality of being simple
ex: simplicity of dress, of style, or of language
simplicity of diet
simplicity of life

s.def: An act or instance of foolishness.
ex: speaking of the great simplicity we commit, in leaving yong children under the government and charge of their fathers and parents.

ety: From the French simplification.

s.def: The act of simplifying or something that has been simplified.
A valid simple argument.

Chinese written using the forms of Chinese characters introduced by the People's Republic of China as script reform. The characters are simplified (with a reduced number of strokes, etc.) compared to their pre-reform shapes.

ety: From the French simplifier, equivalent to simple + -ify.

s.def: To make simpler, either by reducing in complexity, reducing to component parts, or making easier to understand.
To become simpler.

ety: From Middle English symply, symplely; equivalent to simple + -ly, with *-lely simplified to -ly by haplology.

s.def: Merely; solely.
ex: I was simply asking a question.
Rather than scanning a boarding pass or handing over a passport, you simply stare into a camera and you’re verified.

s.def: in a simple manner
In a simple way or state; considered in or by itself; without addition; alone.
Plainly; without art or subtlety
ex: ‘No,’ said Stephen simply.

s.def: Foolishly; stupidly.
absolutely, positively.
ex: That was a simply wonderful dessert.
This type of comportment simply won't be tolerated.
What about the way you love me? / And the way you squeeze me? / Simply beautiful

s.def: Frankly.
ex: Simply, he just fired you.
It was, quite simply, the best there was in stock.

s.def: Having its fundamental group a singleton.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin simulācrum (“image, likeness”), from simul(ā) + -crum (a variant of -culum, from Proto-Indo-European *-tlom, a suffix forming instrument nouns), from similis (“similar (to)”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one; together”).

s.def: A physical image or representation of a deity, person, or thing.
ex: a simulacrum of a New York studio apartment

s.def: A thing which has the appearance or form of another thing, but not its true qualities; a thing which simulates another thing; an imitation; a semblance.
ex: [Y]ou find you have nothing—nothing but a coat and wig and a mask smiling below it—nothing but a great simulacrum.
Certainly a vehicle that seemed to have no inside at all—that appeared to be the mere simulacrum of a vehicle—could not very well contain the two.

ety: First attested in 1652; Borrowed from Latin simulātus, perfect passive participle of simulō (“make like, imitate, copy, represent, feign”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from similis (“like”). See similar.

s.def: To model, replicate, duplicate the behavior, appearance or properties of.
ex: We will use a smoke machine to simulate the fog you will actually encounter.
This video game simulates a pinball machine.

s.def: Feigned; pretended.
ex: under simulate religion

ety: First attested in 1340 as Middle English symulacioun, from Middle French simulation, from Old French simulation/simulacion, from Latin simulātiōnem, from simulō (“imitate”). Morphologically simulate + -ion.

s.def: The process of simulating.
ex: Despite extensive simulation in the design phase, the aircraft failed to behave as expected.

s.def: Something that simulates a system or environment in order to predict actual behaviour.
ex: This exercise is a simulation of actual battle conditions.
The most reliable simulation predicts that the hurricane will turn north.

s.def: A video game designed to convey a more or less realistic experience, as of a sport or warfare.
ex: Some kids in the classroom will be playing simulations after school.

s.def: Assuming an appearance which is feigned, or not true.
The act of falling over in order to be awarded a foul, when no foul has been committed.

ety: From Medieval Latin simultaneus, from simultim (“at the same time, extended”), from Latin simul (“together, at the same time”); compare similar.

s.def: Happening at the same moment.
To be solved for the same values of variables.

s.def: Occurring at the same time.
ex: The cradle-rocking and the song would cease simultaneously for a moment, and an exclamation at highest vocal pitch would take the place of the melody.
The hens woke up squawking with terror because they had all dreamed simultaneously of hearing a gun go off in the distance.

ety: From Classical Persian سیمرغ (sīmurġ).

s.def: A gigantic winged benevolent creature.

s.def: A violation of divine will or religious law.
ex: As a Christian, I think this is a sin against God.

s.def: A misdeed or wrong.
Sinfulness, depravity, iniquity.
A sin offering; a sacrifice for sin.
An embodiment of sin; a very wicked person.
A flaw or mistake.
ex: No movie is without sin.

s.def: sin bin
To commit a sin.
ex: Christine Cooper: It's not wrong to sin. Christ came into this world for the sinners. DCI Tom Barnaby: To call people to repentance, Mrs Cooper.

ety: From Middle English syns, synnes, contraction of earlier sithens, sithence, from sithen (“after, since”) ( + -s, adverbial genitive suffix), from Old English sīþþan, from the phrase sīþ þǣm (“after/since that (time)”), from sīþ (“since, after”) + þǣm dative singular of þæt. Cognate with Dutch sinds (“since”), German seit (“since”), Danish siden (“since”), Icelandic síðan (“since”) Scots syne (“since”).

s.def: From a specified time in the past.
ex: I met him last year, but haven't seen him since.
A short/long time since

s.def: from (time)
From: referring to a period of time ending in the present and defining it by the point in time at which it started, or the period in which its starting point occurred.
ex: I'd known her only since the previous year, so from/since the moment we got married we’ve quarrelled.
I'd been working since six o’clock, and I was getting tired.
Since the 1980s, computers have had increasing roles in all aspects of human life—including an involvement in criminal acts.

s.def: From the time that.
ex: I have loved you since I first met you.
I've known her since I've lived in her street, but I've not seen her out of the house since her husband died.
Since leaving school, I've completely changed.

s.def: Because.
ex: Since you didn't call, we left without you.

s.def: When or that.

ety: From Middle French sincere, from Latin sincerus (“genuine”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together”) (whence English sam) + *ḱer- (“grow”) (whence Latin Ceres, the goddess of harvest, etymon of cereal). Not from sine (“without”) + cera (“wax”), which is a folk etymology; see Wikipedia page.

s.def: Genuine, honest, and free from pretense or deceit; heartfelt.
ex: I believe he is sincere in his offer to help.
Tumid blustering, with more or less of sincerity, which need not be entirely sincere, yet the sincerer the better, is like to go far.
My sincerest apologies to Brother Ron Smith in the December ish.

s.def: Meant truly or earnestly.
ex: She gave it a sincere if misguided effort.

s.def: Clean; pure.

ety: From sincere + -ly, from Latin sincērus (“pure, clean, sound”).

s.def: In a sincere or earnest manner; honestly.
ex: I sincerely hope they make it home safely.

s.def: A conventional formula for ending a letter, used when the salutation addresses the person for whom the letter is intended by his or her name.
ex: Please consider the proposal carefully and let me know what you decide. Sincerely, Fred

ety: From Middle English sinceritie, from Old French sincerité and Medieval Latin sincēritās; both from Latin sincēritās, from sincērus + -tās. Equivalent to sincere + -ity.

s.def: The quality or state of being sincere.
ex: I protest, in the sincerity of love.
If the shew of any thing be good for any thing, I am sure sincerity is better

ety: Borrowed from Latin sinciput (“half a head”; “smoked hog’s cheek or half-jowl”; (transferred senses): “brain”, “head”), whence also the French sinciput.

s.def: The front part of the head or skull (as contradistinct from occiput).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sinos Proto-Italic *sinus Latin sinusbor. English sine Borrowed from Latin sinus (“curve, bend; bosom”), a translation of Arabic جَيْب (jayb, “bosom”), a misidentification of the notation جيب (j-y-b), written without vowel diacritics, standing for Arabic جِيبَ (jība, “sine”), in turn from Sanskrit ज्या (jyā, “sine, chord, bowstring”) through the similar Sanskrit जीव (jīva, “sine, chord, life, existence”). Doublet of sinus.

s.def: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side opposite an angle to the length of the hypotenuse.

ety: Borrowed from Latin [condiciō] sine quā nōn (“[condition] without which not”), an expression which originated in the works of Boethius as a translation of some Aristotelian expression (perhaps Ancient Greek οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ (hoû ouk áneu); compare also Modern Greek εκ των ων ουκ άνευ (ek ton on ouk ánef) / Katharevousa ἐκ τῶν ὧν οὐκ ἄνευ (ek tón ón ouk ánef)), and was later popularized by scholastics.

s.def: An essential or indispensable element, condition, or ingredient.
ex: Near-synonyms: dealbreaker, necessary condition
Literature, instead of being an accessory, is the fundamental sine qua non of complete living.

ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin sine cūrā (literally “without care”), ellipsis of beneficium sine cūrā (“benefice without cure [of souls, i.e. the office of a curate]”), formed from Medieval Latin sine (“without”) + cūrā (“care, charge, cure”).

s.def: A position that requires little to no work, or easy work, but still gives an ample payment; a cushy job.
ex: Miss Briggs was not formally dismissed, but her place as companion was a sinecure and a derision […]
A lucrative sinecure in the Excise was bestowed on Ferguson.

s.def: An ecclesiastical benefice without the care of souls.
Requiring no work for an ample reward.
ex: By the act of union (1800), the offices of Irish secretary, a sinecure post, and lord lieutenant's secretary were combined.

s.def: Having the appearance of functionality without being of any actual use or purpose.
To put or place in a sinecure.

ety: From Middle English synwe, synewe (“tendon; ligament or other connective tissue; muscle; nerve; leaf vein”), from Old English sinu (“tendon, sinew; nerve”), from Proto-West Germanic *sinu, from Proto-Germanic *sinwō, from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon”), from *(s)neh₁- (“to twist (threads), spin, weave”). s.def: A cord or tendon of the body.
A cord or string, particularly (music) as of a musical instrument.
Muscular power, muscle; nerve, nervous energy; vigor, vigorous strength.
That which gives strength or in which strength consists; a supporting factor or member; mainstay.
ex: Good company and good discourse are the very sinews of virtue.

s.def: A nerve.
To knit together or make strong with, or as if with, sinews.

ety: Inherited from Middle English synwy, synewy, synowy (“tendonous”); equivalent to sinew + -y.

s.def: Tough; having strong sinews.

Possessing physical strength and weight; rugged and powerful.

Hawat put a sinewy finger beside his eye.

ety: From Middle English synful, senful, sunful, from Old English synful (“sinful, guilty, wicked, corrupt”), equivalent to sin + -ful. Compare Dutch zondevol (“sinful”), German sündevoll (“sinful”), Danish syndefuld (“sinful”), Swedish syndfull (“sinful”), Icelandic syndfullur (“sinful”).

Constituting a sin; morally or religiously wrong; wicked; evil.
decadent (luxuriously self-indulgent)

ety: From Middle English singen, from Old English singan (“to sing”), from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to recite, sing”). ex: "I really want to sing in the school choir," said Vera.

s.def: To perform a vocal part in a musical composition, regardless of technique.
To express audibly by means of a harmonious vocalization.
ex: sing a lullaby

s.def: To soothe with singing.

a singing kettle

ety: From Singapore (“island and city-state in Southeast Asia”) + -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming agent nouns).

ex: I am a Singaporean, and I lived on the island for 20 years before coming to the United States for my college education.

ety: From Middle English sengen, from Old English senġan, sænċġan (“to singe, burn slightly, scorch, afflict”), from Proto-West Germanic *sangijan (“to burn, torch”), from Proto-Indo-European *senk- (“to burn”). To remove the hair or down from (a plucked chicken, etc.) by passing it over a flame.
A burning of the surface; a slight burn.
Obsolete form of sing.

ety: Inherited from Middle English synger, syngere, singere, singare, equivalent to sing + -er. Cognate with Scots singar, Saterland Frisian Sjunger, West Frisian sjonger, German Low German Singer. ety: From Middle English susterhede; equivalent to sister + -hood (with a modification in the suffix).

ex: After a long day of walking, it was good just to sit and relax.

ex: The dishes are still sitting on the table!

s.def: To assume a low or sunken position.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin situātus, past participle of Medieval Latin situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).

ety: From Middle English skinny (“resembling skin”), equivalent to skin + -y. The meaning associated with lack of fat or muscle possibly derives from the phrase skin and bones; the meaning associated with nudity refers to the exposed skin.

ex: Her recent weight loss has made her look rather skinny than slender

s.def: Of food or a beverage, having reduced fat or calories.
ex: skinny flat white
...into the skinny chocolate milk?
“All right,” said Katz, who, waiting on his skinny milk latte, turned to snap his fingers at the only waiter in the room.

s.def: Naked; nude (chiefly used in the phrase skinny dipping).
ex: Let's take our clothes oft" and go swimming skinny.
We never swam skinny in the river like the hippy kids on the farm across the railway tracks.
When I went in again, the desirable alien was in bed with eyelids closed [...], obviously sleeping skinny, to employ her own term for it.

s.def: Tight-fitting.
ex: skinny jeans

s.def: Synonym of thin (“type of shot where the ball is struck by the bottom part of the club head”).
The details or facts; especially, those obtained by gossip or rumor.
ex: She called to get the skinny on the latest goings-on in the club.

s.def: A state of nakedness; nudity.
ex: Again, she appears nude whilst dipping in the skinny, but this time, instead of being eaten by a shark or a bear, she encounters a Japanese submarine
"Nobody would bother peeking these days," she said ruefully, "in bathing suits or in the skinny."

s.def: A low-fat serving of coffee.
A skinny being.
An obstacle for a horse to jump over, consisting of a narrow fence.

ety: From skin + tight.

s.def: Conforming tightly to the body, snug against the skin.
ex: He'd have to stow the Gun somewhere; no place to conceal it in the skintight bodysuit.
I'mma get your heart racing / In my skin-tight jeans / Be your teenage dream tonight

ety: From Middle English skippen, skyppen, of North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skupjaną, perhaps related to *skeubaną (“to drive, push”), iterative *skuppōną (“to push/move repeatedly, skip”), from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ- (“to push, throw, shake”). Related to Icelandic skopa (“to take a run”), Old Swedish skuppa (“to skip”), modern dialectal Swedish skopa, skimpa (“to skip, leap”), and English shove. See also dialectal English skimp (“to mock”) (Etymology 1), considered by…

s.def: To move by hopping on alternate feet.
ex: She will skip from one end of the sidewalk to the other.

s.def: To disregard, miss or omit part of a continuation (some item or stage).
ex: My heart will skip a beat.
He skipped the second question and moved on.
I will read most of the book, but skip the first chapter because the video covered it.

s.def: Not to attend (some event, especially a class or a meeting).
ex: Yeah, I really should go to the quarterly meeting but I think I'm going to skip it.

s.def: To leap about lightly.
ex: So she drew her mother away skipping, dancing, and frisking fantastically.

s.def: To skim, ricochet or bounce over a surface.
ex: The rock will skip across the pond.

s.def: To throw (something), making it skim, ricochet, or bounce over a surface.
ex: I bet I can skip this rock to the other side of the pond.

s.def: To leave, especially in a sudden and covert manner.
ex: to skip the country
a customer who skipped town without paying her hotel bill
I see ya' little speed boat head up our coast She really want to skip town Get back off me, beast off me Get back you flea-infested mongrel

s.def: To leap lightly over.
ex: to skip the rope

s.def: To jump rope.
ex: The girls were skipping in the playground.

s.def: To cause the stylus to jump back to the previous loop of the record's groove, continuously repeating that part of the sound, as a result of excessive scratching or wear. (of a phonograph record)

ety: From skip (verb) + Jack.

s.def: Any of several not closely related fish.
An upstart.
ex: Tag-rag or other, hogen mogen, vanden, skip-jacks or chouses.

s.def: An elaterid; a click beetle.
A shallow sailboat with a rectilinear or V-shaped cross section.
A medium-sized perciform fish of species Katsuwonus pelamis, in the tuna family.

ety: From Middle English skippere, skyppere, scippere, borrowed from Middle Dutch scipper, schipper, from Old Dutch *skipāri, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz. Piecewise doublet of shipper, from ship + -er.

s.def: The master of a ship.
A coach, director, or other leader.
The captain of a sports team such as football, cricket, rugby or curling.
ex: But even the return of skipper Steven Gerrard from a six-week injury layoff could not inspire Liverpool

s.def: Synonym of detective sergeant, especially as a term of direct address.
To captain a ship or a sports team.
ex: Tourist subs, which could once be skippered by anyone with a U.S. Coast Guard captain’s license

s.def: Agent noun of skip: one who skips.
A person who skips, or fails to attend class.
One who jumps rope.
Any of various butterflies of the families Hesperiidae and its subfamily Megathyminae, having a hairy mothlike body, hooked tips on the antennae, and a darting flight pattern.
ex: Blue skippers in sunny hours ope and shut Where wormwood and grunsel flowers by the cart ruts […]

s.def: Any of several marine fishes that often leap above water, especially Cololabis saira (Pacific saury) and Sprattus sprattus (European sprat).

ety: Compare Icelandic skip, English skipper. See ship.

s.def: A small boat; a skiff.
ex: Vpon the banck they sitting did espy / A daintie damzell, dressing of her heare, / By whom a litle skippet floting did appeare

s.def: A small, round box used for keeping documents and seals or for covering seals attached to documents
An item for play or physical exercise consisting of a length of rope with a handle attached to each end, intended to be swung over and under a person jumping in a continual rhythm.

ety: Originally from Scots and Northern English dialects (as a verb), probably of Old Norse origin; ultimately imitative.

s.def: To make a shrill sound, as of bagpipes.
ex: Drums began to thump in a variety of rhythms. The flautists were not sure what to play. The shawm began to skirl.

s.def: A shrill sound, as of bagpipes.
ex: To a resounding wail headed by the King-Kong skirl, all gangs joined in hauling in the net.

s.def: A blast (of wind-blown snow or rain); a gust (especially if accompanied by snow or rain, or a shill or whistling sound).
ex: Skirls of snow swept over the pavements, and in the roadway the tracks of cars were lined with brownish slush.
... skirls of snow that further obscured her vision and stung her cheeks.
Skirls of snow are swirling across the ice of Indian Lake, meaning things are about to pick up again.

s.def: Alternative form of shirl.

ety: From Middle English skirmish (as a verb), from Old French escarmouche (“skirmish”), from Italian scaramuccia, earlier schermugio. Doublet of escarmouche, Scaramouche, and Scaramucci.

s.def: A brief battle between small groups, usually part of a longer or larger battle or war.
Any minor dispute.
ex: Three people were arrested after a skirmish in a bar.
Fires which have heretofore been one‐alarm skirmishes are now multialarm small wars.

s.def: A type of outdoor military style game using paintball or similar weapons.
To engage in a minor battle or dispute.

ety: From Dutch suikerwortel (literally “sugar-root”).

s.def: An umbelliferous plant (Sium sisarum), cultivated for its sweet edible tuberous roots.
ex: Nicolas Venette, French physician, refers to skirret, a plant that has esculent tubers, for its high aphrodisiac potential.

s.def: A straight-line marking tool consisting of a line of thread wrapped around a holder.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der.? Proto-Germanic *skertaną Proto-Germanic *skurtaz Proto-Germanic *skurtijǭ Old Norse skyrtabor. Middle English skyrte English skirt From Middle English scyrt, skirt, skyrte, skyrthe, skyrtte, from Old Norse skyrta, from Proto-Germanic *skurtijǭ (“apron; skirt”), from *skurtaz (“short; deficient”), from *skertaną (“to cut off”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off; to divide”). Doublet of shirt. Cognates Cognate with Yola shoorth, skoort…

s.def: A separate article of clothing, usually worn by women and girls, that hangs from the waist and covers the lower torso and part of the legs.
A similar part of a dress or robe, etc., that hangs below the waist.
A loose edging to any part of a dress.
A petticoat.
A woman.
ex: But I tell ya, I can't help but like a guy who wants to rescue some skirt he fell for.

s.def: Women collectively, in a sexual context.
Sexual intercourse with a woman.
A border; edge; margin; extreme part of anything.
ex: here in the skirts of the forest, like fringe upon a petticoat.

s.def: A diaphragm, or midriff.
To be on or form the border of.
ex: The plain was skirted by rows of trees.

ety: From skirt + board.

s.def: Synonym of skirting board.
A panel, normally made of wood, between the floor and the interior wall of a structure, or placed in a position that is subject to repeated knocks.

ety: Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Old Norse skjúta (“to shoot, dart, move quickly”), variant of skjóta. Compare flytja (“to move”). Alternately, perhaps a back-formation from skittish, which in turn may derive from Old Norse or another North Germanic language.

s.def: A short comic performance done by amateurs.
A jeer or sally; a brief satire.
ex: That is a mere skit compared with this strange performance.

s.def: A wanton girl; a wench.
A short, sharp shower (of rain).
ex: ... there come on a 'skit' of rain, and I made for one of his barns for shelter.

s.def: Diarrhea, in livestock; the scour.
ex: The Cause and Nature of the Skit, or Scour, of Sheep and Lambs.
... lambs, and on the appearance of the skit or scour, the necessity for a change of food is indicated.

s.def: To make fun of.
To caper; to skip or run lightly and quickly.
ex: Yet soon's she hears me mention Muirland Willie, / She skits an' flings like ony towmont filly- […]
I could feel her eyes skitting over to me after she said something that might have shocked me - but I stayed quiet.

ety: Possibly a frequentative of skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction”) (Scotland, Northern England). The noun is derived from the verb.

s.def: To move hurriedly or as by bouncing or twitching; to scamper, to scurry; to scuttle.
ex: I opened the cabinet and a number of cockroaches went skittering off into the darkness.
Some kinds of ducks in lighting strike the water with their tails first, and skitter along the surface for a few feet before settling down.

s.def: To make a scratching or scuttling noise while, or as if, skittering.
To move or pass (something) over a surface quickly so that it touches only at intervals; to skip, to skite.
A skittering movement.
ex: A skitter of activity. A skitter of gooseflesh.

s.def: To cause to have diarrhea.
To suffer from a bout of diarrhea; to produce thin excrement.
Often skitters: the condition of suffering from diarrhea; thin excrement.
ex: I can't give it my immediate attention, as the cow has the skitter (diarrhoea) and I'm waiting on the Vit (vet).

ety: Probably from skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction (Scotland, Northern England)”) + -ish; compare skitter.

s.def: Easily scared or startled; timid.
ex: The dog likes people he knows, but he is skittish around strangers.

s.def: Wanton; changeable; fickle.
ex: How some men creep in skittish fortune’s hall, Whiles others play the idiots in her eyes!

s.def: Difficult to manage; tricky.

ety: Probably from French esquiver (“slink away”), from Middle French esquiver (“to escape”), from Spanish esquivar (“to avoid, reject, elude”), from esquivo (“contemptuous, loathsome”), itself from Old French eschiver, of East Germanic origin, from Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌷𐍃 (*skiuhs, “afraid, barefaced”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“afraid, frightened”). s.def: To avoid one's lessons or work (chiefly at school or university); shirk.

ex: Mr Smith's history classes are a total skive.

s.def: An act of avoiding lessons or work.
ex: Another school skive! I only realised this when my dentist's receptionist told me to expect a fair wait till I could be seen.

s.def: A rotating iron disk coated with oil and diamond dust used to polish the facets of a diamond.
ex: This accident sometimes occasions a flaw in the diamond, and always damages the skive, by tearing up its surface.

ex: There would be no need for medial heel skive and the heel cup can be of normal depth.

ex: When two pieces of leather have to be overlapped they must be suitably skived.

A skewer.

To skewer, impale.

A close-fitting, long-sleeved T-shirt with a rolled collar.

I put my wetsuit and skivvy on a tree to dry, and laid out my other gear on some grass.

North Macedonia, especially in the Greek media.

s.def: Dishonest, underhanded, or unscrupulous activities or behaviour.
ex: Mr. BURNS wanted to hear from the gentleman from Logan on his amendment, to see whether there was any "sculduggery" about it.

ety: From Middle English sculke, skulke, sculken, of North Germanic origin; compare Danish skulke (“shirk”), Swedish skolka (“play truant”).

ex: "I shall do my duty, Mr. Jackson," replied Newton, "and fear no consequences." / "Indeed! you saw how I settled a skulk just now;—beware of his fate!"

A skulk of fox padded daintily over a stream-slashed meadow, and a herd of deer like iron ornaments stood stock still in their winter pelage.

s.def: A group of people seen as being fox-like (e.g. cunning, dishonest, or having nefarious plans).
ex: […] a skulk of priests flapped out of the Church of San Geronimo, and women kneeling at novena put away their beads […]

ex: Discover’d and defeated of your Prey, You sculk’d behind the Fence, and sneak’d away.

ex: The residue like vnto the bare arssed rebels sculked to and fro; but in the end, they and the others were all dispersed, & durst not to appeare.

s.def: To avoid an obligation or responsibility.

The mind or brain.

The crown of the headpiece in armour.
A shallow bow-handled basket.
The head or master of a college.
To hit in the head with a fist, a weapon, or a thrown object.
To strike the top of (the ball).
ex: Monte swung so hard at the next ball that he skulled it straight right, into the pond: 8 in, 9 out.

ex: She nearly skulled the next drink and, despite feeling a little woozy, she felt a lot better.
He skulled his drink, set the glass down, then grabbed the bottle and ambled over to the other couch.

A yarmulke-like hat.
The calvaria, the top part of the skull, covering the cranial cavity containing the brain.

A torture device for compressing the skull.

A despicable person.
ex: In fact, the term he applied to this species of human being was "skunk," and he used it freely.

s.def: Anything very bad; a stinker.

s.def: A walkover victory in sports or board games, as when the opposing side is unable to score.
A win by thirty or more points. (A double skunk is sixty or more, a triple skunk ninety or more.)
To spray someone with a strong-smelling liquid.
ex: Two girls help me to my feet, hug me, skunking me with perfume.

s.def: To defeat so badly as to prevent any opposing points.
ex: I skunked him at cards.

To go bad, to spoil.

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English sky (“sky; cloud; mist”), also spelled ski, skie, [and other forms], from Old Norse ský (“cloud”), from Proto-Germanic *skiwją (“cloud; sky”), from *skiwô (“cloud; cloud cover, haze; sky”) (whence Old English sċēo (“cloud”) and Middle English skew (“air; sky; (rare) cloud”)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover; to conceal, hide”). ex: I lay back under a warm Texas sky.

All in a hot and copper sky / The bloody sun at noon, / Right up above the mast did stand, / No bigger than the moon.

In an art gallery: the upper rows of pictures that cannot easily be seen; also, the place where such pictures are hung.
A cloud.
To drink (a beverage) from a container without one's lips touching the container.
To hang (a picture on exhibition) near the top of a wall, where it cannot easily be seen; (by extension) to put (something) in an undesirable place.

Of a vibrant light blue colour, like that of the sky on a fine day.

A region of flat, thin ice allowing a submarine to surface.

ety: From sky + -wards.

ety: From sky + way.

ety: Late 18th century dialectal English snob (“cobbler”), of unknown origin. ety: From Middle English snod, from Old English snōd (“headdress, fillet, snood”), from Proto-West Germanic *snōdu, from Proto-Germanic *snōdō (“rope, string”), from Proto-Indo-European *snoh₁téh₂ (“yarn, thread”), from *sneh₁(i)- (“to twist, wind, weave, plait”). Cognate with Scots snuid (“snood”), Swedish snod, snodd (“twist, twine”). Compare also Old Saxon snōva (“necklace”), Old Norse snúa (“to turn, twist”), snúðr (“a twist, twirl”), English needle.

s.def: A band or ribbon for keeping the hair in place, including the hair-band formerly worn in Scotland and northern England by young unmarried women.
ex: “Frida [...] tied her hair in the Grecian snood which her lover used to admire so.”

serious girls with their hair in snoods entered numbers into logbooks […]

s.def: The flap of erectile red skin on the beak of a male turkey.
A short line of horsehair, gut, monofilament, etc., by which a fishhook is attached to a longer (and usually heavier) line; a snell.
A piece of clothing to keep the neck warm; neckwarmer.
To keep the hair in place with a snood.

The situation where the cue ball is in such a position that the player cannot directly hit a legal ball with it.
ex: She put her opponent in a snooker.

ety: From Dutch snoepen (“to pry, eat in secret, sneak”) or maybe Old Norse snópa (“to idle about dismally”), or (“to use a blood found”). Related to Dutch and Low German snappen (“to bite, seize”), Dutch snavel (“beak, bill, pecker, neb”), German Schnabel (“beak, bill, mouth”). More at snap.

ex: If I had not snooped on her, I wouldn't have found out that she lied about her degree.

s.def: To steal.
ex: 'What on earth do Coker and his parcel of tuck matter to us? You're not thinking of snooping his tuck, I suppose, like Bunter.'

s.def: The act of snooping.
One who snoops.
ex: Be careful what you say around Gene because he's the bosses' snoop.

s.def: A private detective.

s.def: To snoop.

s.def: Charlie Brown's pet beagle in the comic strip Peanuts, by Charles M. Schulz; often representing doggish soulfulness.
ex: My daughter calls these "Snoopy eyes" after the childlike presentation of the beagle in Schulz's cartoon Peanuts.
Mary Mann, another sophomore, sits on the roof of a red dog house, giving her most enigmatic Snoopy look.
Being excessive or overzealous only gives the patient a surprised “Snoopy” look.

ety: From Scots snoot, snout (“snout”), from Middle English snowte, from Middle Dutch snute; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *snūt, from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz. Doublet of snout.

s.def: An elitist or snobbish person.
ex: The sidecars— sneer if you will, you purists and gastronomic snoots— at Perino's in Wilshire in Los Angeles.

s.def: A language pedant or snob; one who practices linguistic elitism.
ex: There are lots of epithets for people like this—Grammar Nazis, Usage Nerds, Syntax Snobs, the Language Police. The term I was raised with is SNOOT.

s.def: A nose or snout.
Snout; especially of a dog ("doggo"), cat ("catto"), or snake ("snek").
A cylindrical or conical attachment used on a spotlight to restrict spill light.
To behave disdainfully toward someone.
To apply a snoot attachment to (a light).

ety: Unknown, attested since 18th century. Compare Dutch snoezelen (“to snooze”) or Swedish snusa (“to snore lightly”). Compare also Ancient Greek νυστάζω (nustázō, “to doze, drowse”) and Russian сон (son, “sleep, dream”).

s.def: To sleep, especially briefly; to nap, doze.
ex: The boss caught him snoozing at his desk.

s.def: A brief period of sleep; a nap.
ex: The cat enjoys taking a snooze on a sunny windowsill.

s.def: The snooze button on an alarm clock.
Something boring.
ex: The whole movie was a snooze.

ety: From Middle English snoren, fnoren (“to snore loudly; snort”), from Middle English snore, *fnore (“snore; snort”, noun), from Old English fnora (“snort; sneezing”), from Proto-Germanic *fnuzô, from Proto-Indo-European *pnew- (“to breathe; snort; sneeze”). Compare also Proto-West Germanic *snarkōn, Middle Low German snorren (“to drone”), Dutch snorren (“to hum, purr”). The change fn → sn in this word is regular, seen also in sneeze, from Middle English fnesen (see sneeze for more).

s.def: To breathe during sleep with harsh, snorting noises caused by vibration of the soft palate.
The act of snoring, and the noise produced.
An extremely boring person or event.

ety: Borrowed from German Schnorchel (“(submarine) snorkel”), related to schnarchen (“to snore”). She used a snorkel to breathe while swimming underwater.

s.def: A retractable tube fitted in diesel-engine submarines to allow sufficient ventilation that the engines may be used at periscope depth.
A snorkel parka.
To use a snorkel.
ex: We spent the afternoon snorkeling in the clear blue waters.

ety: From Middle English snorten, from earlier fnorten, from Old English *fnorettan, related to Middle English snoren, fnoren, from Old English fnora. See snore and sneeze for more on the change from fn- to sn-.

s.def: The sound made by exhaling or inhaling roughly through the nose.
A dose of snuff or other drug to be snorted.
A consumed portion of an alcoholic drink.

To express or force out by snorting.
ex: He snorted a derisory reply and turned on his heel.

ex: Snow is white, / And lieth in the dike. And every man lets it lye.

an electromagnetic storm on the photosphere of the Sun

ety: Borrowed from Latin sōlārium (“sundial, place for enjoying sunlight”), from sōl (“sun”) + -ārium (“-arium: indicating related places or devices”).

ex: My brother kept a health-lift a few years ago... and then he had a blue-glass solarium.

An earthen structure constructed by certain ants for the purpose of brood incubation.

[…] lifting his eyes from the solarium set under the aplustre for reference in keeping the course...

ety: From solar + -ize.

Intangible or emotional compensation.

ety: From Middle English souder, soudere, soudur (noun), from Old French soldure, soudeure (noun), from Old French souder, solder (“to solder”, verb) (> Middle English souden (“to solder”)), from Latin solidāre (“make solid”).

ety: Inherited from Middle English soudeour, from Old French soudier or soudeour (“mercenary”), from Medieval Latin soldarius (“soldier (one having pay)”), from Late Latin solidus, a type of coin. ety: From Middle English sole, soule, from Old French sol, soul (“alone”), from Latin sōlus (“alone, single, solitary, lonely”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (reflexive pronoun). ety: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake, excite, cite, to put in motion”).

ety: From Middle English solicitude, from Old French sollicitude, from Latin sollicitūdō (“anxiety”), from sollicitus, solicitus (“anxious, solicitous”). See solicitous.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-der. Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s Proto-Italic *soliðos Latin solidusder. Old French solidebor. Living or being alone; solitary.

ety: Borrowed from Italian solo, from Latin sōlus, probably related to se (“himself”).
