ety: Borrowed from Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of spatha (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”). Doublet of spauld; compare spatha and spathe.

s.def: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flat surface attached to a long handle, used for turning, lifting, or stirring food.
A palette knife.
A kitchen utensil consisting of a flexible surface attached to a long handle, used for scraping the sides of bowls.
A thin hand tool, often made of nickel, for handling chemicals or other materials, when weighing, etc.
A tongue depressor.
A croupier's tool for turning up cards in a casino.
ex: The croupier delicately faced her other two cards with the tip of his spatula. A four! She had lost!

s.def: A sclerotized, T-shaped plate in the prothorax of larvae of flies belonging to family Cecidomyiidae, the gall midges.
To lift with or as if with a spatula.
ex: A book on Pastels referes [sic] to a rough Modeling paste to be spatulaed over cotton duck.
So if you get road-pizzaed, should you have to pay in order to get yourself spatulaed off of the street?
Eddie spatulaed the patty onto a bun and extracted tomatoes, lettuce, and sliced pickles from a Tupperware.

s.def: To strike with a spatula.
ex: I haven't spatulaed anyone in ages...

s.def: Shaped like a spatula; having a rounded, flattened extremity.
ex: For a moment he was sunk in thought, coiling (so it seemed) and uncoiling his long spatulate fingers.

s.def: Of a leaf: having a broad, flat end and tapering into a narrower base.
To treat or mix with a spatula.
To incise the end of (a pliable cylindrical structure) such that the cut end can be splayed apart and flattened.

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English spavein, spaveine (“swelling on horse’s leg causing lameness; disease causing lameness in horses”), from Old French espavain, a variant of esparvain, esprevain, esprevin (modern French éparvin, épervin). The further etymology is unknown; one suggestion is that it is from Frankish *sparwan (“sparrow”), though this is seen as quite tenuous. The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: A similar disease causing a person's leg to be lame.

A bony swelling which develops in a horse's leg where the shank and splint bone meet, caused by inflammation of the cartilage connecting those bones; also, a similar swelling caused by inflammation of the hock bones.
ex: Mr. Field had seen the same horses brought to his forge from day to day, and year to year, with large spavins, yet continuing perfectly sound.

s.def: A disease of horses caused by this bony swelling (etymology 1, noun sense 1.1).

ety: Recorded since 1413; from Middle English spawnen, from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Old French espandre, from Latin expandere (“stretch out; spread out”, verb). Doublet of expand. Compare also Middle English spalden, spolden, spawden (“to cut open (a fish)”).

s.def: To produce or deposit (eggs) in water.
ex: A frog spawns thousands of tadpoles every year.

s.def: To generate, bring into being, especially nonmammalian beings in very large numbers.
To bring forth in general.
ex: The web server spawns a new process to handle each client's request.

s.def: To deposit (numerous) eggs in water.
ex: Alewives are anadromous fish: Born in freshwater, they spend their lives in the ocean, returning annually to their birthplaces to spawn.

s.def: To appear, or cause (something or someone) to appear, spontaneously in a game world at a particular place and time.
ex: We put down torches to stop creepers from spawning.

s.def: The numerous eggs of an aquatic organism.
any germ or seed, even a figurative source; offspring
To induce (aquatic organisms) to spawn.
To plant with fungal spawn.
To reproduce, especially in large numbers.

ety: From Middle English spayen, spaien, from the Anglo-Norman espeier, equivalent to the Old French espeer (“to cut with a sword”), from espee (“sword”), whence the Modern French épée.

s.def: To destroy or remove the ovaries or uterus (of a female animal) to prevent pregnancy.
ex: We’re having our cat spayed as we don’t want her having kittens.

s.def: The act of spaying an animal.
ex: I was queasy about my first spay of a far-gone feral and left it up to my vet.

s.def: Rare form of spayard.
Alternative form of spae (to foretell or divine)

ety: From Middle English speke, speken (“to speak”), from Old English specan (“to speak”). This is usually taken to be an irregular alteration of earlier sprecan, spreocan (“to speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *sprekan, from Proto-Germanic *sprekaną (“to speak, make a sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *spreg- (“to make a sound, utter, speak”). Finding this proposed loss of r from the stable cluster spr unparalleled, Hill instead sets up a different root, Proto-West Germanic *spekan (“to negotiate”)…

s.def: To communicate with one's voice, to say words out loud.
ex: I was so surprised I couldn't speak.
You're speaking too fast.

s.def: To communicate or converse by some means other than orally, such as writing or facial expressions.
ex: He spoke of it in his diary.
Speak to me only with your eyes.
Actions speak louder than words.

s.def: To have a conversation.
ex: It's been ages since we've spoken.

s.def: To deliver a message to a group; to deliver a speech.
ex: This evening I shall speak on the topic of correct English usage.

s.def: To be able to communicate in a language.
ex: He speaks Mandarin fluently.

s.def: To utter.
ex: I was so surprised that I couldn't speak a word.

s.def: To communicate (some fact or feeling); to bespeak, to indicate.
ex: Their behaviour to each other speaks the most cordial confidence and happiness.
There he sat, his very indifference speaking a nature in which there lurked no civilized hypocrisies and bland deceits.

s.def: To understand (as though it were a language).
ex: Sorry, I don't speak idiot.
So you can program in C. But do you speak C++?

s.def: To produce a sound; to sound.
ex: Make all our trumpets speak.

s.def: Of a bird, to be able to vocally reproduce words or phrases from a human language.
ex: Miles tremblingly confessed that it had, but to no purpose; a parrot being able to speak better in three weeks than a brazen head.

ety: Ellipsis of speak of the devil and he shall appear, which can be traced back to “talk of the Devil, and he’s presently at your elbow”, attested in 1666. The idea behind this (namely, that mentioning a dangerous creature may cause it to appear) is found in many cultures around the world; see taboo avoidance.

s.def: An expression sometimes used when a person mentioned in the current conversation happens to arrive on the scene.
ex: A: You know who would appreciate this? Tom. B: Speak of the devil! Look who just walked in!

ety: Deverbal from speak easy (= speak quietly [interj.]); for the history, see Wikipedia at speakeasy § Etymology.

s.def: An illegal saloon or tavern, especially one operated during the American Prohibition period in the 1920s.
ex: Many of the legitimate nightclubs of today sprang like legalized phoenixes from the still-hot ashes of the speakeasies of prohibition days.

Proto-Germanic *sprekaną Proto-West Germanic *sprekan Old English sprecan Old English specan Middle English speken Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere Middle English spekere, speker English speaker From Middle English speker, spekere, an alteration (with change of suffix) of Old English s…

s.def: One who speaks.
ex: There were three different speakers, but I couldn't make out their accents.

s.def: Loudspeaker.
ex: She lost her hearing after standing too close to the speaker at the festival.

s.def: One who makes a speech to an audience.
ex: Near-synonyms: orator, presenter, announcer
hired speaker; motivational speaker
The company hired a motivational speaker to boost morale.

s.def: Speakerphone.
ex: you're on speaker
I'm gonna put you on speaker now

s.def: The chair or presiding officer of certain legislative bodies, such as the U.K. House of Commons or the U.S. House of Representatives.
A book containing passages of text for use in speeches.
The producer of a given utterance, whether speech or text.
A key on a woodwind instrument of the clarinet family (compare octave key on other instruments) which induces the instrument to overblow.
A wooden pole or spike used by hedgers to carry loads on their shoulders. Possibly Dorset dialect.
ex: With a speäker, or stake, he tossed the outlying scraps of fuel on the into the conflagration.

ety: From Middle English spekinge, spekynge, spekinde, spekende, spekande, spekand, from Old English specende, sprecende (“speaking”), from Proto-Germanic *sprekandz (“speaking”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *sprekaną (“to speak”). Equivalent to speak + -ing. Cognate with Scots speikand, speikin (“speaking”), Saterland Frisian spreekend (“speaking”), West Frisian sprekkend (“speaking”), Dutch sprekend (“speaking”), German Low German sprekend (“speaking”), German sprechend (“speaking”).

s.def: Used in speaking.
ex: one's normal speaking voice

s.def: Expressive; eloquent.
ex: The sight was more speaking than any speech could be.
There was no reply, save on the speaking countenance.

s.def: Involving speaking.
ex: It was her first speaking part: she screamed.

s.def: Having the ability of speech.
ex: speaking parrot; speaking clock

s.def: One's ability to communicate vocally in a given language.
ex: I can read and understand most texts in German, but my speaking is awful.

s.def: The act of communicating vocally.
ex: Sometimes, a brawl would erupt, as a result, but, in general, public speakings were peaceful events and essential ingredients for election to office.

s.def: A speaking exercise or exam.
An oral recitation of e.g. a story.
present participle and gerund of speak
ex: Who is that speaking? -Hi. This is José García (speaking).

s.def: Indication that the person requested is the same as the one who is currently speaking.
Speaking of which; relatedly, used to introduce a related topic.
ex: “Speaking of by the way: nice car. I mean that.”
No more songs. This is a restaurant, for Christ’s sake, and speaking of, can somebody tell me where the hell is that veal?
—[…] Speaking of by the way we should go shopping on Saturday or Sunday because Penney’s is having a sale at Fair Oaks.

ety: From Middle English spere, sperre, spear, from Old English spere, from Proto-West Germanic *speru, from Proto-Germanic *speru, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-. Cognates See also West Frisian spear, Dutch speer, German Speer, Old Norse spjǫr, *sparrô, Middle Dutch sparre (“rafter”), Old Norse sparri (“spar, rafter”), sperra (“rafter, beam”); also Latin sparus (“short spear”), Albanian ferrë (“thorn, thornbush”).

s.def: A long stick with a sharp tip used as a weapon for throwing or thrusting, or anything used to make a thrusting motion.
A lance with barbed prongs, used by fishermen to retrieve fish.
To penetrate or strike with, or as if with, any long narrow object; to make a thrusting motion that catches an object on the tip of a long device.
A soldier armed with such a weapon; a spearman.
ex: Now toil'd the Bruce, the battle done , To use his conquest boldly won; And gave command for horse and spear To press the Southron's scatter'd rear
Two of the four spears came directly from Lady Margaret's staff. One was her great-nephew Maurice St John […].

s.def: An illegal maneuver using the end of a hockey stick to strike into another hockey player.
In professional wrestling, a running tackle in which the wrestler's shoulder is driven into the opponent's midsection.
A shoot, as of grass; a spire.
The feather of a horse.
The rod to which the bucket, or plunger, of a pump is attached; a pump rod.
A long, thin strip from a vegetable.
ex: asparagus and broccoli spears

ety: Etymology tree English spear Proto-Indo-European *péysks Proto-Germanic *fiskaz Proto-West Germanic *fisk Old English fisċ Middle English fisch English fish English spearfish From spear + fish.

s.def: Translations
Any of the genus Tetrapturus of marlins, a type of fish with the upper jaw elongated into a spearlike bill.
Any striped marlin (Kajikia audax)
Any quillback (Carpioides cyprinus
To attempt to catch a fish using a spear or spear gun.
ex: Bart, who incidentally has designed an excellent diaphragm‐type call for geese and turkeys, once spearfished commercially in the British West Indies.
A Bajau diver spearfishes in Sulawesi.

s.def: To fish for spearfish by any method.

ety: From Middle English spere-hed; equivalent to spear + head.

s.def: The pointed head, or end, of a spear.
Something or somebody leading or initiating an activity (such as an attack or campaign).
The leading military unit in an attack.
A player who initiates attacking moves.
To drive or campaign ardently for (an effort, project, etc.); to direct.
ex: He spearheaded the entire project from day one.
Newcastle have put themselves within touching distance after a fantastic run which has been spearheaded by the goals of Senegal striker Cisse.
George Monks spearheaded the project to solve this problem with a funicular, and work on the Lynton & Lynmouth Cliff Railway (L&LCR) began in 1887.

ety: Etymology tree English spear Proto-Indo-European *mon- Proto-Germanic *mann- Proto-West Germanic *mann Old English mann Middle English man Middle English -man English -man English spearman From spear + -man.

s.def: One who uses a spear; a soldier or warrior who fights with a spear; a person who hunts with a spear.
ex: The second Adigar is only entitled to twenty-four spearmen and fifteen whipcrackers.
He spoke : the brawny spearman let his cheek Bulge with the unswallow'd piece, and turning stared;
All around here the spearmen would hide, armed with those terrible shovel-balded spears that will kill a bullock at seventy yards.

ety: From spear (“sprout of a plant, spire”) + mint, so named due to its spiry blooms.

s.def: A herb of the mint family (Mentha spicata), commonly used in herb tea, candy and to treat mild stomach ache.

ety: From Middle English sperwort, sperewort, from Old English sperewyrt, i.e. spear + wort.

s.def: Any of various perennial herbaceous plants in the Ranunculus (buttercup) genus.

ety: From Middle English *special, especial, especiall, from Old French especial (whence also French spécial), from Latin speciālis (from speciēs). In this sense displaced native Old English synderlīċ. Doublet of especial.

s.def: Distinguished by a unique, particular, or unusual quality.
ex: a special episode of a television series
her special blend of spices

s.def: Of particular value or interest; dear; beloved.
ex: Everyone is special to someone.
his special friend of many years, Bill

s.def: Of or related to unconventional warfare.
ex: special forces, special operations

s.def: Appointed specifically to examine a single event or issue.
ex: For the few times the U.S. Supreme Court has to actually try a case, they will appoint a special master to do so.
After the Watergate break in, a special prosecutor was appointed.

s.def: Constituting or relating to a species.
ex: Having seven dark spots is a special property unique to Coccinella septempunctata.

s.def: Of or related to disabilities, especially learning or intellectual disabilities.
ex: special education, special needs
He goes to a special school.

s.def: Of, being, or pertaining to sexual intercourse or the genitals.
ex: The parents told the kids not to bother them during special time.
The girl said the man had tried to touch her special place.

s.def: Infused with a drug, especially marijuana; being an edible.
A reduction in consumer cost (usually for a limited time) for items or services rendered; the thing thus sold.
ex: We're running a special on turkey for Thanksgiving.
I didn't have much money, so I bought the special.

s.def: A meal offered only at a certain time by a restaurant, not as a standing fixture of the menu; often, one of a rotation of meals systematically offered for a lower price; also often a dish at a nondiscounted price that is seasonal or otherwise exciting or unusual.
ex: Today's dinner special is wild salmon, which we don't normally get a chance to offer.
The Tuesday lunch special is our tuna melt on rye.

s.def: Translations
Designation for types of administrative division in China, East Timor, and North Korea.
An effect that cannot be reasonably achieved by normal means, as for example by the digital manipulation of previously filmed footage.

ety: 2022, Calque of Russian специа́льная вое́нная опера́ция (speciálʹnaja vojénnaja operácija), a phrase used by Vladimir Putin upon launching an attack on Ukraine on 24 February 2022, when he said he had "decided to launch a special military operation."

s.def: A military campaign resembling a war; especially the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.
An autonomous region of Indonesia. Capital: Yogyakarta.

ety: Borrowed from French spécialiste, equivalent to special + -ist.

s.def: Specialised, involving detailed knowledge of a restricted topic.
Someone who is an expert in, or devoted to, some specific branch of study or research.
A player on a team who primarily employs one particular skill or takes one particular role.
A physician whose practice is limited to a particular branch of medicine or surgery.
ex: Dr. Robert Leroy Hutton, a retired specialist in internal medicine and a well‐known diagnostician, died yesterday here.
Most Americans mistakenly believe that they must see specialists for almost every medical problem.

s.def: An organism that is specialized for a particular environment.
ex: The tree Lepidothamnus laxifolius is a high alpine specialist found in high-altitude bog communities and in scrub.

s.def: Any of several non-commissioned ranks corresponding to that of corporal.
A stenotopic species.
A sixth-former at Eton College.

ety: From special + -ity, from Middle French spécialité, from Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.

s.def: UK standard form of specialty.
ex: They cook well overall, but their true speciality is pasta.

ety: Etymology tree Middle English especial English special Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English specialize From special + -ize.

s.def: To make distinct or separate from what is common
ex: Our Sauiour specialising and nominating the places in which these false prophets should teach his presence to be.

s.def: To become distinct or separate from what is common, particularly
ex: These cells specialized for propagation, however they may originate, are accordingly distinguished by a special name, that of Spores of Sporules.

s.def: To become distinct or separate from what is common
ex: Firms... which have specialised in the manufacture of ‘heavies’...
Blackhead: I might look you up myself one of these days. Do you specialise at all, like? Penny Guy: Yeah. Verbal abuse and colonic irrigation.

s.def: To train (someone) in a specialty.

ety: From Middle English specialte, Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.

s.def: That in which one specializes; a chosen expertise or talent; bailiwick.
ex: Near-synonym: discipline
medical specialty
academic specialty

s.def: A product that originates in and is characteristic of a place.
ex: regional specialty
house specialty

s.def: Particularity.
A particular or peculiar case.
A contract or obligation under seal; a contract by deed; a writing, under seal, given as security for a debt particularly specified.
ex: Let specialties be therefore drawne betweene vs, That couenants may be kept on either hand.

s.def: An attribute or quality peculiar to a species.

ety: Originally in the phrase in specie; from Latin speciē, ablative singular of species. Compare in kind.

s.def: Type or kind, in various uses of the phrase in specie.
Money in the form of coins made from precious metal that has an intrinsic value; coinage.
ex: ‘It was not money or specie he thought himself hunting!’

s.def: singular of species

ety: From Latin speciēs (“appearance; quality”), from speciō (“see”) + -iēs suffix signifying abstract noun. Doublet of spice.

s.def: A type or kind. (Compare race.)
ex: the male species
a new species of war
What is called spiritualism should, I think, be called a mental species of materialism.

s.def: group of plants or animals having similar appearance
An image, an appearance, a spectacle.
ex: I cast the species of the Sun onto a sheet of paper through a telescope.

s.def: Either of the two elements of the Eucharist after they have been consecrated.
Coin, or coined silver, gold, or other metal, used as a circulating medium; specie.
ex: There was, in the splendour of the Roman empire, a less quantity of current species in Europe than there is now.

s.def: A component part of compound medicine; a simple.
plural of specie

ety: Etymology tree English specify Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English specifiable From specify + -able.

s.def: Able to be specified

ety: From Old French specifique, from Late Latin specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind”) + -ific.

s.def: Explicit or definite.
Pertaining to a species, as a taxon or taxa at the rank of species.
ex: Holonyms: generic, familial
Meronyms: infrasubspecific, infraspecific, subspecific
Science and literature, then, are the two achievements of Homo sapiens that most convincingly justify the specific name.

s.def: Special, distinctive or unique.
intended for, or applying to, a particular thing.
Serving to identify a particular thing (often a disease or condition), with little risk of mistaking something else for it.
ex: a highly specific test
specific and nonspecific symptoms

s.def: Being a remedy for a particular disease on a deeper level, rather than just masking the symptoms.
ex: Quinine is a specific medicine in cases of malaria.

s.def: Of a value divided by mass (e.g. specific orbital energy).
Similarly referring to a value divided by any measure which acts to standardize it (e.g. thrust specific fuel consumption, referring to fuel consumption divided by thrust).
Limited to a particular antibody or antigen.
A measure compared with a standard reference value by division, to produce a ratio without unit or dimension (e.g. specific refractive index is a pure number, and is relative to that of air).
An obsolete term for specific heat capacity.

Proto-Germanic *-līkaz Proto-Germanic *-ê Proto-Germanic *-līkê Proto-West Germanic *-līkē Old English -līċe Middle English -ly Middle English -ally English -ally English specifically From specific + -…

s.def: For a specific purpose or reason.
In a specific manner, applying to or naming a particular thing or things, expressly, explicitly.
ex: Unless a rule or statute specifically states otherwise, a pleading need not be verified or accompanied by an affidavit.
Many laws are directed specifically at child abuse.

ety: From Middle French specification, from Medieval Latin specificationem (accusative of specificatio).

s.def: An explicit set of requirements to be satisfied by a material, product, or service.
ex: The contractor followed the architect’s specifications.
Each computer is built to the customer’s exact specification.
The product failed to meet the required safety specifications.

s.def: An act of specifying.

ety: From Middle English specifien, from Old French specifier, especefier, or directly from Medieval Latin specificō, from specificus (“specific”).

s.def: To state explicitly, or in detail, or as a condition.
To include in a specification.
To bring about a specific result.
To speak explicitly or in detail (often used with of).
ex: Forthermar o þis lecheri / Agh i þe noght to specifie[…]

ety: From Latin specimen (“mark, sign, example”), from speciō (“observe, watch”).

s.def: An individual instance that represents a class; an example.
ex: early specimens of the art of Picasso
a specimen of my own handwriting
"You're a nice specimen for a clergyman," he said at length, "with your preachin" an" your psalm-singin', an" your Sunday coat on."

s.def: A sample, especially one used for diagnostic analysis.
An eligible man.

ety: From Middle English speciose, specious, from Anglo-Norman specious, Middle French specieux, and their etymon Latin speciōsus (“good-looking”).

s.def: Seemingly well-reasoned, plausible or true, but actually fallacious.
ex: This idea that we must see through what we have started is specious, however good it may sound.

s.def: Employing fallacious but deceptively plausible arguments; deceitful.
ex: But a third cause of the delusion is, that the Church of Rome has become more specious and deceitful than before the Reformation.

s.def: Having an attractive appearance intended to generate a favorable response; deceptively attractive.
ex: [T]he success of Trajan, however transient, was rapid and specious. The degenerate Parthians, broken by intestine discord, fled before his arms.
This argument, though specious, will not, upon examination, be found solid.

s.def: Beautiful, pleasing to look at.
Alternative form of speciose (“rich in species”).
ex: Coelorinchus is the most specious genus of macrourids with 122 species at the time of writing and more yet to be described.

ety: From Middle English spekke, from Old English specca (“small spot, stain”), from the same ultimate source as Proto-Germanic *sprakô (“spark”). Cognate with Low German spaken (“to spot with wet”).

s.def: A tiny spot or particle, especially of dirt.
ex: a tiny speck of soot

s.def: A very small amount; a particle; a whit.
ex: He has not a speck of money.
not a speck of truth in her story.

s.def: A small etheostomoid fish, Etheostoma stigmaeum, common in the eastern United States.
To mark with specks; to speckle.
ex: paper specked by impurities in the water used in its manufacture
Each flower of slender stalk, whose head though gay / Carnation, purple, azure, or specked with gold, / Hung drooping unsustained, […]

s.def: Fat; lard; fat meat.
A juniper-flavoured ham originally from Tyrol.
The blubber of whales or other marine mammals.
The fat of the hippopotamus.

ety: The noun is from Middle Dutch spekkel; the verb was later coined from the noun, in the late 16th century.

s.def: A small spot or speck on the skin, plumage or foliage.
The random distribution of light when it is scattered by a rough surface.
Kind; sort.
A cluster of interchromatin granules in a nucleus.
To mark with speckles.
Abbreviation of spectacles.
Specifications: plural of spec
third-person singular simple present indicative of spec

ety: From Middle English spectacle, from Middle French spectacle, from Latin spectāculum (“a show, spectacle”), from spectō (“to see, behold”), frequentative of speciō (“to see”). See species. Doublet of spectaculum.

s.def: An exciting or extraordinary scene, exhibition, performance etc.
ex: The horse race was a thrilling spectacle.
But scarcely was it set upon the table when the whole was carried off and plundered by the people who came to see the spectacle of the entertainment

s.def: Drama and excitement in a display, product, performance, exhibition, etc.
ex: I enjoyed her presentation, but it needs more spectacle.

s.def: A frame with different coloured lenses on a semaphore signal through which light from a lamp shines at night, often a part of the signal arm.
An embarrassing or unedifying scene or situation.
ex: He made a spectacle out of himself.

s.def: Attributive form of spectacles.
The brille of a snake.

der: make a public spectacle of oneself

ety: Since some specimens have spectacle-like markings on their faces.

s.def: Tremarctos ornatus, a species of small, short-faced bear native to South America.
A pair of lenses set in a frame worn on the nose and ears in order to correct deficiencies in eyesight or to ornament the face.
ex: He needed to get new spectacles because his original ones had broken.

s.def: Synonym of pair (“score of zero runs in both innings”).

ety: From Latin spectaculum (“a sight, show”) + -ar.

s.def: Amazing or worthy of special notice.
ex: The parachutists were spectacular.

s.def: Related to, or having the character of, a spectacle or entertainment.
ex: the merely spectacular

s.def: Relating to spectacles, or glasses for the eyes.
A spectacular display.
ex: Though business has more or less held up so far, a series of drug-related spectaculars sparked an exodus of the city's upper class this summer.

s.def: A pop-up (folded paper element) in material sent by postal mail.

ex: One study of popular escapistic communications indicates that the recipients regarded the heroes and spokesmen as "trustworthy models and guides."
President Moon Jae-in proposed the plan this week during a meeting with government officials, his spokesman said.

ety: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + person.

s.def: A person who acts as the voice of another person or a group of people.

ety: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + woman.

s.def: A woman who speaks as the voice of a group of people.

ety: From Late Middle English spoliacioun (“looting, robbery, theft; an instance of this; (ecclesiastical) wrongful deprivation of the emoluments of a benefice due to another”), from Anglo-Norman spoliacioun, espolïacion, and directly from their etymon Latin spoliātiō (“plundering, robbing”), from spoliāre + -tiō (suffix forming nouns denoting a process, action, or result of an action). s.def: The action of spoliating, or forcibly seizing property; pillage, plunder; also, the state of having property forcibly seized; (countable) an instance of this; a robbery, a seizure.
The action of destroying or ruining; destruction, ruin.
The action of an incumbent (“holder of an ecclesiastical benefice”) wrongfully depriving another of the emoluments of a benefice.
A lawsuit brought or writ issued by an incumbent against another, claiming that the latter has wrongfully taken the emoluments of a benefice.
The intentional destruction of, or tampering with, a document so as to impair its evidentiary value.
The systematic forcible seizure of property during a crisis or state of unrest such as that caused by war, now regarded as a crime; looting, pillage, plunder; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: Spoliation of Jewish property by Nazi authorities occurred on a large scale during World War II.

s.def: The government-sanctioned action or practice of plundering neutral ships at sea; (countable) an instance of this.

ety: Compare French spoliatif.

s.def: Serving to take away, diminish, or rob.
ex: spoliative bloodletting

ety: From Latin spondēus (“spondee”), from Ancient Greek σπονδεῖος (spondeîos, “associated with a libation”) from σπονδή (spondḗ, “libation”): spondees were often used in melodies sung at libations.

s.def: A word or metrical foot of two syllables, either both long or both stressed.

ety: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). Displaced native Old English swamm (“fungus, sponge”).

s.def: The porous material that synthetic washing sponges are made of.
Any of various marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera, that have a porous skeleton often of silica.
A piece of porous material used for washing (originally made from the invertebrates, now often made of plastic).
A type of light cake.
A type of steamed pudding.
A person who readily absorbs ideas.
A form of contraception that is inserted vaginally; a contraceptive sponge.
A person who takes advantage of the generosity of others (abstractly imagined to absorb or soak up the money or efforts of others like a sponge).
A heavy drinker.
Any sponge-like substance.

A light, soft, baked dessert (commonly layered with cream and jam) that is typically made with flour, sugar, baking powder and eggs, and has a firm, yet well aerated structure, similar to that of a sea sponge.
ex: I made a sponge cake the other day. It was a disaster: I forgot the baking powder! It didn't rise!

s.def: Something that is simple or very easy.

ety: Etymology tree English sponge Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder. Proto-Germanic *-līkaz Proto-West Germanic *-līk Old English -līċ Middle English -like English -like English spongelike From sponge + -like.

A parasitic hanger-on.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin spōnsor (“a surety", in Late Latin "a sponsor in baptism”).

ex: He was my sponsor when I applied to join the club.

s.def: A person or organization that pays all or part of the cost of an event, publication, media program, etc., usually in exchange for advertising.

s.def: The aid or support provided by a sponsor; backing or patronage.

Produced without being planted or without human cultivation or labor.
Sudden, without warning.

ety: Coined by English comedian Arthur Roberts in 1884 as the name of a card game involving deception and nonsense.

ety: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”). Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, spûk (“apparition, ghost”), Middle High German gespük (“a haunting”), German Spuk, Danish spøge (“to haunt”), Swedish spöke (“ghost”).

ety: From Middle English steyen, staien, from Old French estayer, estaier (“to fix, prop up, support, stay”), from estaye, estaie (“a prop, stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade (“a prop, stay, help, aid”) (compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stadi (“a site, place, location, standing”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“a standing, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂t…

s.def: To remain in a particular place, especially for a definite or short period of time; sojourn; abide.
ex: We stayed in Hawaii for a week. I can only stay for an hour.

ex: Wear gloves so your hands stay warm.

ex: My father stays my coming;

s.def: To remain for the purpose of; to stay to take part in or be present at (a meal, ceremony etc.).

s.def: Initialism of subscriber trunk dialling or subscriber toll dialing.
Initialism of short-term disability.
Initialism of save the date.

ety: From Middle English sted, stede (noun) and steden (verb), from Old English stede, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“place”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing, location”). s.def: The position or function (of someone or something), as taken on by a successor.
ex: Had Daniel Ortega not got himself illegally on to this year’s ballot to seek a third term, his wife might have run in his stead.

A relational or circumstantial position; standing.
A place as it relates to situation, circumstance, or status; condition.

I shiver to the cold solitude Overwhelming desire to have a different stead I don't know why I don't know why I'm just afraid to fly […]
The Adidas shirts look fantastic and certainly put us in a different stead.

ex: For he ne wonneth in one certaine stead, / But restlesse walketh all the world around[…].
"[…] I went to another stead in the yard to be further from her cries."

s.def: A place where a person normally rests; a seat.
ex: There now the hart, fearlesse of greyhound, feeds, / And loving pelican in safety breeds; / There shrieking satyres fill the people's emptie steads.

s.def: An inhabited place; a settlement, city, town etc.
An estate, a property with its grounds; a farm; a homestead.
ex: But of course I could not do this by myself, so I took a Hottentot—a very clever man when he was not drunk—who lived on the stead, into my confidence.

s.def: The frame on which a bed is laid; a bedstead.
ex: The genial bed / Sallow the feet, the borders, and the stead.

s.def: To help, support, benefit or assist; to be helpful.
ex: May you stead me? will you pleasure me? shall I know your answer?

ety: From Middle English stedefast, from Old English stedefæst, from Proto-Germanic *stadifastuz, equivalent to stead (“place; spot; position”) + fast (“firm; fixed”). Cognate with Middle Dutch stedevast (“steadfast”), Icelandic staðfestur (“steadfast”), Danish stedfast (“firmly attached, secured”), Danish stadfæste (“to confirm; ratify”), Norwegian Nynorsk stadfesta (“confirm, ratify; establish”), Swedish stadfästa (“to confirm; establish”).

s.def: Fixed or unchanging; steady.
Firmly loyal or constant; unswerving.
ex: steadfast support
steadfast commitment

ety: From Middle English stedy, studi, stidiȝ, perhaps continuing Old English stæþþiġ, ġestæþþiġ (“steadfast, stable, firm, staid”), equivalent to stead + -y; or calquing Middle Low German or Middle Dutch stēdig. Cognate with Saterland Frisian stoadig (“steady”), West Frisian stadich (“slow”), Danish stedig, stadig, steeg, Swedish stadig, Icelandic stöðugur, German stätig, stetig. s.def: Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm.
ex: Hold the ladder steady while I go up.
Their feet steady, their hands diligent, their eyes watchful, and their hearts resolute.

s.def: Constant in feeling, purpose, or pursuit; not fickle, changeable, or wavering; not easily moved or persuaded to alter a purpose; resolute.
ex: a man steady in his principles, in his purpose, or in the pursuit of an object

s.def: Smooth and not bumpy or with obstructions.
ex: a steady ride

s.def: Phlegmatic, calm; not easily upset, excited, or disturbed.
ex: a steady tone of voice

s.def: Regular and even.

s.def: Slow.

Confident and cool-headed under pressure; competent; reliable, adept.
To stabilize; to prevent from shaking.
ex: I took a drink to steady my nerves.

s.def: To become stable.
ex: The ship steadied in the air. Another spray of ballast came, heavier than the last.

ety: From Middle English steike, from Old Norse steik (“roast; meat roasted on a stick”). The verb is either from the noun or from steikja (“to roast”). The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English /ɛː/ to /eɪ/ in the standard language; contrast this with the development of other words such as speak and wreak.

s.def: Beefsteak: a slice of beef, broiled or cut for broiling.
A relatively large, thick slice or slab cut from another animal, a vegetable, etc.
ex: venison steak, pork steak, salmon steak; cauliflower steak, eggplant steaks

s.def: A slice of meat cut across the grain (perpendicular to the spine) from a fish.
To cook (something, especially fish) like or as a steak.
A table knife with a sharp, narrow, and often serrated blade designed for cutting tougher foods such as cooked meats.

ety: From steak + house.

s.def: A restaurant that specializes in good cuts of meat, particularly steak.
ex: They're of the generation that believes that steak houses should be dimly lit and frostily chilled (hell, they actually believe in steak houses).

Cognate with Bavarian stöhn (“to steal”), Dutch stelen (“to steal”), German and Low German stehlen (“to steal”), Luxembourgish stielen (“to steal”), Danish stjæle (“to steal”), Faroese stjala (“to steal”), Icelandic stela (“to steal”), Norwegian Bokm…

s.def: To take illegally, or without the owner's permission, something owned by someone else without intending to return it.
ex: Three irreplaceable paintings were stolen from the gallery.
The problem is the two bicycles stolen from us.
They stole all my money (from me).

s.def: A piece of merchandise available at a very low, attractive price; the act of buying it.
ex: Near-synonyms: bargain, good value, value for money

ex: They stole my idea for a biodegradable, disposable garbage de-odorizer.

ex: He stole glances at the pretty woman across the street.

To move silently or secretly; to pass unnoticed.
ex: He stole across the room, trying not to wake her.

When night had fallen, the she-demon stole forth toward the hall, which she entered unheard and unseen.

s.def: To convey (something) clandestinely.
ex: The fact that European Cuckoos steal their eggs into the nests of other birds has been generally known for more than a thousand years.

s.def: To withdraw or convey (oneself) clandestinely.
ex: They could insinuate and steal themselves under the same by their humble carriage and submission.

s.def: To advance safely to (another base) during the delivery of a pitch, without the aid of a hit, walk, passed ball, wild pitch, or defensive indifference.

ety: From steal + -age.

s.def: Theft.

ety: From Middle English stelthe, from Old English stǣlþ, from Proto-Germanic *stēliþō, to Proto-Germanic *stelaną (“to steal, to sneak”) + *-iþō, equivalent to steal + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Compare Old English stalu (“theft, stealth”), Old High German stāla (“theft”), German Diebstahl (“theft”).

An act of secrecy, especially one involving thievery.
ex: Claudio.[...] But it chances The stealth of our most mutuall entertainment With Character too grosse, is writ on Iuliet.
[The King] thinks it fit[...] that restitution according to this order be made to the petitioners for stealths committed upon them last winter (273).

s.def: To conceal or infiltrate through the use of stealth.
To subject (someone) to stealthing (sexual intercourse without a condom through deception, for example removing the condom mid-act).
Surreptitious; secret; not openly acknowledged.
Having properties that diminish radar signatures.
Hiding one's transgender status (in general or in specific areas of one's life, e.g. at work) after transition.

ety: From Middle English steem, stem, from Old English stēam (“steam, hot exhalation, hot breath; that which emits vapour; blood”), from Proto-Germanic *staumaz (“steam, vapour, breath”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to whirl, waft, stink, shake; steam, haze, smoke”). To project upward, or make an angle with the horizon or with the line of a vessel's keel; said of the bowsprit, etc.
To stow, as bales in a vessel's hold, by means of a steeve.

ety: From a regional use of German Stein (“stone”). Probably a clipping of Steingut (“stoneware”) or Steinkrug (“stone pitcher”). Compare Old English stǣna (“stone jug, a pot of stone or earth”). Doublet of stone. More at stean.

s.def: A beer mug, usually made of ceramic or glass.
ex: A gnome-size German civilian with a red von Hindenburg mustache is dispensing steins of what looks to be mostly head.

ety: From Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē, “upright rock; pillar; column”), plural form στῆλαι (stêlai). Doublet of stela.

s.def: Any carved or engraved surface.
ex: Two large hieroglyphed steles incised upon the face of a projecting mass of boldly rounded cliff.

s.def: An acroterion, the decoration on the ridge of an ancient Greek building such as a temple.
ex: Stele. The ornaments on the ridge of a Greek temple, answering to the antefixæ on the summit of the flank entablatures, are thus designated.

s.def: An upright (or formerly upright) slab containing engraved or painted decorations or inscriptions; a stela.
ex: A superior class of members...had their names inscribed upon a marble stélé or column.
It appears, that when any one of the family died, a stelè to his memory was added to the tomb.
In Egypt [obelisks] belonged to the class of steles (commemorative pillars).

s.def: The central core of a plant's root and stem system, especially including the vascular tissue and developed from the plerome.
ex: The so-called central cylinder, for which Van Tieghem has proposed the name stele (column).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗrder. Proto-Italic *stērlā Latin stēlla Latin stēllārisbor. English stellar Borrowed from Latin stēllāris.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of stars.
Heavenly.
Exceptional, exceptionally good.
ex: The actress gave a stellar performance.
Yet the economic seers are at it again, seemingly unabashed by their somewhat less than stellar performances in 1969.

s.def: The equivalent of solar wind associated with a star not restricted to being the Sun.

ety: Borrowed from Latin stēllātus (“starry”), from stēlla (“star”) + -ātus (“-ate”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to stell(a) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Shaped like a star, having points, or rays radiating from a center.
ex: stellate cells
stellate flowers
Exit wounds can be stellate, slit-like, crescent, circular, or completely irregular (Figure 4.23).

s.def: Ellipsis of stellate cell.
To extend the edges or planes of a polyhedron to form a new shape.

ety: From Latin stēlla (“star”) + -i- + -ferous.

s.def: Filled with stars; starry.
With conditions that support stars.

ety: Latin stelliformis, from stella (“star”), + -iform.

s.def: Shaped like a star.

ety: From Latin stellio (“a newt with starlike spots on its back”), from stella (“star”).

s.def: A lizard (Laudakia stellio or Stellagama stellio). It is olive-green with small stellate spots, commonly found in the rocky areas around the Mediterranean.

ety: From Latin stellula, diminutive of stella (“a star”).

s.def: Having the shape or appearance of little stars; stellate; stellated; radiated.
Marked with star-like spots of colour; star-spangled.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *sth₂mnís Proto-Germanic *stamniz Proto-West Germanic *stamni Old English stemn Middle English stemme English stem From Middle English stem, stemme, stempne, stevin, from Old English stemn (“stem”), from Proto-West Germanic *stamni, from Proto-Germanic *stamniz (“stem, tree stalk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, stay”). Cognate…

s.def: The above-ground stalk (technically axis) of a vascular plant, and certain anatomically similar, below-ground organs such as rhizomes, bulbs, tubers, and corms.
ex: After they are shot up thirty feet in length, they spread a very large top, having no bough nor twig in the trunk or the stem.

s.def: The main part of an uninflected word to which affixes may be added to form inflections of the word. A stem often has a more fundamental root. Systematic conjugations and declensions derive from their stems.
The stock of a family; a race or generation of progenitors.
A branch of a family.
ex: This is a stem / Of that victorious stock.

s.def: An advanced or leading position; the lookout.
ex: Wolsey sat at the stem more than twenty years.

s.def: A slender supporting member of an individual part of a plant such as a flower or a leaf; also, by analogy, the shaft of a feather.
ex: the stem of an apple or a cherry

s.def: A narrow part on certain man-made objects, such as a wine glass, a tobacco pipe, a spoon.
A person's leg.
The penis.
ex: Waves of ecstasy roll through him as the moustachioed Casanova slides his stem in and out of the spaced-out chick.

s.def: A vertical stroke of a letter.
A primal undifferentiated cell from which a variety of other cells can develop through the process of cellular differentiation.

ety: From Middle English stench, from Old English stenċ (“stench, odor, fragrance”), from Proto-Germanic *stankwiz (“smell, fragrance, odor”), from Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ- (“to push, thrust”). Cognate with Dutch stank (“stench, odor”), German Stank, Gestank (“stench, odor, smell”), Danish stank (“stench”), Swedish stank (“stench”), Icelandic stækja (“stench”).

s.def: a strong foul smell; a stink.
A foul quality.
ex: the stench of political corruption

s.def: A smell or odour, not necessarily bad.
To cause to emit a disagreeable odour; to cause to stink.
ex: Dead bards stench every coast

s.def: To stanch.

ety: Likely a nominalization of Middle English stencellen (“to garnish with bright hues”), borrowed from Middle French estinceller (“to glisten”), from Old French estenceler (“to spark”), from Old French estencele (“spark”), from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, from metathesis of Latin scintilla (“spark”). The verb is from the noun.

s.def: A thin sheet, either perforated or using some other technique, with which a pattern may be produced upon a surface; a utensil that contains a perforated sheet.
ex: You do not necessarily need to have a stencil brush to paint over a stencil.

s.def: A pattern produced using such a utensil.
A two-ply master sheet for use with a mimeograph.
To print with a stencil.

ety: From steno- + -graph.

s.def: A production of stenography; anything written in shorthand.
A shorthand character.
A stenography machine.
To write or report in stenographic characters.

ety: From stenography + -er.

s.def: Someone skilled in the writing of shorthand or the use of a stenotype machine, especially for the purpose of rapid transcription of speech. One employed in such a role: a professional transcriptionist who employs shorthand.
One who invents or studies systems of shorthand.

ety: From steno- (“narrow”) + -graphy.

s.def: The practice of transcribing speech (primarily for later dictation or testimony), usually using shorthand

ety: From steno- + phyllous.

s.def: Having narrow leaves.

ety: From New Latin stenōsis, from Ancient Greek στένωσις (sténōsis, “narrowing”), from στενόω (stenóō, “to confine, to contract”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix), equivalent to steno- + -osis.

s.def: An abnormal narrowing or stricture in a blood vessel or other tubular organ.
A reduction in either mental or physical capacity.

ety: From steno- + -type.

s.def: A keyboard machine used to record a version of shorthand using a series of phonetic symbols.
Any of the characters used in this shorthand system.
To record using a stenotype.

ety: Unclear. Possibly named after dentist Charles Stent. The English surname is a variant of Stein.

s.def: A slender tube inserted into a blood vessel, a ureter or the oesophagus in order to provide support and to prevent disease-induced closure.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Stentōr, from Ancient Greek Στέντωρ (Sténtōr), the name of a herald in the Iliad who had a loud voice.

s.def: Any protozoan of the genus Stentor.
ex: When the stentors become too numerous it is a simple matter to subdivide the culture and add the requisite amount of spring water to each culture.

s.def: A part of the amplification system of a carillon.
ex: The unit is completely automatic in operation and tower stentors, matching the power output of the amplifier, are provided for roof or tower mounting.

s.def: A howler monkey.
A person with a powerful or stentorian voice.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *stapjaną Proto-West Germanic *stappjan Old English stæppan Middle English steppen English step From Middle English steppen, from Old English steppan (“to step, go, proceed, advance”), stepe (“step”), from Proto-West Germanic *stappjan, from Proto-Germanic *stapjaną (“to step”), *stapiz (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“to support, stomp, curse, be amazed”). Cognate with West Frisian stappe (“to step”), North Frisian stape (“to walk, trudge”), Dutch stap…

s.def: An advance or movement made from one foot to the other; a pace.
intransitive: to move the foot in walking
A rest, or one of a set of rests, for the foot in ascending or descending, as a stair, or a rung of a ladder.
ex: The breadth of every single step or stair should be never less than one foot.
Through the open front door ran Jessamy, down the steps to where Kitto was sitting at the bottom with the pram beside him.

s.def: The part of a spade, digging stick or similar tool that a digger's foot rests against and presses on when digging; an ear, a foot-rest.
The button joining a glass's stem to its foot.
A distinct part of a process; stage; phase.
ex: He improved step by step, or by steps.
The first step is to find a job.

s.def: A running board where passengers step to get on and off the bus.
ex: The driver must have a clear view of the step in order to prevent accidents.

s.def: The space passed over by one movement of the foot in walking or running.
ex: One step is generally about three feet, but may be more or less.

s.def: A small space or distance.
ex: It is but a step.

s.def: A print of the foot; a footstep; a footprint; track.

der: a journey of a thousand miles begins wi…

s.def: Gradually and steadily.
ex: Like many a successful YouTuber, she built up her following step by step, amassing subscribers as her video library grew.
Rail technology advanced step by step - albeit electrification was a good stride, rather than a short step.

s.def: From one stage to the next in sequence.
ex: She assembled the toy step by step, following the instructions carefully.
We were shown the process step by step.

s.def: To get involved; to act.
To act as a replacement or substitute.
A ladder with steps or treads instead of rungs that is hinged in the middle to form an inverted V, with stays to keep the two halves at a fixed angle.
The player over whom another player marks to take a spectacular mark.
To cheat on someone; to be unfaithful to a lover.
ex: Nikki, who is stepping out on her main squeeze Lee,
I could tell from the way she acted that night that she had never stepped out on her man.

ety: From Middle English step-, from Old English stēop- (“deprived of a relative, step-”, prefix), from Proto-West Germanic *steupa-, from Proto-Germanic *steupa- (“orphaned, step-”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push, strike”). Cognate with Scots step- (“step-”), West Frisian stiep- (“step-”), Dutch stief- (“step-”), Low German steef- (“step-”), German stief- (“step-”), Swedish styv- (“step-”), Icelandic stjúp- (“step-”). Related to Old English stīepan (“to deprive, bereave”). Not, howev…

s.def: A prefix used before father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, child, and so forth, to indicate that the person being identified is not a blood relative but is related through the marriage of a parent.

ety: From Armenian Ստեփանակերտ (Stepʻanakert). Named after Stepan Shahumyan, a communist revolutionary active throughout the Caucasus.

s.def: The capital of the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew- Proto-Germanic *steupa- Proto-West Germanic *steupa- Old English stēop- Middle English step- English step- Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr Proto-Germanic *brōþēr Proto-West Germanic *brōþer Old English brōþor Middle English brother English brother English stepbrother From step- + brother.

s.def: The son of one's stepparent by a previous relationship.
The stepson of one's parent who is not one's half-brother.

ety: From Middle English stepchild, stepchyld, from Old English stēopċild (“stepchild”), equivalent to step- + child. Compare Dutch stiefkind (“stepchild”), German Stiefkind (“stepchild”), Swedish styvbarn (“stepchild”).

s.def: The child of one's spouse from a previous relationship.
A bereaved child; one who has lost father or mother.

ety: From Middle English stepdoughter, stepdoghter, steopdohter, from Old English stēopdohtor (“stepdaughter”), from Proto-Germanic *steupaduhtēr (“stepdaughter”), equivalent to step- + daughter. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Stäifdochter (“stepdaughter”), West Frisian styfdochter (“stepdaughter”), Dutch stiefdochter (“stepdaughter”), German Low German Steevdochter (“stepdaughter”), German Stieftochter (“stepdaughter”), Danish steddatter (“stepdaughter”), Swedish styvdotter (“stepdaughter”), Icelan…

s.def: The daughter of one's spouse from a previous relationship.
ex: Shannon Spann had an infant, Jake, to care for and two stepdaughters to suddenly raise by herself.

ety: Deverbal from step down.

s.def: Used to decrease the secondary voltage relative to the primary voltage.
A gradual reduction.

ety: From Middle English stepfader, from Old English stēopfæder, from Proto-Germanic *steupafadēr (“stepfather”), equivalent to step- + father. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Stäiffoar (“stepfather”), Dutch stiefvader (“stepfather”), German Low German Steevvader (“stepfather”), German Stiefvater (“stepfather”), Swedish styvfar (“stepfather”), Icelandic stjúpfaðir (“stepfather”).

s.def: The husband of one's biological mother after her initial marriage to or relationship with one's biological father.
The husband of one's parent distinct from one's biological father or person with a similar relationship.
ex: In suboptimal cases the gynaecologist takes sperm from anonymous donors. In this case the husband can only be stepfather of the child.

ety: Borrowed from French Stéphanie. The standard English feminine form of Stephen. Doublet of Stephania.

s.def: A female given name from French.

ety: From Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος (Stéphanos), from στέφανος (stéphanos, “crown, wreath”), from στέφω (stéphō, “to put round, to surround”). From *stegʷʰ- (“to enlace”) + -νος (-nos, suffix forming an adjective or noun) from Proto-Indo-European *-nós (suffix forming a verbal adjective from a verb stem).

s.def: A male given name from Ancient Greek.
The first Christian martyr.
ex: And Steuen full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people.

s.def: A female given name.
ex: Even in her fourteenth year Miss Stephen Norman gave promise of striking beauty; beauty of a rarely composite character.

s.def: A surname originating as a patronymic.
A minor city in Marshall County, Minnesota, United States, named after George Stephen.
Alternative form of step ladder.

ety: From Middle English stepmoder, from Old English stēopmōdor, from Proto-Germanic *steupamōdēr (“stepmother”), corresponding to step- + mother. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Stäifmuur (“stepmother”), Dutch stiefmoeder (“stepmother”), German Low German Steevmoder (“stepmother”), German Stiefmutter (“stepmother”), Danish stedmor (“stepmother”), Swedish styvmor (“stepmother”), Icelandic stjúpmóðir (“stepmother”). Compare also West Frisian styfmem (“stepmother”).

s.def: wife of one's biological father, not one's biological mother
A woman who is a subsequent wife or partner of a person's parent, usually following the divorce or separation of their parents, or the death of one's biological mother.
Synonym of co-mother (“the non-birth mother of a child in a lesbian couple”).
Clipping of stepmother's blessing.
A viola, especially Viola tricolor, heartsease.
ex: The second came up about ten days later in the lee of the channel marker, and it was called stepmother, or love-in-idelness.

ety: From step- + mother-in-law or stepmother + -in-law.

s.def: A stepmother of one's spouse.

ety: From German Steppe or French steppe, in turn from Russian степь (stepʹ, “flat grassy plain”) or Ukrainian степ (step). There is no generally accepted earlier etymology, but there is a speculative Old East Slavic reconstruction *сътепь (sŭtepĭ, “trampled place, flat, bare”), related to топот (topot), топтать (toptatĭ).

s.def: The grasslands of Eastern Europe and Asia.
ex: Nevertheless be it remarked, that even a Russian steppe has tumuli and gold ornaments […]

s.def: A vast, cold, dry, grassy plain.
Alternative form of stepping stone.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew- Proto-Germanic *steupa- Proto-West Germanic *steupa- Old English stēop- Middle English step- English step- Proto-Indo-European *swé Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ Proto-Indo-European *su-h₁ésh₂-ōr? Proto-Indo-European *swé Proto-Indo-European *-sōr ? Proto-Indo-European *swésōrder. Proto-Germanic *swestēr Proto-West Germanic *swester Old English sweostor Middle English suster English sister English stepsister From step- + sister.

s.def: The daughter of one's stepparent by a previous relationship.
The stepdaughter of one's parent which is not one's half-sister.

ety: From Middle English stepsone, stepsune, from Old English stēopsunu (“stepson”), from Proto-Germanic *steupasunuz (“stepson”), equivalent to step- + son. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Stäifsuun (“stepson”), West Frisian styfsoan (“stepson”), Dutch stiefzoon (“stepson”), German Low German Steevsöhn (“stepson”), German Stiefsohn (“stepson”), Danish stedsøn (“stepson”), Swedish styvson (“stepson”), Icelandic stjúpsonur (“stepson”).

s.def: The son of one's spouse from a previous relationship.

ety: From Latin stercorāceus, from stercus (“dung”).

s.def: Consisting of, resembling or pertaining to feces.
ex: He had reason to believe the stercoraceous flavour, condemned by prejudice as a stink, was, in fact, most agreeable to the organs of smelling.
[W]e find it hard today to see the entertaining aspects of, for instance, stercoraceous jokes.

ety: From French stère, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”), because the unit was used for solid commodities such as firewood.

s.def: A measure of volume used e.g. for cut wood, equal to one cubic metre.

ety: A shortened form of stereotype, stereoscope or stereophonic, all originally derived, via stereo-, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”).

s.def: Any object or device equipped with audio components that reproduces sound in stereo, such as a stereo console in the home.
ex: He liked to listen to classical music on his stereo.

s.def: A system of recording or reproducing sound that uses two or more channels, each playing a portion of the original sound at different locations in order to simulate the separation of sources along at least one spatial dimension.
A stereotype.
A genre of Western-style pop and rock music.
Of sound, music, etc, recorded in stereo.
Of a pair of images: one depicting the view as would be seen from one eye and the other from the other eye, so that when viewed appropriately, they combine to give an impression of three dimensions.
ex: One could easily do this with stereo photographs, but one could also do it by making a pseudoscope, with a short cardboard tube and mirrors, […]

s.def: To create a stereophotographic image of.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ster-der. Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós) Ancient Greek στερεο- (stereo-)der. English stereo- English chemistry English stereochemistry From stereo- + chemistry.

s.def: the branch of chemistry that involves the spatial arrangement of the atoms of molecules, and studies how this affects the physical and chemical properties of such species
the effect of such spatial arrangement on the chemistry of a particular compound
The painting of murals using pigments mixed with water glass

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ster-der. Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós) Ancient Greek στερεο- (stereo-)der. English stereo- English isomer English stereoisomer From stereo- + isomer.

s.def: One of a set of the isomers of a compound that exhibits stereoisomerism.

ety: From stereo- + -phonic, by analogy with stereoscopic.

s.def: Of or pertaining to sound reproduction using two or sometimes more channels played at different locations to simulate the separation of sources along at least one spatial dimension.

ety: Borrowed from French stéréotype (adjective), equivalent to stereo- + type. Printing sense is from 1817; the “conventional, formulaic, and oversimplified conception, opinion, or image” sense is recorded from 1922 in Walter Lippmann’s book Public Opinion.

s.def: A conventional, formulaic, and often oversimplified or exaggerated conception, opinion, or image of (a person or a group of people).
ex: Not all Zumbetonians wear plimsolls. That's just a stereotype.
Instead we notice a trait which marks a well known type, and fill in the rest of the picture by means of the stereotypes we carry about in our heads.
Heartwarming: Trans girl breaks stereotypes by being the worst on the girls swim team

s.def: A metal printing plate cast from a matrix moulded from a raised printing surface.
A person who is regarded as embodying or conforming to a set image or type.
An extensibility mechanism of the Unified Modeling Language, allowing a new element to be derived from an existing one with added specializations.
To make a stereotype of someone or something, or characterize someone by a stereotype.
To prepare for printing in stereotype; to produce stereotype plates of.
ex: to stereotype the Bible

s.def: To print from a stereotype.
To make firm or permanent; to fix.
ex: Powerful causes tending to stereotype and aggravate the poverty of old conditions.

s.def: Of an edition: printed in stereotype.
Synonym of stereotyped.

ety: From Middle French stérile, from Latin sterilis (“barren, futile”). See also Ancient Greek στεῖρα (steîra).

s.def: Unable to reproduce (or procreate).
Terse; lacking sentiment or emotional stimulation, as in a manner of speaking.
Fruitless, uninspiring, or unproductive.
Germless; free from all living or viable microorganisms.
ex: a sterile kitchen table

s.def: Permanently uninhabitable (as in a planet like Earth) to all life, including even microbes.
Free from dangerous objects, as a zone in an airport that can be only be entered via a security checkpoint.
Of weapons: foreign-made and untraceable to the United States.

ety: From Middle English sterylite, sterylyte, from Latin sterilitās. By surface analysis, sterile + -ity.

s.def: The state or quality of being sterile.

ety: From sterilize + -able.

s.def: Able to be sterilized; able to go through sterilization.
ex: One should not wear leather gloves in the laboratory, because they are not sterilizable.

ety: From sterile + -ization or sterilize + -ation.

s.def: The process of treating something to kill or inactivate microorganisms.
ex: Heat sterilization is used during canning so the food can be safely stored for long periods.

s.def: A procedure to permanently prevent an organism from reproducing.
ex: Spaying a cat is a form of sterilization to limit the population growth.

s.def: An instance of a sterilization procedure.
ex: The vet performed several sterilizations this week.

s.def: A monetary policy operation used to offset a foreign exchange intervention.
ex: The Federal Reserve is responsible for foreign exchange sterilization.

s.def: The process of permanently rendering a planet like Earth completely uninhabitable to all life, including even microbes, leading to their complete extinction.

ety: Etymology tree English sterile Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English sterilize From sterile + -ize.

s.def: To deprive of the ability to procreate.
To make unable to produce; to make unprofitable.
To kill, deactivate (denature), or destroy (break apart) all living, viable microorganisms and spores on a surface, in a fluid, or contained in a compound, such as culture media or a medical product.
To render a planet like Earth permanently uninhabitable to all life, including even microbes, causing their complete extinction.
To redact (a document), removing classified or sensitive material.

ety: From Russian сте́рлядь (stérljadʹ).

s.def: A smaller, common Eurasian sturgeon, of the species Acipenser ruthenus.

ety: From Middle English sterling, possibly from Old English *steorling, from steorra (“star”) and -ling, in reference to the stars that appeared on certain English pennies. Alternatively, the first element may be *stēre, meaning “strong” or “stout” (compare the etymology of solidus).

s.def: The currency of the United Kingdom, also called the pound sterling
ex: [A]mong the objects stolen was the famous parure of Black Diamonds, for which a bid of half a million sterling had just been made and accepted.

s.def: An English silver penny first introduced by the Normans.
ex: In England sterlings and nobles were struck, both of them often counterfeited.

s.def: A penny issued in other countries, such as Scotland.
Short for sterling silver (“an alloy containing not less than 92.5 percent silver, the remainder usually being copper; articles made from this alloy collectively”).
ex: Many of the women cleaned house for other women, soaping fine china and polishing heavy sterling, […]

s.def: Former British gold or silver coinage of a standard fineness (0.91666 for gold and 0.925 for silver).
Synonym of pennyweight (“a unit of mass equal to 24 grains, or ¹⁄₂₀ of a troy ounce”)
ex: [E]ight of them [carats] make but one Sterlin, and a Sterlin is the 24 part of an ounce.

s.def: Money generally.
The standard degree of fineness.
Of or relating to the currency of the United Kingdom, or former types of English or British coinage.
ex: The doctrine of the Old Testament is the religion of England. […] It believes in a Providence which does not treat with levity a pound sterling.

s.def: Of silver: being of standard quality.

ety: From Middle English stern, sterne, sturne, from Old English styrne (“stern, grave, strict, austere, hard, severe, cruel”), from Proto-Germanic *sturnijaz (“angry, astonished, shocked”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“rigid, stiff”). Cognate with Scots stern (“bold, courageous, fierce, resolute”), Old High German stornēn (“to be astonished”), Dutch stuurs (“glum, austere”), Swedish stursk (“insolent”).

s.def: Having a hardness and severity of nature or manner.
ex: stern as tutors, and as uncles hard

s.def: Grim and forbidding in appearance.
ex: The remark earned me a stern rebuke.
these barren rocks, your stern inheritance

s.def: The rear part (after end) of a ship or other vessel.
ex: Holonyms: watercraft < vessel

s.def: The post of management or direction.
ex: and sit chiefest stern of public weal

s.def: The hinder part of anything.
The tail of an animal; now used only of the tail of a dog.
To steer, to direct the course of (a ship).
To propel or move backward or stern-first in the water.
A bird, the black tern, seabird.

ety: From sternum + -al.

s.def: Of, relating to, or near the sternum.

ety: From sterno- + -tomy.

s.def: An incision into the sternum.

ety: From stern + post.

s.def: A timber or steel bar extending from the keel to the main deck at the stern of a vessel.

ety: Borrowed from New Latin sternum, related to Old English steorn (“forehead”), German Stirn (“forehead”).

s.def: The breastbone, consisting of the manubrium, gladiolus, and xiphoid process.
ex: The neckline fell into a V, showing the bone of his sternum.

s.def: The sclerotized ventral plate of spiders, between the coxae, marking the floor of the cephalothorax.

ety: Latin sternutatio.

ety: From Latin stultus (“stupid, foolish”), + -ify. Compare Late Latin stultificō.
