ex: chief ruler and principal head everywhere, not suffragant and subsidiary
They constituted a useful subsidiary testimony of another state of existence.

s.def: Secondary or subordinate.
ex: a subsidiary stream

s.def: Of or relating to a subsidy.
ex: subsidiary payments to an ally
George the Second relied on his subsidiary treaties.

s.def: A company owned by a parent company or a holding company, also called daughter company or sister company.
A subordinate theme.
One who aids or supplies; an assistant.

ety: Etymology tree English subsidy Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English subsidize From subsidy + -ize.

s.def: To assist (someone or something) by granting a subsidy.

ety: From Middle English subsidy, subsidie, from Anglo-Norman subsidee, subsidie, from Old French subside, from Latin subsidium (support, assistance), from subsido from sub- (“below”) + sīdō (“sit”).

s.def: Financial support or assistance, such as a grant.
ex: Manufacturing firms are supported by government subsidies in some countries.
You don't have to be Einstein to work out that this level of government subsidy is unsustainable.

s.def: Money granted by parliament to the British Crown.

ety: From Latin subsistō (“halt, stop”), from sub (“below”) + sistō (“stand, place”). Compare consist, desist, exist, insist, persist.

s.def: To survive on a minimum of resources.
To have ontological reality; to exist.
ex: Subject to section 5(1), copyright subsists only by virtue of this Act.

s.def: To retain a certain state; to continue.
To supply sustenance or subsistence to or for.

ety: From Middle English subsistence; partly from Middle French subsistence (modern French subsistance) and partly from its etymon Late Latin subsistentia (“substance, reality, in Medieval Latin also stability”), from Latin subsistēns, present participle of subsistere (“to continue, subsist”). Perhaps also partly from subsist + -ence.

s.def: Something (food, water, money, etc.) that is required to stay alive.
ex: In the general course of human nature, a power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will.
His viceroy could only propose to himself a comfortable subsistence out of the plunder of his province.

s.def: Real being; existence.
ex: the human nature loseth its proper subsistence , and is assumed into the subsistence of the divine nature

s.def: The act of maintaining oneself at a minimum level.
Inherency.
ex: the subsistence of qualities in bodies

s.def: Embodiment or personification or hypostasis of an underlying principle or quality.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- English soil English subsoil From sub- + soil.

s.def: The layer of earth that is below the topsoil.
ex: In the few areas underlain by horizontally bedded limestone, the surface soil is dark gray to black and peatlike, and the subsoil gray and marllike.

s.def: To turn up the subsoil of.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- English solar English subsolar From sub- + solar.

s.def: directly beneath the sun
between the tropics; equatorial

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- Proto-Indo-European *swónh₂os Latin sonus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English sonic English subsonic From sub- + sonic.

s.def: having a frequency too low to be audible
very quiet, almost inaudible
ex: The noise of the ship was all around her. The faint subsonic rumble of the reactor and drive. (Leviathan Wakes, James S. A. Corey)

s.def: (aviation) less than the speed of sound (in the same medium, and at the same temperature and pressure)
with a Mach number such that 0.3 < Ma < 0.8 (approximately - the exact limits vary between sources)
an aircraft whose maximum speed is less than the speed of sound

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- English species English subspecies From sub- + species.

s.def: A rank in the classification of organisms, below species.
A taxon at that rank, often indicated with trinomial nomenclature (such as Felis silvestris silvestris in zoology and Pinus nigra subsp. salzmannii in botany).
A subdivision of a species in other scientific disciplines.

ety: Inherited from Middle English substance, from Old French substance, from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist”, literally “stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”). Displaced native Old English andweorc.

s.def: The essential part of anything; the most vital part.
ex: Heroic virtue did his actions guide, / And he the substance, not the appearance, chose.
1684-1690, Thomas Burnet, Sacred Theory of the Earth This edition is the same in substance with the Latin.
It is insolent in words, in manner; but in substance it is not only insulting, but alarming.

s.def: Material possessions; estate; property; resources.
ex: a man of substance
And there wasted his substance with riotous living.

s.def: physical matter; material — see also matter
Physical matter; material.
Substantiality; solidity; firmness.
ex: Some textile fabrics have little substance.

s.def: Drugs (illegal narcotics)
ex: substance abuse

s.def: Ousia, essence; underlying reality or hypostasis in the philosophical sense.
To give substance to; to make real or substantial.
ex: If life were nothing but what gets phrased and substanced, the world might as well be rolled up and laid away again in darkness.
The calm ruminating / Reverie, substancing / Intellect into emotion, / Is shelter enough for love / Unhumiliated by faith.

s.def: An overindulgence in and dependence on a drug or other chemical.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-der. Proto-Germanic *standaną Frankish *standan Proto-Indo-European *kret-der.? Proto-Germanic *harduz Proto-Indo-European *-yos Proto-Indo-European *-yós Proto-Germanic *-jaz Proto-West Germanic *-ī Frankish *hard(ī) Frankish *standahardbor.? Old French estendre? Old French estandartbor. Middle English standard English standard English substandard From sub- + standard.

s.def: Of inferior quality; not meeting the minimum quality requirements.
ex: They built this with substandard parts. No wonder it collapsed.
[...] the fence provided by NR was substandard and poorly maintained, such that unauthorised access to the railway was straightforward.

s.def: Not conforming to the standard variety; nonstandard.

ety: Scientific Latin, from substantia (“substance”) + nigra (“black”).

s.def: A brain structure located in the mesencephalon (midbrain) that plays an important role in reward, addiction, and movement, damage to which occurs in Parkinson's and Parkinsonian patients.
ex: Their location was established in the 1950s as the substantia nigra, a layer of grey matter in the midbrain.

ety: From Middle English substancial, substantiall, from Old French substanciel, substantiel and its etymon Latin substantiālis.

s.def: Having a substance; actually existing.
ex: substantial life

s.def: Not imaginary; real; actual; true; veritable.
Corporeal; material; firm.
Having good substance; strong; stout; solid; firm.
ex: substantial cloth
a substantial fence or wall

s.def: Addressing the substance of an injury
ex: Substantial damages (i.e. damages set at a level that exactly covers the plaintiff's losses; synonym: compensatory damgages)

s.def: Possessed of goods or an estate; moderately wealthy.
ex: a substantial freeholder

s.def: Large in size, quantity, or value; ample; significant.
ex: He inherited a substantial amount of money from his uncle.
A substantial number of people went to the event.
The blind man laughed and a substantial coin found its billet in the caretaker's never-reluctant palm.

s.def: Most important; essential.
Satisfying; having sufficient substance to be nourishing or filling.
ex: I don't just want a snack; I need something substantial.
Teddy had a few crackers in his backpack, but he needed something more substantial if he was to survive a three-day trek.

s.def: Anything having substance; an essential part.

ety: Etymology tree English substantial Middle English -ly English -ly English substantially From substantial + -ly.

s.def: In a strong or substantial manner; considerably.
To a great extent; in essence; essentially.
Without material qualifications.

ety: From Medieval Latin substantiatus (“given substance”), from the verb substantiare, first used 1657.

s.def: To verify something by supplying evidence; to authenticate or corroborate.
ex: substantiate allegations
substantiate a claim
The lawyer was asked to substantiate her claims.

s.def: To give material form or substance to something; to embody; to record in documents

ety: From Middle English substantif, from Old French substantif.

s.def: Of the essence or essential element of a thing.
ex: substantive information
In one sense the first debate achieved the worst of all worlds: it managed to be technical, even dull, without being substantive or especially honest.

s.def: Having substance; enduring; solid; firm; substantial.
ex: Once more then, strength and magnitude are qualities which impress the imagination in a powerful and substantive manner;

s.def: Applying to essential legal principles and rules of right.
ex: substantive law

s.def: Not needing the use of a mordant to be made fast to that which is being dyed.
Depending on itself; independent.
Of or pertaining to a substantive.
Actually and legally held, as distinct from an acting, temporary or honorary rank or appointment.
Ellipsis of noun substantive or substantive noun, a noun or a group of words (a noun phrase) that act as a noun (in a sentence).
Part of a text that carries the meaning, such as words and their ordering.
To make a word belonging to another part of speech into a substantive (that is, a noun) or use it as a noun.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- English station English substation From sub- + station.

s.def: Any subordinate station.
ex: The utility now wants the network to be undergrounded in the urban areas, which would mean substations with 33 kV distribution swtichgear.
"We've got power upgrades at substations dotted all the way along the Piccadilly line.

ety: From Middle English substituten, from Latin substitutus, past participle of substituō, from sub- (“under; beneath”) + statuō (“to put up; establish”). Displaced native Old English spala (“a substitute”) and spelian (“to substitute”).

s.def: To use in place of something else, with the same function.
ex: I had no shallots so I substituted onion.

s.def: To use X in place of Y.
ex: I had to substitute new parts for the old ones.

s.def: To use Y in place of X; to replace X with Y.
ex: I had to substitute old parts with the new ones.

s.def: To remove (a player) from the field of play and bring on another in his place.
ex: He was playing poorly and was substituted after twenty minutes

s.def: To serve as a replacement (for someone or something).
ex: Accumulation of wealth by this route may substitute for personal saving.

s.def: A replacement or stand-in for something that achieves a similar result or purpose.
ex: Here we go. AK-47. The very best there is. When you absolutely, positively got to kill every motherfucker in the room, accept no substitutes.

s.def: A player who is available to replace another if the need arises, and who may or may not actually do so.
ex: Dean Whitehead opened the scoring shortly after the break with a low finish and substitute Peter Crouch sealed the win with a tap-in.

s.def: A substitute teacher.
One who enlists for military service in the place of a conscript.
Abbreviation of substitute good.

ety: From Middle French substitution, from Late Latin substitutio.

s.def: The expansion of the lexicon of a language by native means in correspondence to a foreign term.
The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.
ex: In this football tournament, three substitutions can be made during the match.

s.def: A substitute or replacement.
ex: Gary is off this weekend, so Jeff will be his substitution.

s.def: The replacement of an atom, or group of atoms, in a compound, with another.
a reaction in which one functional group is replaced with another

ety: Anglicization of substratum.

s.def: An underlying layer; a substratum.
The substance lining the bottom edge of an enclosure.
ex: The substrate of an aquarium can affect the water's acidity.
Stream substrate affects fish longevity.

s.def: A substance acted upon, as by an enzyme.
A surface on which an organism grows, or to which an organism or an item is attached.
ex: The rock surface of a rockpool is the substrate for a sessile organism such as a limpet.

s.def: A language that is replaced in a population by another language and that influences the language imposed on its speakers.
A metal which is plated with another metal which has different physical properties.
A surface to which a substance adheres.
To strew or lay under.
ex: The melted glass being supported by the substrated sand.

s.def: Having very slight furrows.

ety: From sub- + stratosphere.

s.def: The area of the atmosphere directly below the stratosphere.

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin substrātum, nominalisation of the neuter of Latin substrātus, perfect passive participle of substernō. By surface analysis, sub- + stratum.

s.def: A layer that lies underneath another.
The underlying cause or basis of something.
ex: However exaggerated an estimate this might be, the substratum of truth was solid and auriferous enough to dazzle the imagination.

s.def: A substrate.

ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subsūmere, from sub- + sūmō (“to take”). Compare English consume.

s.def: To place (any one cognition) under another as belonging to it; to include or contain something else.
ex: Near-synonym: comprise

s.def: To consider an occurrence as part of a principle or rule.

ety: From sub- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

s.def: The act of subsuming.
Something subsumed.
The premise of a syllogism that contains the minor term.

ety: From sub- + temperate.

s.def: Of or relating to the cooler parts of the temperate regions.

ety: From Latin subtendere, from sub (“under”) + tendere (“to stretch, extend”), itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνω (hupoteínō, “to subtend”), from which hypotenuse also derives. See tend.

s.def: To extend or stretch opposite something; to be part of a straight or curved line that is opposite to and delimits an angle.
ex: A hypotenuse subtends the right angle of a right triangle.
An arc measuring about 0.75 meters on a circle with a radius of 1 meter subtends an angle of about 43°.

s.def: To use an angle to delimit (mark off, enclose) part of a straight or curved line, for example an arc or the opposite side of a triangle.
ex: A 43° angle subtends an arc of about 0.75 meters on a circle with a radius of 1 meter.

s.def: To form the central angle of a circle underneath an arc.
ex: The points A and B on the circumference form the arc AB, which subtends the central angle θ.

s.def: To stand beneath or close to, as a bract at the base of a flower.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge m, from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).

s.def: An indirect or deceptive device or stratagem; a blind. Refers especially to war and diplomatics.
ex: Overt subterfuge in a region nearly caused a minor accident.
How’s the spy hunt going? Uncovered any subterfuge?

s.def: Deception; misrepresentation of the true nature of an activity.

ety: From Latin subterrāneus + -an. Compare subterrane and subterraneous.

s.def: Below ground, under the earth, underground.
ex: And you were in the parking lot / Subterranean by your own design

s.def: Secret, concealed.
Someone or something that is subterranean.
ex: Prue found an ample subterranean, neatly furnished; […]
Above: a stretch of the walls of the old Cathedral of S. Reparata in the subterraneans of the Duomo.

ety: From Latin subtilis (“fine, thin, slender, delicate”).

s.def: Archaic spelling of subtle.
ex: I burst into mirth at this—I liked him even better when he was subtile than when he was simple.

ety: From French subtiliser; equivalent to subtle + -ize.

s.def: To make subtle; to make thin or fine; to make less gross or coarse.
To refine; to spin into niceties.
ex: to subtilize arguments
Nor as yet have we subtilized ourselves into savages.

s.def: To use subtle arguments or distinctions.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- Etruscanbor.? Latin titulusbor. Old English titul Middle English title English title English subtitle From sub- + title.

s.def: Textual versions of the dialogue in films (and similar media such as television or video games), usually displayed at the bottom of the screen.
A heading below or after a title.
To create subtitles for the dialogue in a film.
in which the dialogue is translated into another language, and displayed, in text, at the bottom of the screen.

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English sotil, soubtil, subtil (“of a person, the mind, etc.: clever, ingenious, penetrating; cunning, sly; insidious; delicate, fine; not dense, light, thin; finely powdered; narrow, slender; etc.”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman sotel, subtil, sutil, Middle French soutil, subtil, sutil, and Old French sotil, soutil, subtil, sutil (“of an object: skilfully designed or made; delicate, fine; slender, thin; of an intangible thing: difficult to understand; of a pe…

s.def: Senses relating to intangible things.
ex: The difference between the tones is subtle, but you can hear it if you listen carefully.

s.def: Senses relating to tangible things.
People or things that are subtle (adjective sense) as a class.
To make (something) subtle (“giving only a slight impression; also, skilfully restrained or understated”).
To burn (someone or something) to ash.

ety: From Middle English sotilte, from Old French sutilté, inherited from Latin subtīlitās, from subtīlis (“subtle”). Equivalent to subtle + -ty. Doublet of subtility.

s.def: An instance of being subtle, a subtle thing, especially a subtle argument or distinction.
ex: The subtleties of this overture are often overlooked.
It is your turn now […] to support your philosophical subtilties against the dictates of plain reason and experience.
His body was as insensitive to pain as was his mind to subtleties.

s.def: quality or act of being subtle
The quality of being subtle.
ex: the subtlety of the Mona Lisa’s smile
[H]e had a lifetime of skill in interpreting his father's gestures: those bent knees meant that something of great subtlety was about to be revealed.

s.def: An ornate medieval illusion dish or table decoration, especially when made from one thing but crafted to look like another.
ex: At the king's coronation feast, several subtleties were served between main courses.
the seruice […] was sumpteous, with many subtleties, straunge deuises, with seuerall poses, and many deintie dishes.

s.def: The quality of being clever in surreptitious or deceitful behaviour; an act or argument that shows this quality.
ex: When eyther Hare or Deare, or any other chase vseth subtleties to deceyue the houndes, we saye they crosse or double.
[She] resolued now with plainnesse to winne trust, which trust she might after deceyue with a greater subtletie.
[…] the Spy was deceiv’d rather by the Art and Subtlety of Ulysses, than by his Falshood.

s.def: A trick that creates a false appearance.
ex: You doe yet taste / Some subtleties o’ th’ Isle, that will not let you / Beleeue things certaine:

s.def: The property of having a low density or thin consistency.
The property of being able to penetrate materials easily.
ex: Hence we see the amazing Subtlety of this Fire, which pervades Glass as readily as if nothing were in the Way.

ety: From Middle English sotilly; equivalent to subtle + -ly.

s.def: With subtleness, in a subtle manner; with cleverness rather than brute force.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub-der. English sub- English total English subtotal From sub- + total.

s.def: The total for a part of a list of numbers being summed.

ety: Borrowed from Latin subtractus, perfect passive participle of subtrahō (“to draw from beneath; withdraw, remove”); from sub (“under”) + trahō (“to draw, pull, drag”).

s.def: To remove or reduce; especially to reduce a quantity or number.
ex: If you subtract the $100 for gas from the total cost, it was a fairly inexpensive trip.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin subtractio, subtractionis. Can be decomposed to subtract + -ion.

s.def: The process of subtracting a number from another.
A calculation involving subtracting.
ex: The teacher has set us ten subtractions to do by tomorrow.

s.def: The removal of something.
ex: The subtraction of the wealth from the economy will result in recession.

ety: 1670s, from Latin subtrahendus numerus (“number to be subtracted”), form of subtrahō (“to pull out from under, to subtract”) (English subtract). By surface analysis, subtract + -end (“patient (recipient) of action”).

s.def: A number or quantity to be subtracted from another.
ex: In the subtraction 10 − 4, 4 is the subtrahend.

ety: From Latin sūbulātus.

s.def: Awl-shaped; tapering into a sharp point from a broader base.

ety: From Old French suburbe, subburbe, from Latin suburbium (from sub- (“under-”) + urbs (“city”)). Displaced native Old English underburg (literally “underborough”).

s.def: A residential area located on the outskirts of a city or large town that usually includes businesses that cater to its residents; such as schools, grocery stores, shopping centers, restaurants, convenience stores, etc.
ex: [London] could hardly have contained less than thirty or forty thousand souls within its walls; and the suburbs were very populous.

s.def: Any subdivision of a conurbation, not necessarily on the periphery.
The outer part; the environment.
ex: the suburbs […] of sorrow
the suburb of their straw-built citadel

ety: Etymology tree English suburban Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs)der. Latin -ītēslbor. French -iteder. English -ite English suburbanite From suburban + -ite.

s.def: Someone who lives in the suburbs.
ex: Don't call me a suburbanite just because I live in Oak Grove!
I would suggest that we give the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company a chance to correct the existing faults before condemning the scheme. A SUBURBANITE.
The line was doubled in the nineties and Hillfoot station added for suburbanites in 1900.

ety: PIE word *upó From suburb + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns, the names of collections of things, etc.), perhaps modelled after Latin suburbia (“suburbs”), the plural of suburbium.

s.def: The suburbs as a whole and all that characterizes or pertains to them; (sometimes derogatory) the suburbs as encapsulated or represented by the typical characteristics or qualities of the people living there, especially complacency, conformity, conservativeness, dullness, etc.
ex: Outside a new day is dawning / Outside suburbia is sprawling everywhere
Let's take a ride and run with the dogs tonight / In suburbia / You can't hide, run with the dogs tonight / In suburbia

ety: From Latin subveniō (“come to the aid of”), from sub (“under, up towards”) + veniō (“come”).

s.def: To arrive or happen so as to help or support.
ex: A future state must needs subvene to prevent the whole edifice from falling into ruin.

s.def: To subsidize or defray.

ety: From Middle French subvention, from Late Latin subventio, from Latin subvenio (assist).

s.def: A subsidy; provision of financial or other support.
ex: […] the said religious shall […] pay all papal impositions, subventions, and contributions […]
[…] the Crown-Prince, contrary to wont, broke silence, and begged some dole or subvention for these poor people; but there was nothing to be had.

s.def: The act of coming under.
The act of relieving, as of a burden; support; aid; assistance; help.
To subsidise.

ety: Inherited from Middle English subversion, subversioun, from Old French subversion.

s.def: The act of overthrowing a government or a ruler; dethronement.
A systematic attempt to overthrow a government by working from within; undermining.
The act of subverting; overturning; flipping from beneath.
The condition of being subverted.
A revision considered more similar to preceding subversions than a revision deemed a new "version" is to preceding versions.

ety: From Middle English subverten, from Old French subvertir, from Latin subvertō (“to overthrow”, literally “to underturn, turn from beneath”).

s.def: To overturn from the foundation; to overthrow; to ruin utterly.
ex: He […] razeth your cities, and subverts your towns.
, Book IV, Chapter XVIII This would be to subvert the principles and foundations of all knowledge.

s.def: To pervert, as the mind, and turn it from the truth; to corrupt; to confound.
ex: The oppressive regime stays in power only as long as they manage to subvert the will of the people.

s.def: To upturn convention from the foundation by undermining it (literally, to turn from beneath).
An advertisement created by subvertising.

ety: From sub- + way.

s.def: An underground railway, especially for mass transit of people in urban areas.
ex: He is going to Westminster by subway.

s.def: A train that runs on such an underground railway.
ex: Just before you leave, the subway comes. You get on. It stops at the next station.

s.def: A rapid transit system, regardless of the elevation of its right of way; a metro system.
An underground walkway, tunnel for pedestrians (called pedestrian underpass in US).
ex: Heading beneath the tracks via the subway to the immediate north of the station takes us to the Didcot Railway Centre.

s.def: An underground route for pipes, sewers, etc.
An underground route for creatures (e.g. bats).
To travel by underground railway.
ex: I suppose I could have subwayed around town in search of froufrou French pastry shops.

ety: Modern Latin, neuter singular of Latin succēdāneus (“acting as substitute”).

s.def: A substitute, replacement for something else, particularly of a medicine used in place of another.

ety: From Old French succeder, from Latin succedere (“to go under, go from under, come under, approach, follow, take the place of, receive by succession, prosper, be successful”). Partly displaced English speed, of which the original sense “to succeed” only survives in a few fossilized expressions such as Godspeed.

s.def: To follow something in sequence or time.
ex: Autumn succeeds summer.
Destructive effects […] succeeded the curse.

s.def: To replace or supplant someone in order vis-à-vis an office, position, or title.
ex: The king's eldest son succeeds his father on the throne.
After a contentious election, Jones succeeded Smith as president of the republic.

s.def: To come after or follow; to be subsequent or consequent; (often with to).

To come in the place of another person, thing, or event; to come next in the usual, natural, or prescribed course of things; to follow; hence, to come next in the possession of anything; (often with to).
ex: Following the death of his mother, he succeeded to the throne.
So, if the issue of the elder son succeed before the younger, the crown (or: property) falls to me.

s.def: To prevail in obtaining an intended objective or accomplishment; to prosper as a result or conclusion of a particular effort.
ex: The persecution of any righteous practice has never succeeded in the face of history; in fact, it can expedite the collapse of the persecutory regime.
She succeeded in her efforts to repair the tank.

s.def: To prosper or attain success and beneficial results in general.
ex: voted most likely to succeed

s.def: To turn out, fare, do (well or ill).
To support; to prosper; to promote or give success to.
ex: Succeed my wish and second my design.

s.def: To descend, as an estate or an heirloom, in the same family; to devolve; (often with to).
To fall heir to; to inherit.
ex: (iv) By Transmission of Shares: A person may become a member by registration if he succeeds the estate of a deceased member.

der: if at first you don't succeed, try try…

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin successus, from succēdō (“succeed”), from sub- (“next to”) + cēdō (“go, move”).

s.def: The achievement of one's aim or goal.
ex: His third attempt to pass the entrance exam was a success.
a glowing success

s.def: Financial profitability.
ex: Don't let success go to your head.

s.def: One who, or that which, achieves assumed goals.
ex: Scholastically, he was a success.
The new range of toys has been a resounding success.

s.def: The fact of getting or achieving wealth, respect, or fame.
ex: She is country music's most recent success.

s.def: Something which happens as a consequence; the outcome or result.
A successful person or thing, serving as a model for others.
ex: Challenge yourself and become a success story!
This program has become a success story.

s.def: Anecdotal evidence for the benefits of some product or policy.
ex: You can read about our success stories on our official website.

ety: From success + -ful.

ety: From Middle English suspecioun, borrowed from Latin suspīciō, suspīciōnem, from suspicere, from sub- (“up to”) with specere (“to look at”). Perhaps partly through the influence of Old French sospeçon (or rather the Anglo-Norman form suspecioun). Equivalent to suspect + -ion.

s.def: The act of suspecting something or someone, especially of something wrong.
ex: "When it comes to strangers with guns," I told her, "I think suspicion is more likely to keep you alive than trust."

s.def: Uncertainty, doubt.
The condition of being suspected.
A trace, or slight indication.
ex: a suspicion of a smile
The features are mild but expressive, with just a suspicion[…]of saturnine or sarcastic humor.
Keep hot for 3 minutes, then turn right side up, polish the top with a suspicion of butter, cut in quarters, and send to table.

s.def: The imagining of something without evidence.
To suspect; to have suspicions.
ex: “Well, what’s more dangerous than coming here in the day time!—anybody would suspicion us that saw us.”
"I've been suspicioning here was where they got their information right along," the sheriff commented, and slipped the handcuffs on the landlord.

der: Caesar's wife must be above suspicion

ety: From Old French sospecious, from Latin suspiciosus, suspitiosus.

s.def: Arousing suspicion.
ex: His suspicious behaviour brought him to the attention of the police.

s.def: Expressing suspicion
ex: She gave me a suspicious look.

s.def: Distrustful or tending to suspect.
ex: We know he has a suspicious attitude to get-rich-quick schemes.

ety: Late Middle English, from Latin suspīrāre. Cognate with Old French sospirer (modern soupirer) and Spanish suspirar.

s.def: To breathe, especially to exhale
ex: Fireflies that suspire / In short, soft lapses of transported flame.
To him that yesterday did suspire.

s.def: To sigh.
A long, deep breath; a sigh.

ety: From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).

s.def: To maintain, or keep in existence.
ex: The professor had trouble sustaining students’ interest until the end of her lectures.
The city came under sustained attack by enemy forces.
Sam managed to sustain his erection for two straight hours.

s.def: To provide for or nourish.
ex: provisions to sustain an army
We rode five farsakhs today, sustained by a single bowl of curds and tortured by the wooden saddles.

s.def: To encourage or sanction (something).
To experience or suffer (an injury, etc.).
ex: The building sustained major damage in the earthquake.
[…] if you omit The offer of this time, I cannot promise But that you shall sustain moe new disgraces, With these you bear already.
Shall Turnus then such endless Toil sustain, In fighting Fields, and conquer Towns in vain:

s.def: To confirm, prove, or corroborate; to uphold.
ex: to sustain a charge, an accusation, or a proposition
After the vote is taken, the Chairman states that the decision of the Chair is sustained, or reversed, as the case may be.

s.def: To allow, accept, or admit (e.g. an objection or motion) as valid.
To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support.
ex: A foundation sustains the superstructure; an animal sustains a load; a rope sustains a weight.

s.def: To aid, comfort, or relieve; to vindicate.
ex: His Sons, who seek the Tyrant to sustain, And long for Arbitrary Lords again,

s.def: To be a long-lasting sound.
ex: I like how long that drum sustains.

s.def: A mechanism which can be used to hold a note, as the right pedal on a piano.
ex: To call this music bland is to ignore the down-the-drain vocal fade-aways, the extended sax sustains […]

ety: Etymology tree English sustain Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Proto-Italic *-tāts Latin -tās Latin -abilitas Middle French -abletébor. Middle English -ablete English -ability English sustainability From sustain + -ability.

s.def: The ability to sustain something.
ex: The making of buggy whips is the proverbial exemplar of a business without sustainability in the face of technological change.

ety: Etymology tree English sustain Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English sustainable From sustain + -able.

s.def: Able to be sustained.
Able to be produced or sustained for an indefinite period without damaging the environment, or without depleting a resource; renewable.
ex: sustainable economy
Some critics have asserted that sustainable food is "elitist"; that it's too expensive and not widely available.

ety: From Middle English sustenaunce, from Old French sustenance, from sustenir with the suffix -ance, from Vulgar Latin *sustenire, from Latin sustinere. Compare also Late Latin sustinentia. Equivalent to sustain + -ance.

s.def: Something that provides support or nourishment.

ety: From Latin sustentaculum; compare sustentate. Attested since the eighteenth century.

s.def: A supporting structure, a body part that supports one or more other parts.
ex: While of only moderate size, the sustentaculum is very thick and prominent; its astragalar facet is of irregularly oval shape and nearly plane.

ety: First attested in 1382: from the Old French sustentacion, from the Latin sustentātio, from sustentō; compare the Italian sostentazione, the Occitan sustentacion, the Portuguese sustentação, and the Spanish sustentación. Doublet of sustentatio.

s.def: The act or the result of sustaining; sustainment; sustention.
The aggregate of the functions by which a living organism is maintained in a normal condition of weight and growth.

The scheme by which the ministers of the Free Church of Scotland are supported by voluntary contributions not local or congregational, but with a national altruism or solidarity paid into a great central fund, out of which equal stipends are paid to all alike.

ety: First attested in 1868: a nominalisation of sustain, by analogy with detain → detention, retain → retention, etc., coined for contradistinction with sustentation.

s.def: sustentation

ety: From Latin susurratio.

s.def: A low and indistinct whispering sound; a murmur.
ex: Halleck nodded, heard the faint sussuration^([sic]) and felt the air shift as a lockport swung open beside him.

ety: From Dutch soeteler (modern zoetelaar).

s.def: A person who follows an army, selling provisions.
A modern business that provides period uniforms and supplies to reenactors.

ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit सूत्र (sū́tra, “thread, yarn, string; rule”). Doublet of sutta; more distantly related to sew and suture.

s.def: A rule or thesis in Sanskrit grammar or Hindu law or philosophy.
A scriptural narrative, especially a discourse of the Buddha.

ety: From Sanskrit सती (satī́, “good and virtuous or faithful wife”), from सत् (sát, “true, good, right etc.”). In English usage since 1786. Doublet of sin.

s.def: The traditional custom of a Hindu woman giving herself up to be cremated on her husband’s funeral pyre as a sign of her devotion.

ety: From Middle English suture, from Latin sūtūra (“suture”), from suere (“sew, join or tack together”) + -tūra (forms action nouns).

s.def: A seam formed by sewing two edges together, especially to join pieces of skin in surgically treating a wound.
Thread used to sew or stitch two edges (especially of skin) together.
An area where separate terrane join together along a major fault.
A type of fibrous joint bound together by Sharpey's fibres which only occurs in the skull.
A seam or line, such as that between the segments of a crustacean, between the whorls of a univalve shell, or where the elytra of a beetle meet.
The seam at the union of two margins in a plant.

The procedure by which a subject comes to be identified with its own representation, as in the identification of the speaker with the sign “I” within a certain discourse; (by extension) any process by which the content of something is determined or supplied from outside itself.
To sew up or join by means of a suture.

ety: Borrowed from Fijian Suva, from suva (“mound”), from Proto-Central Eastern Oceanic *supa.

s.def: capital of Fiji
The capital city of Fiji.
ex: Suva is the capital of the Fiji Islands

ety: Borrowed from Arabic السُّوَيْدَاء (as-suwaydāʔ).

s.def: A city in southern Syria.
A governorate in southern Syria.

ety: From French suzerain, based on sus (“up, above”) (from Latin sursum) with the ending of souverain (whence also English sovereign).

s.def: A dominant nation or state that has control over the international affairs of a subservient state which otherwise has domestic autonomy.
ex: The origin of these conflicts is to be sought in the position which Rome acquired about 275 b.c. as suzerain and protector of all Italy.

s.def: A feudal landowner to whom vassals were forced to pledge allegiance.

ety: Named for the discoverer, Akira Suzuki.

s.def: The organic reaction of an aryl- or vinyl-boronic acid with an aryl- or vinyl-halide or pseudohalide, such as triflates, catalyzed by a palladium(0) complex, widely used to synthesize polyolefins, styrenes, and substituted biphenyls.

ety: Borrowed from Old Norse Svalbarð n probably through Norwegian. From svalr (“cool”) + barð (“edge, brim”), thus roughly meaning “cold shore”, probably alluding to the treeless landscape mostly covered with grass. The name was first attested in annales referring to year 1194, but it’s uncertain whether it referred to the modern archipelago. Cognate with Faroese Svalbarð, Icelandic Svalbarði and Norwegian Svalbard.

s.def: An archipelago, territory, and unincorporated area of Norway northeast of Greenland, in the Arctic Ocean.

ety: Borrowed from French svelte, from Italian svelto (“stretched out”), past participle of svellere (“to pluck out, root out”), from Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from ex + vellere (“to pluck, stretch”).

s.def: Attractively thin; gracefully slender.
ex: My first priority was to help Trumps lose her pudgy look and gain a healthier, svelter size.

s.def: Refined, delicate.
A city in North Macedonia

ety: Mid 17th century (in the sense 'mop for cleaning the decks'): back-formation from Middle English swabber (“sailor detailed to swab decks”), from Middle Dutch zwabber, from a Germanic base meaning 'splash' or 'sway', also found as nautical German Schwabber and Volga German Schwabber ("scrubber, mop, swab")

s.def: A sample taken with a swab (piece of absorbent material).
A mop, especially on a ship.
A small piece of soft, absorbent material, such as gauze, used to clean wounds, apply medicine, or take samples of body fluids. Often attached to a stick or wire to aid access.
A piece of material used for cleaning or sampling other items like musical instruments or guns.
A sailor; a swabby.
ex: As for that swab, he's good and dead, he is.

s.def: A naval officer's epaulet.
To use a swab on something, or clean something with a swab.
ex: swab the deck of a ship

ety: From Middle English swathlen (“to bind; swaddle”), from Middle English swathel, swethel, from Old English swaþul, swæþel, sweþel, sweoþol (“swaddling cloth”), equivalent to swathe (“to wrap with fabric”) + -le (agent/instrumental suffix), the word then underwent th-stopping (its voiced th became a d). Cognate with Middle Dutch swadel (“swaddling; bandage”), Old High German swedili (“poultice”), Old English sweþian, besweþian (“to wrap; swaddle”).

s.def: To bind (a baby) with long narrow strips of cloth.
To beat; cudgel.
Anything used to swaddle with, such as a cloth or band.
ex: They put me in bed in all my swaddles.
The baby is awake, trying to escape the swaddle I have imprisoned her in.

ety: From Middle English swaþelynge; equivalent to swaddle + -ing.

s.def: The practice of wrapping infants in clothing that restricts movement.
Clothing of this kind.
A garment, made of strips of cloth, used to bind an infant and restrict movement of its limbs.
An early period in development, infancy, the beginnings of something; inception.
ex: The steel—industry wore swaddling clothes when the first walkout occurred exactly 100 years ago.

ety: Named after the American linguist Morris Swadesh.

s.def: A list of vocabulary with universal test meanings and concepts.

ety: Inherited from Middle English swagen, a late collateral form of *swawen possibly originating from Lancashire and Yorkshire (possibly continued in Scots swaw (“wave”); parallel to e.g. drag for draw), from Old Norse *svaga (“to swerve, sway”), of unclear origin. Compare dialectal Norwegian svaga (“to sway, swing, stagger”).

s.def: To (cause to) sway.
ex: 1790, William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, The Argument, p. 1, Hungry clouds swag on the deep
Soap/soak the mop into the mop bucket, squeeze it out slightly, swag it back and forth across the piss stained concrete, mop it dry.

ex: so laid, they are more apt in swagging down, to pierce with their points, then in the jacent Posture
I swagge as a fatte persos belly swaggeth as he goth.

ex: Detective Inspector Douglas Browne, the flesh of whose cheeks hung in swags, had the friendly aspect of a large brown-eyed dog.

ex: Now this dude got swag, and he was pushing up on me but, it wasn't like we was kicking it or anything!

s.def: Branded handout, freebies, or giveaways, often distributed at conventions; merchandise.

ety: Inherited from Middle English swage, from Middle French souage, from Old French souage (“decorative groove”), from soue (“rope”), from Vulgar Latin *soca, from Gaulish *souca (“cord”), from Proto-Celtic *soukā, from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to twist, bend”).

s.def: A tool, used by blacksmiths and other metalworkers, for shaping of a metal item.
ex: "I made a swage and hammered out the test bars to the required .615 inch plus or minus .003, the thickness of a sheet of paper. […]

Obsolete form of assuage.
ex: apt words have power to swage

ety: A frequentative form of swag (“to sway”), first attested in A Midsummer Night's Dream (1595), see quotations.

s.def: To behave (especially to walk or carry oneself) in a pompous, superior manner.
To boast or brag noisily; to bluster; to bully.
ex: To be great is not […] to swagger at our footmen.
“They say there’s something wrong with our president!” Mr. Trump swaggered at his indoor Tulsa rally in June,[…]

s.def: To walk with a swaying motion.
ex: It's the injustice… he is so unjust— whiskey-blind, swaggering home at five.

s.def: Confidence, pride.
A bold or arrogant strut.
A prideful boasting or bragging.
Fashionable; trendy.
ex: Mrs. Morton was well known for her Americanisms, her swagger dinner parties, and beautiful Paris gowns.

s.def: Someone carrying a swag; a swagman.
ex: There were now more swaggers passing down Ferry Street and more coming to ask for food […].

ety: Borrowed from Swahili Mswahili / Kiswahili, from Arabic سَوَاحِلِيّ (sawāḥiliyy, “(people) of the coasts”), from سَوَاحِل (sawāḥil, “coasts”), broken plural of سَاحِل (sāḥil, “coast”).

s.def: An agglutinative language of the Bantu branch widely spoken in East Africa. Born in its modern form from the hybridization of the Arabic and Bantu cultures, it was the language of the traders in East Africa, and spread along the routes of trade.
ex: Similarly, Swahili evolved as the trading language in East Africa and is described as having an Arab vocabulary upon an African grammar.

ety: From Middle English swayn, swain, sweyn, swein, from Old English sweġen (attested also as personal name Swein, Sweġen), from Old Norse sveinn, from Proto-Germanic *swainaz (“relative, young man, servant”), from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“oneself; separate; apart”), thus properly one's own. Cognate with Danish svend (“hireling, young man”), Norwegian svein (“lad, young man, servant”) Icelandic sveinn (“boy, lad, servant”), Swedish sven (“swain, servant”), Low German Sween, dialectal German Schwe…

s.def: A young man or boy in service; a servant.
A knight's servant; an attendant.
A country labourer; a countryman, a rustic.
A rural lover; a male sweetheart in a pastoral setting.
ex: Why thus from the Plain does my Shepherdess rove Forsaking Her Swain and neglecting his love?
You're the belle of the ball, and these are all your swains, hoping for a glimpse of ankle.

ety: From Middle English swolwen, from Old English swelgan, from Proto-West Germanic *swelgan, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą (“to swallow, revel, devour”), from Proto-Indo-European *swelk- (“to gulp”). Cognate with Dutch zwelgen (“to revel, carouse, guzzle”), German schwelgen (“to delight, indulge”), Danish svælge (“to swallow”), Norwegian Bokmål svelge (“to swallow”), Norwegian Nynorsk svelgje (“to swallow”), Swedish svälja (“to swallow, gulp”), Faroese svølgja (“to swallow”), Icelandic svelgja (“t…

s.def: To cause (food, drink etc.) to pass from the mouth into the stomach; to take into the stomach through the throat.
ex: Clothes are to be worn and food is to be swallowed: they remain trapped in the physical world.

s.def: To take food down into the stomach; to make the muscular contractions of the oesophagus to achieve this, often taken as a sign of nervousness or strong emotion.
ex: My throat was so sore that I was unable to swallow.
She swallowed nervously then, appearing near sick with what she had to say.

s.def: To accept easily or without questions; to believe, accept.
ex: this humbug was readily swallowed by men who were supposed to be intelligent,
Most newspapers we saw swallowed whole an S.R. estimate that it would cost £20m to equip the Region with point heaters.
Be careful of the Commie Lies / swallow them and freedom dies / The USA must realize / that she's the biggest prize.

s.def: to take in, to consume
The amount swallowed in one gulp; the act of swallowing.
ex: He took the aspirin with a single swallow of water.
She took a swallow of milk and made a face. "This milk is blinky."

To take (something) in so that it disappears; to consume, absorb.
ex: The necessary provision of the life swallows the greatest part of their time.

ex: Homer excels […] in this, that he swallowed up the honour of those who succeeded him.

s.def: To retract; to recant.
ex: to swallow one's opinions
Left her in her tears, and dried not one of them with his comfort; swallowed his vows whole

s.def: To put up with; to bear patiently or without retaliation.
ex: to swallow an affront or insult

ety: From swallow + tail.

s.def: Any of various butterflies of the family Papilionidae, many of which have a long extension to each hindwing.
Anything, such as a burgee, of a similar forked shape.
The forked tail of a swallow.
A type of tailcoat with two long tapering tails.
Alternative form of swallow-wort.

ety: Borrowed from Hindi स्वामी (svāmī), from Sanskrit स्वामिन् (svāmín).

s.def: A Hindu ascetic or religious teacher.
A Hindu religious idol.

ety: Early attestations (starting in 1624) are from North America, but the term was probably in local use in Britain earlier. The etymology is not entirely certain; it is probably a fusion of Middle English swam (“swamp, muddy pool, bog, marsh”, also “fungus, mushroom”) — from Old English swamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz — and Middle English sompe (“marsh, morass”), from either Middle Dutch somp, sump (“marsh, swamp”) or Midd…

s.def: An area of wet (water-saturated), spongy (soft) land, often with trees, generally a rich ecosystem for certain plants and animals but ill-suited for many agricultural purposes. (A type of wetland. Compare marsh, bog, fen.)
ex: Some small Marshes and Swamps there are, but more profitable than hurtfull.

s.def: A place or situation that is foul or where progress is difficult.

ex: I have been swamped with paperwork ever since they started using the new system.
"I'm being swamped now with calls from parents and young people who are upset that there are not many options for employment this summer," he said.

ex: The Whig majority of the house of Lords was swamped by the creation of twelve Tory peers.
Having swamped himself in following the ignis fatuus of a theory[…]

a person who travels by foot but has his belongings on a wagon.

ex: The old swamper shifted his broom and held it between his elbow and his side while he held out his hand for the can.

To travel or move about in an aimless, idle, or pretentiously casual way.

ety: From dialectal swank (“to strut, behave ostentatiously”), perhaps from an unrecorded Old English root, derived from Proto-Germanic *swankijaną (“to cause to sway, swing”) or from Proto-Germanic *swankaz (“lithe, bendsome, slender”), related to the Scots swank and the Middle High German swanken, modern German schwanken (“to sway”).

Ostentation; bravado.

ety: From Middle English swappen (“to swap”), originally meaning "to hurl" or "to strike", the word alludes to striking hands together when making an exchange; probably from Old English *swappian, a secondary form of Old English swāpan (“to swoop”). ex: I'll swap out the dead battery for a new one.

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English swerd, sward (“rind, skin; leather strap; sod, turf”) [and other forms], from Old English sweard (“rind; skin”), from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind; tough skin; turf”); further etymology unknown. The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: Earth which grass has grown into the upper layer of; greensward, sod, turf; (countable) a portion of such earth.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin syllabus (“list”), which arose from accusative plural syllabōs appearing as a corruption of sittybās (accusative plural of sittyba, from Ancient Greek σιττύβα (sittúba, “parchment label; table of contents”)) in a 1470s edition of Cicero's “Ad Atticum” IV.5 and 8, influenced by the stem of Ancient Greek συλλαμβάνω (sullambánō, “to put together”).

s.def: A summary of topics which will be covered during an academic course, or a text or lecture.
ex: ‘I checked online for a beginner syllabus,’ she say. ‘A syllabus is a plan for how we would work, what I can teach you.’

s.def: The headnote of a reported case; the brief statement of the points of law determined prefixed to a reported case.

ety: From Latin syllepsis, from Ancient Greek σύλληψις (súllēpsis), from συλλαμβάνω (sullambánō).

s.def: A figure of speech in which one word simultaneously modifies two or more other words such that the modification must be understood differently with respect to each modified word; often causing humorous incongruity.
Growth in which lateral branches develop from a lateral meristem, without the formation of a bud or period of dormancy, when the lateral meristem is split from a terminal meristem.

ety: From Old French silogisme (“syllogism”), from Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”). Doublet of syllogismus.

s.def: An argument whose conclusion is supported by two premises, of which one contains the term that is the predicate of the conclusion, and the other contains the term that is the subject of the conclusion; common to both premises is a term that is excluded from the conclusion.
A trick, artifice; an extremely subtle, sophisticated, or deceptive argument; a sophism.

ety: From Middle French sillogiser, ultimately from Ancient Greek συλλογίζεσθαι (sullogízesthai).

s.def: To reason by means of syllogisms.
To deduce consequences from.

ety: First attested in 1657. From New Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century. The coinage may derive from Latin sylvestris (“of the woods”) and nympha (“nymph”). Ultimately from the root silva (“woods, forest”). Related to sylvan. More at Wikipedia.

s.def: An invisible being of the air.
ex: Her heart fluttered with expectation—her step was buoyant with hope, and she sprung into the carriage with the lightness of a sylph.

s.def: The elemental being of air, usually female.
A slender woman or girl, usually graceful and sometimes with the implication of sublime station over everyday people.
Any of the mainly dark green and blue hummingbirds (genus Aglaiocercus), the male of which has a long forked tail.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sylvanus, possibly via Middle French sylvain, from Latin silvanus, cognate with Latin Silvānus (“Roman god of the woods”), from silva (“forest”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”). The ⟨y⟩ in sylvanus and its descendants is due to influence from Ancient Greek ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood, matter”), transliterated in the Latin style as hyle. Analysable as sylva (“silva”) + -an.

s.def: Pertaining to the forest, or woodlands.
ex: Over the course of the nineteenth century, an entity known as the 'German forest' arose out of Central Europe's sylvan diversity.

s.def: Residing in a forest or wood.
Wooded, or covered in forest.

ety: From Latin sylvāticus. See sylvan. Doublet of savage.

s.def: Of or pertaining to woods or woodland organisms; sylvan
Of or pertaining to wild rather than domestic animals
Of or pertaining to diseases or parasites borne or transmitted by sylvatic organisms
A wild animal

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Proto-Hellenic *ksún Ancient Greek σύν (sún) Ancient Greek σῠν- (sŭn-) Ancient Greek σῠμ- (sŭm-) English sym- From Ancient Greek συμ- (sum-), variant of συν- (sun-), from σύν (sún, “with, in company with, together with”).

s.def: variant of syn-, used before the letters b, m and p.

ety: From sym- + -biont.

s.def: An organism that lives in a symbiotic relationship.

ety: From Ancient Greek συμβίωσις (sumbíōsis, “living together”). By surface analysis, sym- + -biosis.

s.def: A relationship of mutual benefit, especially among different species.
The close and long-term relationship or interaction between two or more different species.
ex: Bees and flowers display symbiosis. The bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.

s.def: The state of people of different types, races, cultures, communities, etc., living together.
The occurrence of two different or opposing things in the same time and place.
ex: In this peculiar and deadly symbiosis the presence of warfare stimulates trade and the presence of trade stimulates warfare.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon)bor. Latin symbolumbor. French symboleder. English symbol From French symbole, from Latin symbolus, symbolum (“a sign, mark, token, symbol, in Late Latin also a creed”), fro…

s.def: A character or glyph representing an idea, concept or object.
ex: "$" is the symbol for dollars in the US and some other countries.
Chinese people use word symbols for writing.

s.def: object meant to represent another
A thing considered the embodiment or cardinal exemplar of a concept, theme, or other thing.
ex: The lion is the symbol of courage; the lamb is the symbol of meekness or patience.

s.def: A type of noun whereby the form refers to the same entity independently of the context; a symbol arbitrarily denotes a referent. See also icon and index.
A summary of a dogmatic statement of faith.
ex: The Apostles, Nicene Creed and the confessional books of Protestantism, such as the Augsburg Confession of Lutheranism are considered symbols.

s.def: The numerical expression which defines a plane's position relative to the assumed axes.
That which is thrown into a common fund; hence, an appointed or accustomed duty.
ex: They do their work in the days of peace […] and come to pay their symbol in a war or in a plague.

s.def: Share; allotment.
ex: The persons who are to be judged […] shall all appear to receive their symbol.

s.def: An internal identifier used by a debugger to relate parts of the compiled program to the corresponding names in the source code.
A signalling event on a communications channel; a signal that cannot be further divided into meaningful information.

ety: From symbolical + -ly or symbolic + -ally.

s.def: In a symbolic manner.
By means of symbols or a symbol.
As symbols or a symbol.

ety: From symbol + -ism, sense 2 being a semantic loan from French symbolisme.

s.def: Representation of a concept through symbols or underlying meanings of objects or qualities.

An art movement originating in late 19th-century France and Belgium, seeking to represent absolute truths symbolically through language and metaphorical images, mainly as a reaction against naturalism and realism.
A combining together of parts or ingredients.

ety: From Middle French symboliser.

s.def: To be symbolic of; to represent.
ex: Doves often symbolize peace.
The broken chain symbolizes freedom.

s.def: To use symbols; to represent ideas symbolically.
To convert something into a symbol.
To resemble each other in qualities or properties; to correspond; to harmonize.
ex: They both symbolize in this, that they love to look upon themselves through multiplying glasses.

s.def: To hold the same faith; to agree.
ex: The believers in pretended miracles have always previously symbolized with the performers of them.

ety: From Latin Sȳmē.

s.def: An island of the Dodecanese, Greece.
A municipality of Rhodes regional unit, Greece.

ety: Either from French symétriser or symmetry + -ize.

s.def: To make or become symmetric.

ety: From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría), from σύμμετρος (súmmetros, “symmetrical”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, sym- + -metry.

s.def: Exact correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center or axis.
The satisfying arrangement of a balanced distribution of the elements of a whole.

ety: Mid 17th century in the sense “relating to an affinity or paranormal influence”, from Latin sympathēticus. By surface analysis, sympathy + -etic (“pertaining to”); compare pathetic. Displaced native Old English efnþrōwiende.

s.def: of a person: attracting the liking of others
Of, related to, feeling, showing, or characterized by sympathy.
ex: John looked very upset. I gave him a sympathetic look.

s.def: Attracting the liking of others. (of a person)
Relating to, producing, or denoting an effect which arises through an affinity, interdependence, or mutual association.
ex: Sympathetic magic is based on imitation or correspondence.
sympathetic ink

s.def: Relating to or denoting the part of the autonomic nervous system consisting of nerves arising from ganglia near the middle part of the spinal cord, supplying the internal organs, blood vessels, and glands, and balancing the action of the parasympathetic nerves.
ex: Sympathetic innervation involves epinephrine.

s.def: A sympathetic nerve.

ety: Borrowed from French sympathiser. By surface analysis, sympathy + -ize. Displaced native Old English efnþrōwian (literally “to suffer with or together”).

s.def: To have, show or express sympathy; to be affected by feelings similar to those of another, in consequence of knowing the person to be thus affected; to feel for.
ex: The wives were sympathizing with each other in slightly raised voices.

s.def: To support, favour, have sympathy (with a political cause or movement, a side in a conflict / in an action).
ex: He’d go to […] Soviet Russia—now giving us the whole story, that he sympathized with the Reds and admired Lenin […]
President Obama in a speech this past week said that we should solve the nation's bee problem. Oh, God, we elected a guy who sympathizes with bees?

s.def: To say in an expression of sympathy.
ex: “How much he slapped my sons—you should see their swollen faces, Panditji,” said Dukhi. […] “Poor children,” sympathized Pandit Lallaram.

s.def: To have a common feeling, as of bodily pleasure or pain.
ex: […] the mind will sympathize so much with the anguish and debility of the body, that it will be […] too distracted to fix itself in meditation.

s.def: To share (a feeling or experience).
To agree; to be in accord; to harmonize.

ety: Etymology tree English sympathize Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English sympathizer From sympathize + -er.

s.def: A person who sympathizes (with a political cause, a side in a conflict, etc.); a supporter.
ex: His reputation was ruined when it was revealed that he had been a Nazi sympathizer before the war.
[…] she exposed herself to the fury of the sympathizers with slavery, without fear, and suffered their blows without flinching.

s.def: A person who has, shows or expresses sympathy (with another person or people); a person who enters into the feelings of another.
ex: Not a mood of his but what found a ready sympathiser in Margaret; not a wish of his that she did not strive to forecast, and to fulfil.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής (sŭmpăthḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, “-y”, nominal suffix). Equivalent to sym- (“acting or considered together”) + -pathy (“feeling”).

s.def: feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another — see also compassion
A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.
Inclination to think or feel alike; emotional or intellectual accord; common feeling.
ex: Many people in Hollywood were blacklisted merely because they were suspected of Communist sympathies.

s.def: An affinity, association or mutual relationship between people or things such that they are correspondingly affected by any condition.
ex: A peculiarity of were-animals is the sympathy that exists between their animal form and that of the human with whom it is connected.
Sympathy likened anything to anything else in universal attraction, e.g. the fate of men to the course of the planets.

s.def: Characteristic of a symphony.
ex: symphonic poem
She enjoyed the rich symphonic sound of the concert.
The band incorporated symphonic elements into their rock music.

s.def: An extended piece of music of sophisticated structure, usually for orchestra.
ex: classical symphony
compose a symphony
full symphony orchestra

s.def: An instrumental introduction or termination to a vocal composition.
Harmony in music or colour, or a harmonious combination of elements.
ex: She described the city at night as a symphony of lights and sounds.

s.def: A symphony orchestra.
A large orchestra that traditionally plays Western classical orchestral music.

ety: Borrowed from New Latin symphysis.

s.def: The process of two originally separate bones growing together as the subject matures, as with the pubic bones or lower jawbones in humans.

A place where two bones are closely joined in the median plane of the body, either forming an immovable joint (as between the pubic bones in the center of the pelvis) or completely fused (as at the midline of the lower jaw).

ety: From Latin symposiacus.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a symposium.
ex: The ancient custome in Symposiack meetings was to weave chaplets of roses about their heads.
symposiac disputations amongst my acquaintance

s.def: A conference or conversation of philosophers at a banquet.
Any similar gathering.

ety: From Ancient Greek συμποσίαρχος (sumposíarkhos). By surface analysis, symposium + -arch.

s.def: The master of a feast.

ety: Borrowed from Latin symposium, from Ancient Greek συμπόσιον (sumpósion, “drinking party”) from συμπίνω (sumpínō, “drink together”), from συν- (sun-, “together-”) + πίνω (pínō, “drink”). Morphologically compare compotation.

s.def: A conference or other meeting for discussion of a topic, especially one in which the participants make presentations.
A drinking party in Ancient Greece, especially one with intellectual discussion.
A collection of essays, articles or papers on a particular subject by a number of contributors.

ety: From Middle English sinthoma, from Medieval Latin sinthoma, altered by Late Latin symptoma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of συμπίπτω (sumpíptō, “Ι befall”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”). See also syn-, -oma, -ome.

s.def: A perceived change in some function, sensation or appearance of a person that indicates a disease or disorder, such as fever, headache or rash; strictly, a symptom is felt or experienced by the patient, while a sign can be detected by an observer.
ex: The doctor told that his coughing and sneezing was the symptom of standing for too long in the rain.
Swollen breasts, morning sickness, and a missed period are classic symptoms of pregnancy.
Sometimes a change in olfactory experience is the only symptom in a patient who is otherwise healthy.

s.def: A signal; anything that indicates, or is characteristic of, the presence of something else, especially of something undesirable.
ex: Lying, hiding one's true feelings, and having affairs are typical symptoms of a doomed marriage.
Some people see birth outside of marriage as a social problem—a sign of a breakdown in the traditional family and a symptom of moral decay.

ety: Borrowed from French symptomatique, from New Latin symptomaticus, from Ancient Greek συμπτωματικός (sumptōmatikós, “of or pertaining to a chance (or a symptom), casual”), from σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a symptom”). By surface analysis, symptom + -atic.

s.def: Showing symptoms.
Constituting a symptom or indication; characteristic, indicative.
ex: The city's problems are symptomatic of the crisis that is spreading throughout the country.
Symptomatic of a shallow understanding and an unamiable temper.

s.def: Of a treatment, that only affects the symptoms of a disease without targeting the underlying cause.
Relating to symptomatics.

ety: From Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “symptom (of diseases)”) and -λογία (-logía, “study, branch of knowledge”) (i.e., symptomato- and -logy). Compare French symptomatologie.

s.def: The scientific study of the symptoms of diseases, as an aspect of clinical medicine, differential diagnosis, public health, and so on.
ex: Big Pharma has redefined the symptomatology of medical conditions in such a way as to expand enormously the market for its drugs.

s.def: The aggregate of symptoms of a particular disease; the pattern of symptoms, and their timing, that is characteristic of it.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Proto-Hellenic *ksún Ancient Greek σύν (sún) Ancient Greek σῠν- (sŭn-)der. English syn- From Ancient Greek συν- (sun-), from σύν (sún, “with, in company with, together with”). Compare Sanskrit सम्- (sam-).

s.def: identical
ex: syn- + -onym → synonym
syn- + glyph → synoglyph

s.def: with, together
ex: syn- + chron- → synchronize

s.def: concomitant
ex: syn- + esthesia → synaesthesia

ety: Inherited from Middle English synagoge, from Old French synagoge, from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”), from σῠ́ν (sŭ́n, “with, together”) & ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead”). By surface analysis, syn- + -agogue.

s.def: A place of worship for Jews.
A congregation of Jews for the purpose of worship or religious study.
Any assembly of folk.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύναψις (súnapsis, “conjunction”), from συνάπτω (sunáptō, “to clasp”). Introduced by neurophysiologist Charles Scott Sherrington.

s.def: The junction between the terminal of a neuron and either another neuron or a muscle or gland cell, over which nerve impulses pass.

ety: From Ancient Greek σῠ́νᾰψῐς (sŭ́năpsĭs, “contact”).

s.def: The association of homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes during the initial part of meiosis.
Alternative form of synapse.

ety: From syn- + -carp, New Latin syncarpium. See syncarpous.

s.def: A kind of aggregate fruit in which the ovaries cohere in a solid mass, with a slender receptacle, as in the magnolia.
A similar multiple fruit, such as a mulberry.

ety: By surface analysis, syn- + chron- + -ic; historically, see synchronous § Etymology.

s.def: Relating to the study of a language at only one point in its history.
Occurring at a specific point in time.

ety: From synchron(ous) + -icity. From Jungian psychology in the 1920s. By surface analysis, syn- + chron- + -icity; historically, see synchronous § Etymology.

s.def: The state of being synchronous or simultaneous.
Coincidences that seem to be meaningfully related; supposedly the result of "universal forces".

ety: By surface analysis, syn- + chron- + -ism.

s.def: The state of being synchronous.
A temporal relationship between events.
The tabular arrangement of contemporary events etc. in history.

s.def: The state or property of being synchronized.
ex: The generator went off line when it lost synchronization with the power line.
Synchronization, the coordinated dynamics of many units to the same timing is found throughout the natural world.

s.def: The arrangement of military actions in time, space, and purpose to produce maximum relative combat power at a decisive place and time.

s.def: cause two events to have coordinated timing
To cause two or more events or actions to happen at exactly the same time or same rate, or in a time-coordinated way.
ex: The path of this great empire, through its arch of progress, synchronized with that of Christianity.

s.def: To set (a clock or watch) to display the same time as another.
ex: We synchronized our watches and agreed to meet at four o'clock precisely.

s.def: To cause (a set of files, data, or settings) on one computer or device to be (and try to remain) the same as on another.
To agree, be coordinated with, or complement well.
ex: Gay men often have interests and concerns that don't synchronize with the issues considered top priorities by lesbians.

s.def: To coordinate or combine.
A swimming event where swimmers perform a synchronised routine of dance moves in the water.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos, “contemporaneous”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, syn- + chron- + -ous = synchrony + -ous; however, all related words (e.g., synchronic, synchrony, synchronicity, diachronous, diachronic, diachrony, diachronicity) were coined later, either as back-formations from, or otherwise by analogy with the surface analysis of, synchronous.

s.def: At the same time, at the same frequency.
ex: There is a synchronous tie between the motors in each machine room to ensure that the span remains level during raising and lowering.

s.def: Interacting with other elements in series; blocking; interacting with the same program or thread as other operations, thereby preventing those operations from resuming until the operation of interest is complete.

ety: From Ancient Greek σύν (sún, “with, together”) + κλαστός (klastós, “broken in pieces”) + -ic.

s.def: curved toward the same side in all directions
of a surface whose Gaussian curvature is positive at all points

ety: From syn- + -clinal.

s.def: A synclinal fold.

ety: From syn- + -cline.

s.def: A concave-upward fold in rock strata

ety: From Medieval Latin syncopātus, past participle of syncopō, from Late Latin syncopa, from Ancient Greek σύν (sún, “with”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “cut”).

s.def: to omit a vocalic or consonantal sound or a syllable from a word; to use syncope
to stress or accentuate the weak beat of a rhythm; to use syncopation

s.def: A loss of consciousness when fainting.
ex: Schneider, the father of rhinology, mentions a woman in whom the odor of orange-flowers produced syncope.
[…]the rapidly-whitening face, the miserable fixed smile, meant a syncope within the next few bars.

s.def: The elision or loss of a sound from the interior of a word, especially of a vowel sound with loss of a syllable.
A missed beat or off-beat stress in music resulting in syncopation.

ety: Back-formation from syncretism: by surface analysis, syncret(ize) + -ic.

s.def: Combining disparate elements in one system, especially as in forms of religious observance, philosophical systems, or artistic creations.

ety: From Latin syncretismus, from Ancient Greek συγκρητισμός (sunkrētismós, “federation of Cretan cities”), from συγκρητίζω (sunkrētízō, “to unite against a common enemy”), from σύν (sún, “together”) (see English syn-) + Κρῆτες (Krêtes, “Cretans”). By surface analysis, syn- + Crete + -ism (“Crete joining together”).

s.def: The reconciliation or fusion of different systems or beliefs (religious, cultural, or otherwise cosmologic or ontologic).
ex: Kraft's functional view of Anthropology eventually leads to syncretism because God is understood as working within a modern, humanistic paradigm.

s.def: The fusion of different inflexional forms.
ex: In this chapter, I will investigate whether they deserve this name by looking at syncretisms between clusivity and other person markers.

s.def: Alternative form of syndactyle.

ety: From Ancient Greek σύνδεσμος (súndesmos, “binding, fastening, ligament”).

s.def: ligament

ety: Borrowed from New Latin syndesmōsis.

s.def: A slightly movable articulation or joint where the contiguous bony surfaces are rough and are united by an interosseous ligament (e.g. between the fibula and tibia at the ankle).
ex: He was diagnosed with syndesmosis in his left ankle, the same injury that cost Ryan Hoffman a place in last year's grand final.

ety: From Latin syndeticus, from Ancient Greek συνδετικός (sundetikós), from σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding”) + -κός (-kós, “-ic: forming adjectives”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”).

s.def: Of or related to syndeton, the use of a conjunction.
ex: Guns and butter is a syndetic phrase.
Asymmetry in pronominal sequencing is a recurrent feature of syndetic coordination, though with considerable variation in relation to literary genre.

s.def: Synonym of connective, serving to connect.
ex: With the syndetic juxtaposition of distinct members, the article is not often repeated.

s.def: Synonym of crossreferenced.
ex: Syndetic, applied to an alphabetical subject catalogue or dictionary catalogue which includes cross-references as connecting links between subjects.
The dictionary includes syndetic references.
