s.def: A government official having different duties depending on the country; also, a magistrate, especially one of the Chief Magistrates of Geneva, Switzerland.
ex: A syndic shall be appointed for every canal not being administered by a corporation or other public body on behalf of any part of the community.
In 1760 one Intendant went so far as to dissolve the militia altogether and appointed syndics to carry on the local government.

s.def: An agent of a corporation, or of any body of people engaged in a business enterprise; specifically, in the University of Cambridge, a member of the senate appointed to carry out specific duties.
ex: In France, syndics are appointed by the creditors of a bankrupt to manage the property.

s.def: A layperson who is given official responsibility for the finances, care, and civil administration of the nonreligious details of a convent or religious community.

ety: From French syndicalisme.

s.def: Control of both industry and government by labor unions, especially as achieved through revolutionary direct action; advocacy for attempts to bring it about.

ety: Anglicized from French syndicat (“office of a syndic; board of syndics; trade union”) on the basis of -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a group formed of people of this same office), equivalent to syndic (“syndic; representative; (especially) chief magistrate of Geneva”) + -at (“-ate”, forms nouns denoting rank or office), from Medieval Latin *syndicātus, from syndicus (“representative of a corporation or town; syndic”) (from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate for a defendant”…

s.def: A group of individuals or companies formed to transact some specific business, or to promote a common interest; a self-coordinating group.
ex: a gambling syndicate

s.def: The office or jurisdiction of a syndic; a body or council of syndics.
To become a syndicate.
To put under the control of a group acting as a unit.
To release media content through a syndicate to be broadcast or published through multiple outlets.

ety: From the verb syndicate (1925).

s.def: The act of syndicating a news feature by publishing it in multiple newspapers etc, simultaneously

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ, “concurrence of symptoms, concourse”), from σύνδρομος (súndromos, “running together”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + δρόμος (drómos, “running, course”).

s.def: A recognizable pattern of signs, symptoms and/or behaviours, especially of a disease or medical or psychological condition.
ex: Down syndrome; acquired immune deficiency syndrome; restless-leg syndrome; battered-wife syndrome

s.def: Any set of characteristics regarded as identifying a certain type, condition, etc., usually adverse.
ex: not-in-my-backyard syndrome; tip-of-the-tongue syndrome

ety: From Middle English syne, syn, sin, a contracted form of sithen (“since”). More at sithen.

s.def: Subsequently; then.
ex: At last he comes, and on his knee The wee tots a'thegether cling, An' ilk yen strives to catch his ee, Syne tugs his cwoat an' bids him sing.
Sic a pair o' friends aa nivvor seed either before or syne.

s.def: Late.
ex: [Each rogue] shall be discovered either soon or syne.
"I had rather it came to-morrow than a month hence. Come, I know, it will; and, as your country folks say, better soon than syne […]

s.def: Before now; ago.
Since.
ex: I've niver set fute i' Gibb's Ha' syne his father's death.
Shoo's […] gitten fair pratty, syne Maister Allen gat wed.

ety: Borrowed from Latin synecdochē, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).

s.def: A figure of speech that uses the name of a part of something to represent the whole, or the whole to represent a part, or a specific kind or instance to represent the general category, or the general category to represent a specific kind or instance, or the constituent material to represent the thi…
ex: Synecdoche the whole for part will take, Or part for whole, just for the metre's sake.
"Holocaust" can become a tired synecdoche for war crimes in general.

s.def: The use of this figure of speech.
Alternative spelling of synaeresis.

ety: From synergy + -etic.

s.def: Relating to synergetics.
Relating to synergy; synergistic.
synergy
The theological doctrine that salvation is brought about by a combination of human will and divine grace

s.def: Of or pertaining to synergy or synergism; synergic; co-operative, working together, interacting, mutually stimulating.
ex: Farber and Lasker struck up a synergistic partnership that would stretch over decades.

ety: From Ancient Greek συνεργία (sunergía, “cooperation”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, syn- + -ergy.

s.def: A synonym of binding energy.
The cooperation of two or more nerves, muscles, organs, etc.
ex: the digestive synergy

s.def: The combined action of two or more drugs where the effects are stronger than their mere sum.
Benefits resulting from combining different groups, people, objects or processes.
ex: Others argued that the notion of a targeted war on a particular disease inevitably distracted from natural synergies with other areas of research.

Descent from a common ancestor.
The theory that the germ formed by the union of spermatozoon and ovum contains the germs of all future generations.

s.def: The fusion of two syllables into one without the formation of a recognized diphthong, especially to fit a certain poetic meter.
A dense clumping of chromosomes on one side of the nucleus of a cell, sometimes occurring prior to cell division.
Occlusion of the pupil of the eye, resulting in loss of vision.

s.def: An ecclesiastic council or meeting to consult on church matters.

An administrative division of churches, either the entire denomination, as in the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, or a mid-level division (middle judicatory, district) as in the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America
An assembly or council having civil authority (formal); a legislative body.
ex: A third part of the Gods, in synod met / Their deities to assert; who, while they feel / Vigour divine within them, can allow / Omnipotence to none.

s.def: A conjunction of two or more of the heavenly bodies.

ety: From Middle English sinonyme, from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). By surface analysis, syn- + -onym.

s.def: A term (word or phrase) which is synonymous with others.
ex: Near-synonyms: near-synonym, parasynonym, plesionym
“Happy” is a synonym of “glad”.
The proportion of English words that have an exact synonym is small.

s.def: Any of the various names that could in theory be used for a taxon in accordance with the relevant rules.
An alternative (often shorter) name defined for an object in a database.
ex: Synonyms are part of the SQL standard and are used frequently by Oracle DBAs. Note that Oracle includes both private and public synonyms.

s.def: To make synonymous.
ex: […] if that properly belongs to the Saltatorii section, which Fabricius seems to believe by his synonyming it with his C. Viminalis […]

ety: From Medieval Latin synōnymus, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos). By surface analysis, synonym + -ous.

s.def: Having a similar (sometimes identical) meaning. (See Usage notes below)
ex: He was not far wrong, for nothing strikes me more forcibly than the universal tendency to grumble: conversation and complaint are synonymous terms.
For much of the time that incels have self-described as such, their collective worldview has been synonymous with the ‘blackpill’.

s.def: Of, or being a synonym.
Such that both its forms yield the same sequenced protein.

ety: From French synonymie and its etymon Late Latin synōnymia, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía), from συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “of like name”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, synonym + -y or syn- + -onymy. Doublet of synonymia.

s.def: A certain degree of similarity between the meaning(s) of several (synonymous) words or phrases. (See Usage notes below.)
A list or collection of synonyms, often compared and contrasted.
The use of synonyms to clarify or explain one's meaning.
The study of synonyms.
A system of synonyms.
The state of not being the name to be used, of being a synonym.
ex: sink into synonymy
In 1924 this name was reduced to synonymy.

s.def: A group or list of synonyms.
ex: The synonymy of Tachina is extensive.
Descriptions are followed by a synonymy of the names that have been applied in the literature .

ety: From Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning whole view.

s.def: A brief summary of the major points of a written work, either as prose or as a table; an abridgment or condensation of a work.
ex: The following Synopsis is intended as a monograph of those species of the order hitherto discovered…
In the following synopsis of the history of the United States the principal events are briefly mentioned…
A Synopsis, on the other hand, should be short enough and general enough so that a person who has not yet begun to study the language can follow it…

s.def: A reference work containing brief articles that taken together give an overview of an entire field.
A prayer book for use by the laity of the church.

ety: From New Latin syntacticus, from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós).

s.def: Of, related to or connected with syntax.
ex: The sentence “I saw he” contains a syntactic mistake.

s.def: Containing morphemes that are combined in the same order as they would be if they were separate words e.g. greenfinch

ety: Coined analogously with syntactic sugar.

s.def: A feature of a programming language intended to serve as a guardrail against writing code with an unintended meaning.

ety: Attributed to British computer scientist Peter Landin.

s.def: Additions to the syntax of a programming language that make code easier for humans to read or write, but that do not change the functionality or expressiveness of the language.

ety: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

s.def: A set of rules that govern how words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
The formal rules of formulating the statements of a computer language.
The study of the structure of phrases, sentences, and language.

ety: From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”), from συντίθημι (suntíthēmi, “put together, combine”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “set, place”). Doublet of sandhi.

s.def: The formation of something complex or coherent by combining simpler things.
Creation of a complex waveform by summation of simpler waveforms.
The reaction of elements or compounds to form more complex compounds.
A deduction from the general to the particular, by applying the rules of logic to a premise.
The combination of thesis and antithesis.
In intelligence usage, the examining and combining of processed information with other information and intelligence for final interpretation.
An apt arrangement of elements of a text, especially for euphony.
The uniting of ideas into a sentence.
The reunion of parts that have been divided.
An Ancient Roman dining-garment.
ex: The Saturnalia was apparently the only occasion, however, when the synthesis could be worn in public with decorum.

ety: From synthesis + -ize. First attested in 1830.

s.def: To combine two or more things to produce a new product.
ex: synthesize data
synthesize information
Her theory synthesizes ideas from several different disciplines.

s.def: To be combined producing a new, more complex product.
To produce a substance by chemical synthesis.
ex: The lab was able to synthesize a new compound.

s.def: To be produced by chemical synthesis.
To adjust two electronic circuits or devices to operate on the same frequency.

ety: From New Latin syphilis, originally the title of a poem, circa 1530, by Girolamo Fracastoro concerning “Syphilus”, a shepherd boy who insulted the Greek god Apollo and was punished by that god with a horrible disease. Syphilis in the Old World began circa 1495. More in Wikipedia at History of syphilis.

s.def: A disease spread via sexual activity, caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum.
ex: I saw a film the other day about syphilis. Ugh! It was too awful. I couldn't let a man touch me for a week. Is it true you can get it from kissing?

ety: Ultimately from Persian سِیرْدَرْیَا. Doublet of Sirdaryo.

s.def: A major river in Central Asia, running parallel to the Amu Darya.

ety: Borrowed from French Syracuse, from Latin Syrācūsae, from Ancient Greek Συρᾱ́κουσαι (Surā́kousai) attested from 8th century BC, from a Pre-Greek name, possibly Phoenician 𐤔𐤄𐤓𐤀𐤇 (šhrʾḥ, “to feel ill”) in reference to the ancient port's proximity to a swamp. With modified form of suffix -εις (-eis). As a surname, an anglicized form of Italian Siracusa. Doublet of Siragusa. Compare Sicilian Saragusa.

s.def: A placename:
A habitational surname from Italian.

ety: From Middle English Sirie, from Latin Sȳria, from Ancient Greek Σῠρῐ́ᾱ (Sŭrĭ́ā), apheretic form of Ἀσσυρία (Assuría, “Assyria”), from Akkadian 𒀾𒋗𒊏𒅀 (Aššūrāyu), from 𒀸𒋩 (Aššur, “Assur”). The land corresponding to modern Syria was originally called Aram by its ancient inhabitants, the Arameans. After the Assyrian conquest of Aram, the Greeks applied the name Syria to this territory. Over time, Syria came to denote the broader Levant, while Assyria referred to Mesopotamia. Herodotus (5th cen…

s.def: A country in West Asia in the Middle East. Official name: Syrian Arab Republic. Capital: Damascus.

A historical region of West Asia, extending from modern-day southeast Turkey to the north, the Euphrates and Arabian Desert to the east, the Sinai Peninsula to the south, and the Mediterranean sea to the west.
An ancient Roman province between 64 BCE and 198 CE.
A cultural region of Western Asia consisting of the eastern Mediterranean countries, i.e. Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan and Cyprus; the Levant.

ety: From Latin Syriacus (“Syrian”), from Ancient Greek Συριακός (Suriakós, “Syrian”, adjective), from Συρία (Suría) [the Greek name for Aram, and probably based on the name Ἀσσυρία (Assuría, “Assyria”)] + -ακός (-akós).

ex: In contrast to the political dynamics of the preunion period, these struggles were heavily influenced by the new prominence of Syrian capitalists[…]

s.def: Of or relating to the Syriac language or alphabet.
ex: But how about the words which Christ used from the common speech of the people? These are simply written in Syrian letters, and need no translation.

s.def: Of, from, or pertaining to Assyria or the Assyrian people.
A person from Syria or of Syrian descent.
A person from Assyria or of Assyrian descent.

s.def: Official name of Syria: a country in West Asia, in the Middle East.

ety: From Dutch or Middle Low German from Latin sȳrinx from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pan pipes”).

s.def: Sweet mock orange (Philadelphus coronarius).
Any of the several flowering plants of the genus Philadelphus, such as now in the Western United States Philadelphus lewisii.
Any of the several flowering plants, of the genus Syringa, such as the lilacs.

ety: From Middle French syringe (“syringe”), from Latin sȳringem, accusative of sȳrinx (“reed, panpipe”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”). Doublet of syrinx.

s.def: A device used for injecting or drawing fluids through a membrane.
A device consisting of a hypodermic needle, a chamber for containing liquids, and a piston for applying pressure (to inject) or reducing pressure (to draw); a hypodermic syringe.
ex: an ear syringe

s.def: To clean or rinse by means of a syringe.
ex: Have your ears syringed! They're so dirty!

s.def: To inject by means of a syringe.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sȳrinx (“reed; reed pipe, panpipes”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “panpipes; pipe-shaped object”), from Pre-Greek. Doublet of syringe. The plural form syringes is a learned borrowing from Latin sȳringes.

s.def: A set of panpipes.
ex: Inside, somebody was playing a duet on syrinx and lyre. Lew thought he knew the tune, but then it went off in some direction he couldn't follow.

s.def: Chiefly in the plural: a narrow channel cut in rock, especially in Ancient Egyptian burial chambers.
Any of several abnormal tube-shaped structures in the body, especially a rare, fluid-filled neuroglial cavity in the brain stem or within the spinal cord.
The voice organ in birds, located at or near where the trachea and the bronchi join.

ety: From Middle English sirup, from Old French sirop, from Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Doublet of sirop. Related to sorbet, sherbet, sharbat. Compare French sirop, Italian siroppo, sciroppo, Spanish jarabe, jarope, Portuguese xarope, and Dutch siroop and stroop. The first known use of the spelling sirup was in the 14th century.

s.def: Any thick liquid that has a high sugar content and which is added to or poured over food as a flavoring.

peaches in syrup

s.def: Any viscous liquid.
Anything overly sweet or sentimental.
A wig.
To convert or process into syrup.
To add syrup to.
To sabotage (a vehicle) by pouring syrup into the gas tank.
The junction of bones by intervening muscles.

ety: From Latin systalticus (“drawing together”), from Ancient Greek συσταλτικός (sustaltikós), from συστέλλω (sustéllō). Compare systole.

s.def: Capable of, or taking place by, alternate contraction and dilatation.
ex: the systaltic action of the heart

s.def: In Ancient Greek music: having a depressing influence.

ex: Followers should have a system to follow that works in their interests, not against them.

s.def: The conceptual model that defines the behavior, structure, and more views of a system.

s.def: Embedded within and spread throughout and affecting a whole system, group, body, economy, market, or society.
Pertaining to an entire organism.
The part of blood circulation which carries oxygenated blood away from the heart, to the body, and returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart.
A systemic autoimmune disease (or autoimmune connective tissue disease), where the immune system attacks the body's cells and tissue and causes inflammation and tissue damage.

s.def: The rhythmic contraction of the heart, by which blood is driven through the arteries.
A shortening of a naturally long vowel.
The shortest noncontractible loop on a compact metric space.
The contraction of the contractile vesicles in certain algae, plasmodia, and zoospores.
A municipality, the capital of Şırnak district and Şırnak Province, Turkey.
A province in southeastern Turkey, with a Kurdish majority.
A district of Şırnak Province, Turkey.
